divergences.note: The chapter ends on a balanced antithesis Machiavelli weighs like a ledger: 'una infamia sanza odio' against 'una infamia con odio.' Both courses cost the prince his good name — 'infamia' either way — so the choice is decided by the one thing that can actually unseat him: hatred. Meanness earns contempt but no hatred; the rapacity bred by failed generosity earns both. We keep the parallel flat and unsoftened, because the whole grim economy of the chapter resolves into this single weighing: a prince can survive being thought a miser, but not being hated, and so he should choose the reproach that comes without the hatred.

divergences.phrase: è molto più sicuro essere temuto che amato, quando si abbia a mancare dell'uno de' dua
divergences.older: it is much safer to be feared than loved, when, of the two, either must be dispensed with (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: it is much safer to be feared than loved, if one of the two must be given up
divergences.note: The most quoted line in the book, and we hold it flat to the Italian, refusing every temptation to soften it. Machiavelli does not say a prince should prefer fear, but that fear is the safer of two goods a prince would ideally hold together — 'si abbia a mancare dell'uno de' dua,' if one of the two must be lacked. The whole cold calculus that follows depends on this conditional: love is a bond men cut whenever it pays ('rotto da ogni occasione di utilità propria'), while fear is held by 'timore di pena che non ti abbandona mai,' a dread of punishment that never deserts you. We keep 'feared than loved' bare and unhedged, since the chapter's force is precisely that it weighs affection as an instrument and finds it the weaker tool.

divergences.phrase: gli uomini sdimenticano più presto la morte del padre che la perdita del patrimonio
divergences.older: men more quickly forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: men sooner forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony
divergences.note: The chapter's bleakest aphorism, and we render it word for word with the tradition, since any softening would be a betrayal of its point. The verb 'sdimenticano' is flatly 'forget'; the shock is in the comparison Machiavelli draws without flinching — a man will get over his father's killing faster than over being robbed of his inheritance. We keep 'patrimony' rather than the looser 'property' here (though we use 'property' for 'roba' just above), because 'patrimonio' is specifically the estate handed down, the thing a man means to pass on, and the line cuts deepest when that exact sense is preserved. It is the cold ground of the whole counsel to be feared without being hated: shed blood if you must, with cause, but never touch what men own.

divergences.phrase: la sua inumana crudeltà
divergences.older: his inhuman cruelty (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: his inhuman cruelty
divergences.note: Machiavelli's example of cruelty put to perfect use, and we keep the blunt word he wrote — 'inumana crudeltà,' inhuman cruelty — without laundering it into 'severity' or 'sternness,' as is the temptation throughout this chapter. The point is deliberately scandalous: it was precisely this cruelty, joined to his 'virtù infinita' (rendered here as boundless prowess, per this edition's settled handling of virtù), that held a vast army of mixed races together through every reverse, where Scipio's praised leniency bred mutiny. We render 'virtù' as prowess, not 'valour' or 'virtue,' so the argument stands clear: cruelty is not the opposite of a commander's excellence but, well used, an indispensable part of it — and the 'short-sighted writers' who admire Hannibal's results while condemning their cause have simply failed to follow the logic.

divergences.phrase: la golpe e il lione
divergences.older: the fox and the lion (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: the fox and the lion
divergences.note: The most famous image in the book, and we hold it word for word with the tradition. The Italian is 'debbe di quelle pigliare la golpe e il lione; perché il lione non si difende da' lacci, la golpe non si difende da' lupi.' The lesson is built on a precise crossing: each beast is helpless against exactly what the other masters — the lion's strength is blind to the trap ('lacci,' snares), the fox's cunning is defenseless against the wolf's force. So the prince needs both, 'fox to recognize the traps, lion to frighten off the wolves.' We keep the bare animal nouns and the chiasmus intact, since the whole argument that force and craft are inseparable rests on it; softening either beast into a mere metaphor of 'courage' or 'wit' collapses the figure.

divergences.locus: paragraph 7 (the closing maxim, the most misquoted line in Machiavelli)
divergences.phrase: si guarda al fine
divergences.older: one judges by the result (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: one judges by the result
divergences.note: This is the line the world has turned into 'the end justifies the means' — a sentence Machiavelli never wrote. The Italian is 'nelle azioni di tutti gli uomini, e massime de' principi, dove non è iudizio a chi reclamare, si guarda al fine.' 'Si guarda al fine' is flatly 'one looks to the end / the outcome.' Machiavelli is not laying down a moral license that good ends purify foul means; he is making a cold observation about how men actually judge — with no higher court to appeal to ('non è iudizio a chi reclamare'), a prince is assessed only by how things came out. We keep Marriott's exact 'one judges by the result,' and refuse the popular gloss, because the famous distortion inverts a description of human judgment into a principle of moral accounting Machiavelli did not assert.

divergences.phrase: parere ... religioso
divergences.older: to appear ... religious (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: to seem ... devout / religious
divergences.note: Of the five qualities a prince must counterfeit, Machiavelli singles out religion as the one it is most necessary to seem to have — 'non è cosa più necessaria a parere di avere, che questa ultima qualità.' The shock is deliberate: the appearance of piety is named the most useful of all the masks, and the chapter's veiled target (Ferdinand of Aragon, who 'preaches nothing but peace and good faith' while making war on both) is the living proof. We keep the bare verb 'seem' running through the whole passage — seem merciful, seem faithful, seem devout — never letting it slide toward 'be,' since Machiavelli's separation of seeming from being is the engine of the chapter, and religion is where he drives it home hardest.

divergences.phrase: uno de' più potenti remedii ... è non essere odiato dallo universale
divergences.older: one of the most efficacious remedies that a prince can have against conspiracies is not to be hated and despised by the people (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: One of the most effective safeguards a prince can have against conspiracies is simply not to be hated by the people at large
divergences.note: This is the chapter's structural heart, and it is easily confused with the more famous maxim 'the best fortress is not to be hated by the people' — but that line belongs to Chapter XX, not here. In Chapter XIX the Italian is 'uno de' più potenti remedii che abbia uno principe contro alle congiure, è non essere odiato dallo universale.' 'Lo universale' is the whole body of the people, the public at large, set against the handful of conspirators. The logic is cold and exact: a plotter banks on pleasing the people by killing the prince; make the people love the prince, and the plotter is left with no reward and every risk. We keep 'the people at large' for 'lo universale' to mark that it is the mass, not a faction, whose goodwill disarms the conspiracy.

divergences.phrase: vario, leggieri, effeminato, pusillanime, irresoluto
divergences.older: fickle, frivolous, effeminate, mean-spirited, irresolute (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: fickle, frivolous, soft, cowardly, or irresolute
divergences.note: Machiavelli's five vices of contempt are flung down in a flat hammering line — 'vario, leggieri, effeminato, pusillanime, irresoluto' — each the negation of a quality he demands two clauses later (greatness, courage, gravity, strength). 'Effeminato' we render 'soft' rather than the literal 'effeminate,' and 'pusillanime' as 'cowardly': the point is not effeminacy as such but the want of nerve and weight that makes a ruler beneath notice. We keep the bare asyndeton so the list lands as five blows, since the whole argument of the chapter — hated for what you do, despised for what you are — turns on holding these against the virtues of greatness and strength that answer them.

divergences.locus: paragraph 16 (Severus, the fox and the lion)
divergences.phrase: seppe bene usare la persona del golpe e del lione ... uno ferocissimo lione et una astutissima golpe
divergences.older: he knew well how to counterfeit the fox and the lion ... a most valiant lion and a most cunning fox (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: he knew how to play the part of the fox and the lion ... a most ferocious lion and a most cunning fox
divergences.note: The fox-and-lion image was set out in Chapter XVIII; here Severus is its proof — the new prince who held power by being both at once. The Italian is 'seppe bene usare la persona del golpe e del lione' — literally to use the 'persona,' the role or mask, of each. Marriott's 'counterfeit' tips it toward mere fakery; we keep 'play the part,' which holds both the performance and the genuine doubleness Machiavelli means. The closing verdict, 'lo troverrà uno ferocissimo lione et una astutissima golpe,' we render 'a most ferocious lion and a most cunning fox,' keeping the superlatives and the order; Marriott's 'valiant' softens 'ferocissimo,' which is sheer ferocity, not valor. This is the model the chapter finally holds up — Severus' prowess, not Marcus' virtue, is what a new prince must learn.

divergences.phrase: armandoli, quelle arme diventono tue ... di sudditi si fanno tua partigiani
divergences.older: by arming them, those arms become yours ... and your subjects become your adherents (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: by arming them, those arms become yours ... and your subjects become your partisans
divergences.note: The cold mechanism at the heart of the chapter, and we hold it flat to the Italian: 'armandoli, quelle arme diventono tue, diventono fedeli quelli che ti sono sospetti, e quelli che erano fedeli si mantengono, e di sudditi si fanno tua partigiani.' The logic is one of ownership, not gratitude — the weapon you put in a man's hand is now yours, because he wields it for you, so arming the doubtful converts them. We keep 'partisans' for 'partigiani' rather than the paler 'adherents,' since Machiavelli means men actively committed to your side, not mere followers. The point is counter-intuitive and must not be softened: a new prince makes himself safer by handing out arms, never by confiscating them.

divergences.phrase: la migliore fortezza che sia, è non essere odiato dal populo
divergences.older: the best possible fortress is — not to be hated by the people (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: the best fortress there is, is not to be hated by the people
divergences.note: The hammer-blow the whole chapter is built to deliver, and we keep it bare and word-for-word with the tradition. The Italian is 'la migliore fortezza che sia, è non essere odiato dal populo; perché, ancora che tu abbi le fortezze, et il populo ti abbi in odio, le non ti salvono.' Machiavelli's stone-and-mortar word 'fortezza' is turned against itself: the only wall that holds is the people's goodwill, and no actual fortress will save a hated prince, because 'foreigners are never lacking to come to the aid' of a people in arms. We render 'odiato' as the blunt 'hated,' never softening it to 'disliked' or 'resented,' since the negative form is the argument — Machiavelli does not promise that being loved is a fortress, only that being hated dissolves every other one.

divergences.phrase: la contessa di Furlì ... non essere odiata dal populo che avere le fortezze
divergences.older: the Countess of Forli ... it would have been safer for her, both then and before, not to have been hated by the people than to have had the fortresses (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: the Countess of Forlì ... both then and earlier it would have been safer for her not to have been hated by the people than to have had her fortresses
divergences.note: The single test case Machiavelli allows, and he turns it against fortresses even so. Caterina Sforza's castle at Forlì did save her once, after her husband Count Girolamo Riario was murdered — but only because circumstances barred any foreigner from backing the rising. When Cesare Borgia came and the people sided with him, the same fortress was worthless. We keep the proper nouns and the historical exactness intact (Girolamo killed, help awaited from Milan, then Borgia's attack), because the example is the proof: the one time a fortress worked, it worked by luck of circumstance, and the moment the people's hatred and a foreign army combined, the walls counted for nothing. The verdict 'safer not to have been hated than to have had the fortresses' must land flat, with no consolation added to the stones.

divergences.phrase: vero amico, o vero nimico
divergences.older: a true friend or a downright enemy (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: a true friend or a downright enemy
divergences.note: The cold heart of the chapter, and we hold it word for word with the tradition. The Italian is 'È ancora stimato uno principe quando elli è vero amico o vero inimico, cioè quando sanza alcuno respetto si scuopre in favore di alcuno contro a un altro.' Machiavelli's whole counsel here cuts against the prudent instinct to keep your options open: a prince earns esteem precisely by refusing to hedge — by 'discovering' himself, declaring openly and without reservation. We keep 'downright enemy' (rather than a flatter 'real enemy') because the doubled bluntness of 'vero ... vero' is the point: it is the open, unmistakable commitment, friend or foe, that wins respect, and the man who will not choose wins only contempt.

divergences.phrase: li principi mal risoluti ... il più delle volte rovinano
divergences.older: irresolute princes, to avoid present dangers, generally follow the neutral path, and are generally ruined (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: irresolute princes, to escape the dangers of the moment, usually take the neutral road, and usually come to ruin
divergences.note: Machiavelli's verdict on neutrality, and we keep its grim symmetry. The Italian is 'E li principi mal risoluti, per fuggire e' presenti periculi, seguono il più delle volte quella via neutrale, e il più delle volte rovinano.' The repeated 'il più delle volte' (most of the time) is the sting: neutrality is the coward's road, taken to dodge today's risk, and most of the time it does not save him — it destroys him. Neutrality earns the hatred of the victor (whose prey you become) and the contempt of the loser (who will not shelter you); to sit out a war between your neighbors is to be left, in the Roman legate's words, 'the prize of whoever wins.' Nothing is softened: irresolution is named for the ruin it brings.

divergences.phrase: tenendo occupati li animi di quelli baroni ... non pensando a innovare
divergences.older: he held the minds of the barons of Castile occupied in thinking of the war and not anticipating any innovations (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: he kept the minds of the barons of Castile so absorbed in the war that they never saw what was being prepared
divergences.note: The mechanism beneath Ferdinand's 'great enterprises,' and the chapter's quiet lesson in misdirection. The Italian is 'tenne occupati li animi di quelli baroni di Castiglia, li quali, pensando a quella guerra, non pensavano a innovare.' The great campaign is not only glory — it is a screen: while the barons' minds are fixed on Granada, Ferdinand is quietly building 'reputazione e imperio sopra di loro,' reputation and authority over them, without their noticing. We render 'non pensavano a innovare' as 'never saw what was being prepared' rather than the stiff 'not anticipating any innovations,' to keep the cold point that grand undertakings serve to occupy and distract a prince's own people while he tightens his grip on them.

divergences.phrase: l'uno intende da sé, l'altro discerne quello che altri intende, e il terzo non intende né sé né gli altri
divergences.older: one which comprehends by itself; another which appreciates what others comprehended; and a third which neither comprehends by itself nor by the showing of others (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: one that understands things for itself; one that grasps what another has understood; and one that understands neither for itself nor through anyone else
divergences.note: The chapter's most famous passage, and the rhythm is the argument: three minds set out in flat parallel and then graded — 'quel primo è eccellentissimo, el secondo eccellente, el terzo inutile.' The crux is the middle term, 'discerne quello che altri intende': not merely 'appreciates,' which softens it, but discerns or grasps what someone else has worked out. Machiavelli's point is precise and unflattering to Pandolfo — the second-best ruler cannot originate, but he can recognize a good idea when his minister brings it. We keep the three clauses bare and balanced and hold the single verb 'understand' across all three (intende), so the descending scale lands cleanly: understands for himself, understands what another understood, understands nothing at all.

divergences.phrase: quando tu vedi el ministro pensare più a sé che a te, e che in tutte le azioni vi ricerca dentro l'utile suo
divergences.older: when you see the servant thinking more of his own interests than of yours, and seeking inwardly his own profit in everything (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: When you see the minister thinking more of himself than of you, and seeking his own profit in everything he handles
divergences.note: Marriott renders 'ministro' as 'servant' throughout, but Machiavelli's 'ministro' is the high officer who runs the prince's affairs — the secretary or chief counselor, not a household servant. We use 'minister' to keep the rank exact, since the whole chapter is about the men closest to power. The test itself is kept blunt and unsoftened: the disqualifying sign is the man who 'pensa più a sé che a te' and hunts his own 'utile' (profit, advantage) in every action. Machiavelli draws no moral line here, only a structural one — a man who keeps any part of his attention for himself cannot be wholly the prince's, and so cannot be trusted with the prince's state.

divergences.phrase: onorandolo, faccendolo ricco, obligandoselo, partecipandogli li onori e carichi
divergences.older: honouring him, enriching him, doing him kindnesses, sharing with him the honours and cares (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: to honor him, make him rich, put him in his debt, share with him both honors and burdens
divergences.note: The prince's method for binding a good minister is a cold piece of engineering, not generosity, and we keep it so. 'Obligandoselo' is not vaguely 'doing him kindnesses' but putting him under obligation — making him owe — so the bond runs the prince's way. 'Carichi' we render 'burdens' rather than Marriott's softer 'cares': the prince shares the weight of office, not merely worries. The aim, stated plainly in what follows, is that the minister be so loaded with honors, riches, and office that he can want no more and so has nothing to gain by turning — he 'cannot stand without the prince.' The whole calculus is one of dependence deliberately manufactured, and nothing in it should read as warmth.

divergences.phrase: dipoi deliberare da sé a suo modo
divergences.older: and afterwards form his own conclusions (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: and afterwards decide for himself, in his own way
divergences.note: The hinge of the whole method. After questioning his wise men widely, the prince must 'deliberare da sé a suo modo' — deliberate by himself, in his own fashion. Marriott's 'form his own conclusions' catches the sense but loses the two stressed words: 'da sé' (alone, by himself) and 'a suo modo' (his own way, on his own terms). We keep both, because the chapter's argument turns on them — counsel is gathered from many, but the decision is the prince's alone, and the discipline of deciding alone is exactly what saves him from being pulled apart by his advisers, as Maximilian is.

divergences.phrase: come ognuno ti può dire el vero, ti manca la reverenzia
divergences.older: but when every one may tell you the truth, respect for you abates (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: But once everyone may speak the truth to you, your reverence dwindles
divergences.note: The cold paradox the chapter is built on. The only guard against flatterers is to show that truth-telling does not offend you; but if you throw that door open to everyone, 'ti manca la reverenzia' — you lose your reverence, the awe that holds men in check. Marriott's 'respect abates' is accurate but flat; we keep the stronger 'reverenzia' as 'reverence,' since Machiavelli's point is not mere esteem but the distance that makes a prince obeyed. The third course — a few licensed truth-tellers, no more — is his exit from the trap, and the trap only bites if 'reverence' carries its full weight.

divergences.phrase: li buoni consigli, da qualunque venghino, conviene naschino dalla prudenza del principe, e non la prudenza del principe da' buoni consigli
divergences.older: good counsels, whencesoever they come, are born of the wisdom of the prince, and not the wisdom of the prince from good counsels (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: good counsel, wherever it comes from, must be born of the prince's own wisdom, and not the prince's wisdom of good counsel
divergences.note: The chapter's hammer-blow, and we hold it tight to the Italian's chiasmus. Machiavelli reverses the comfortable assumption that a clever council can prop up a dull prince: the causation runs the other way. 'Conviene naschino dalla prudenza del principe' — good counsel must be BORN of the prince's own prudence; it is his judgment that makes counsel good, sifts it, and reconciles it, not the counsel that makes him wise. We keep 'prudenza' as 'wisdom' (the settled rendering here) and preserve the exact mirrored clauses, since the whole chapter exists to drive this reversal home: nothing is softened, nothing added — a prince who is not wise himself cannot be saved by good advice.

divergences.phrase: non accusino la fortuna, ma la ignavia loro
divergences.older: do not let our princes accuse fortune for the loss of their principalities ... but rather their own sloth (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: let our princes ... not blame fortune but their own sloth
divergences.note: This is the cold hinge of the chapter, and it must land bare. The Italian is 'non accusino la fortuna, ma la ignavia loro' — let them blame not fortune but their own 'ignavia,' indolence, slackness, the failure to act. Per this edition's settled rendering, fortuna stays 'fortune' (never softened to 'bad luck' as an excuse), since the whole point is that the princes reach for fortune precisely as an excuse, and Machiavelli yanks it away: the fault was never chance but their own sloth. We keep 'sloth' over 'indolence' for its blunt force and hold the antithesis flat, fortune against sloth, so the accusation cannot be dodged.

divergences.phrase: è comune difetto delli uomini, nelle bonacce, non pensare alle tempeste
divergences.older: it is a common defect in man not to make any provision in the calm against the tempest (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: it is the common failing of men not to reckon on the storm while the weather is fair
divergences.note: Machiavelli reaches for a sailor's image: 'nelle bonacce, non pensare alle tempeste' — in the dead calm ('bonaccia'), to give no thought to the storms. Marriott's 'provision in the calm against the tempest' keeps the sense but stiffens it. We render it 'reckon on the storm while the weather is fair' to keep the weather metaphor alive and the rebuke plain — the failing is not bad luck but a refusal of foresight, the same fault Machiavelli faults the Romans for not having in Chapter III. Nothing is added; the storm is already in the Italian.

divergences.phrase: quelle difese solamente sono buone, sono certe, sono durabili, che dependono da te proprio e dalla virtù tua
divergences.older: those only are reliable, certain, and durable that depend on yourself and your valour (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: the only defenses that are sound, sure, and lasting are those that depend on yourself and your own prowess
divergences.note: The chapter's final verdict and the whole book in miniature. The Italian rings three flat adjectives — 'buone ... certe ... durabili' — and turns on 'da te proprio e dalla virtù tua': on yourself and your own virtù. Per this edition's settled rendering, virtù is 'prowess' here, not Marriott's 'valour' (too narrowly martial) and never moral 'virtue,' since the argument is that only the force and skill you command yourself can be relied on. We hold the triad bare and end on 'your own prowess,' so the cold rule lands: borrowed defenses fail, only your own hold.

divergences.phrase: fiume rovinoso ... ripari e argini
divergences.older: one of those raging rivers ... defences and barriers (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: one of those raging rivers ... banks and dykes
divergences.note: The chapter's governing image, and we hold it close to the Italian: fortune is a 'fiume rovinoso' that floods in flood-time and can be controlled only by works thrown up in calm weather. Machiavelli's 'ripari e argini' are flood-control works — embankments, dykes, the channeling of a river — and we render them 'banks and dykes' rather than Marriott's vaguer 'defences and barriers,' because the metaphor must stay hydraulic for the lesson to land: fortune is not resisted by walls in the abstract but by foresight built up in quiet times. The whole point is that the works are raised before the flood, never during it — fortune ruins only where 'no skill has been prepared to resist her.' Note too that 'virtù' here ('dove non è ordinata virtù a resisterle') is rendered 'skill,' this edition's settled term, never moral 'virtue': it is the prepared, prudent capacity to build the banks in advance.

divergences.phrase: la Fortuna è donna ... batterla ed urtarla
divergences.older: fortune is a woman, and if you wish to keep her under it is necessary to beat and ill-use her (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: fortune is a woman, and if you mean to keep her under you must beat her and knock her about
divergences.note: The most notorious line in the book, and we render it faithfully, not euphemized. The Italian is 'la Fortuna è donna; ed è necessario, volendola tener sotto, batterla ed urtarla' — to beat her and knock her about, strike and shove her. Machiavelli's image is unmistakably one of force used on a woman, and the misogyny is not incidental but the very mechanism of the metaphor: fortune yields to mastery, and the bold young man 'commands' her where the cautious one is rebuffed. We keep the violence of 'batterla ed urtarla' intact ('beat her and knock her about'), since softening it would falsify both the line and the cold, brutal logic Machiavelli draws from it — that fortune favors the aggressor. A modern reader should see the image for exactly what it is: a fifteenth-century equation of mastering chance with mastering a woman by force, repugnant in its terms and inseparable from the argument it carries.

divergences.phrase: rispettivo / impetuoso ... col tempo / col modo del procedere
divergences.older: cautious / impetuous; conform ... to the spirit of the times (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: cautious / bold (headlong); match one's way of acting to the temper of the times
divergences.note: The chapter's analytic core, where the river image is cashed out as practical doctrine. Machiavelli's claim is not that boldness always wins but that success depends on the fit between a man's fixed nature and the shifting 'qualità de' tempi' — the temper of the times. We render 'rispettivo' as 'cautious' and 'impetuoso' as 'bold' or 'headlong' (used of Julius II), keeping the pairing sharp because the whole argument is a study in mismatch: the cautious man is ruined precisely when the times call for boldness, and cannot change because 'he cannot break from the bent his nature gives him.' Marriott's 'spirit of the times' is a touch lofty; we keep the plainer 'temper of the times' so the doctrine reads as the cold, almost mechanical calculus it is — fortune is half-mastered not by courage as such but by the rare man whose nature happens to suit the hour, or rarer still, who can bend his nature to it.

divergences.phrase: sanza capo, sanza ordine, battuta, spogliata, lacera, corsa
divergences.older: without head, without order, beaten, despoiled, torn, overrun (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: without a head, without order, beaten, despoiled, torn, overrun
divergences.note: The emotional pivot of the whole chapter, and we hold it almost word for word with the tradition, because its force is in the bare hammering list. The Italian piles six blows in a single breath — 'sanza capo, sanza ordine, battuta, spogliata, lacera, corsa' — Italy stripped of leadership, of order, then physically beaten, plundered, ripped, and trampled by armies passing through ('corsa,' overrun, raided across). Machiavelli first builds the Moses/Cyrus/Theseus parallel, where captivity was the necessary condition that revealed a redeemer's skill (virtù), then drops Italy into that mold: her degradation is the dark soil from which an Italian deliverer must spring. We keep every term flat and unsoftened so the list lands like the indictment it is.

divergences.phrase: rimasta sanza vita, espetta qual possa essere quello che sani le sue ferite
divergences.older: Italy, left as without life, waits for him who shall yet heal her wounds (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: Italy, left as if without life, waits for the one who will heal her wounds
divergences.note: Here the Moses image turns messianic. 'One man' who lately showed 'qualche spiraculo' — some spark, some glimmer — and seemed 'ordinato da Dio per sua redenzione' is Cesare Borgia, whom fortune cast off 'nel più alto corso delle azioni sue,' at the very height of his career. So Italy lies 'as if without life,' a body waiting for the one who will heal her — the redeemer language ('redenzione,' 'redentore') is deliberate and biblical, and we keep it, since the whole exhortation casts the new prince as a savior answering a nation's prayer. We render 'sani le sue ferite' as 'heal her wounds' and keep the run of concrete griefs (the ravaging of Lombardy, the bleeding and taxing of the Kingdom and Tuscany, the festering sores) so the sacred image stays grounded in real, bodily suffering.

divergences.phrase: Dio non vuole fare ogni cosa, per non ci tòrre el libero arbitrio e parte di quella gloria che tocca a noi
divergences.older: God is not willing to do everything, and thus take away our free will and that share of glory which belongs to us (Marriott 1908)
divergences.lectio: God will not do everything, for He will not take from us our free will and the share of the glory that is ours
divergences.note: The theological heart of the exhortation, and we hold it close to the Italian. Machiavelli has just rolled out the miracles of the Exodus — the sea parted, the cloud, water from the rock, manna — as signs that God has already prepared Italy's way; then, at the brink of pure providentialism, he pulls the burden back onto the man: 'el resto dovete fare voi' (the rest you must do yourselves). The reason is the famous one: God leaves part undone on purpose, so as not to rob us of 'el libero arbitrio' (free will) and of the 'gloria' that is our portion. This is the exact hinge between fortuna and virtù that the book turns on — grace supplies the opening, but the glory must be won. We keep 'free will' and 'glory' bare and the causal 'for He will not take from us' tight, so the line reads as the goad to action it is, not a pious aside.

divergences.phrase: Virtù contro al Furore / Prenderà l'arme; e fia 'l combatter corto: / Ché l'antico valore / Ne gli italici cor non è ancor morto
divergences.older: Virtue against fury shall advance the fight, / And it i' th' combat soon shall put to flight: / For the old Roman valour is not dead, / Nor in th' Italians' brests extinguished (Edward Dacre, 1640)
divergences.lectio: Valor against fury / shall take up arms; and the fight shall be short; / for the ancient courage / in Italian hearts is not yet dead.
divergences.note: Machiavelli ends the book not on his own words but on four lines of Petrarch (from the canzone 'Italia mia'), and the borrowed close is the point: the old poet's faith that Italy can still rise is offered as prophecy fulfilled by the new prince. We render the Italian plainly rather than lean on Dacre's 1640 couplets, which inflate 'l'antico valore' into 'the old Roman valour' — Petrarch wrote only 'the ancient courage,' with no 'Roman,' so we keep it. 'Virtù' here we render 'valor' rather than this edition's usual 'skill,' since in Petrarch's line it is plainly martial courage set against blind 'furore' (fury, the foreign rage); and 'fia 'l combatter corto' is kept as the confident 'the fight shall be short.' The original Italian is preserved here for the reader who wants the poet's own music: 'Virtù contro al Furore / Prenderà l'arme; e fia 'l combatter corto: / Ché l'antico valore / Ne gli italici cor non è ancor morto.'

sections.label: Chapter I
sections.title: The Kinds of Principalities
How Many Kinds of Principalities There Are, and By What Means They Are Acquired

segments.text: All states, all dominions that have held and hold power over men, have been and are either republics or principalities.

Every state, every power that has ever held sway over men, has been and is either a republic or a principality. Principalities are either hereditary, where the ruling family has held power for generations, or they are new.
Principalities are either hereditary, where one bloodline has ruled for a long time, or they are new.

The new ones are either new outright, as Milan was to Francesco Sforza, or they are like limbs grafted onto the hereditary state of the prince who acquires them, as the kingdom of Naples is to the King of Spain.

Dominions acquired this way are accustomed either to living under a prince or to being free; and they are acquired either with the arms of others or with one's own, either by fortune or by virtù — a man's own skill and nerve.

New principalities are either wholly new, as Milan was to Francesco Sforza, or they are limbs grafted onto the hereditary state of the prince who acquires them, as the kingdom of Naples was to the King of Spain. Dominions taken this way are either used to living under a prince or used to being free; and they are won either by the prince's own arms or by the arms of others, by luck or by skill.

sections.label: Chapter II
sections.title: Hereditary Principalities
Concerning Hereditary Principalities

segments.text: I will leave republics aside, since I have discussed them at length elsewhere. I will turn only to principalities, taking up the threads laid out above, and ask how these principalities can be governed and kept.

I will set aside any discussion of republics, since I have written about them at length elsewhere, and address myself to principalities alone. Keeping to the order I laid out above, I will examine how such principalities are to be governed and held.

I say at once that hereditary states, accustomed to the bloodline of their prince, are far less difficult to hold than new ones. It is enough not to break the customs of one's ancestors, and to play for time when events turn; then a prince of ordinary industry will always keep his state, unless some extraordinary and overwhelming force strips him of it — and even stripped of it, he wins it back the moment the usurper stumbles.

I say at once that hereditary states, long accustomed to the line of their prince, are far less troublesome to hold than new ones. It is enough for the prince not to break with the customs of his ancestors, and to bend with circumstances as they arise; a man of merely ordinary ability can keep his footing, unless some extraordinary and overwhelming force strips him of it. And even if he is stripped of it, the moment any setback befalls the one who seized his place, he wins it back.

Italy gives us an example in the Duke of Ferrara, who held out against the assaults of the Venetians in '84, and of Pope Julius in '10, for no other reason than that his house was old in that dominion. For the hereditary prince has fewer reasons to give offense, and less need to; hence he is more loved; and unless outrageous vices make him hated, it stands to reason that his own people are naturally well disposed toward him. In the age and continuity of his rule, the memories of innovation and the causes of it are extinguished — for one change always leaves jutting brickwork for the next to build on.

Take, for example, the Duke of Ferrara here in Italy. He could not have withstood the assault of the Venetians in '84, nor that of Pope Julius in 1510, had he not been long settled in his domains. For the hereditary prince has less reason and less need to give offense, and so he is the more loved; and unless monstrous vices make him hated, it stands to reason that his subjects will be naturally well disposed toward him. In the long age and continuity of his rule, the memories and motives that drive men to change are extinguished — for one upheaval always leaves behind the toothing on which the next is built.

sections.label: Chapter III
sections.title: Mixed Principalities
Concerning Mixed Principalities

segments.text: But in the new principality the difficulties begin. First, if it is not new through and through but a limb joined to a larger state (call the whole thing, taken together, a mixed principality), its instability springs first of all from a natural difficulty found in every new principality: men change masters willingly, believing they will be better off, and that belief puts arms in their hands against the man who rules them. In this they are deceived, for experience soon teaches them that they are worse off. And that follows from another necessity, natural and ordinary: a new prince is always forced to injure the very people he acquires, both with his soldiers and with the countless other abuses a new conquest drags behind it.

The real difficulties begin with a new principality. Take first the case of one that is not entirely new but joined onto a state the ruler already holds, so that the two together make up what we might call a mixed principality. Here the trouble comes from a flaw built into every new acquisition: men are willing to change rulers because they believe the change will improve their lot, and that belief moves them to take up arms against the man in power. They are wrong, of course. Experience soon teaches them they have only made things worse. And that follows from another natural and ordinary necessity: a new prince is always forced to burden the people he has just taken over with his troops, and with countless other hardships that conquest brings in its train.

So you have for enemies everyone you injured in seizing the principality, and you cannot keep as friends the men who put you there, since you cannot satisfy them as they had expected — and you cannot use strong medicine against them either, being in their debt. For however strong your armies, you always need the goodwill of the locals to enter a province.

So you find that you have made enemies of everyone you injured in seizing the principality, while you cannot keep the friendship of those who put you in power, since you are unable to satisfy them as fully as they expected — and you cannot move hard against them either, because you are in their debt. For however strong your army, you always need the goodwill of the local people to take and hold a province.

For these reasons Louis the Twelfth, King of France, took Milan quickly and lost it quickly; and to take it from him the first time, Lodovico's own forces were enough. For the people who had opened the gates to him, finding themselves cheated of the future they had promised themselves, could not stomach the abuses of the new prince. It is quite true that when rebel territory is taken a second time it is not lost so easily, for the prince, with fewer scruples now, uses the rebellion as his license to punish the guilty, expose the suspects, and reinforce himself wherever he is weakest. So the first time, to make France lose Milan, it was enough for Duke Lodovico to raise a revolt on the borders; to make her lose it the second time took the whole world combined against her, her armies destroyed and driven out of Italy — and that came about for the reasons given above.

These are the reasons why Louis XII, King of France, took Milan in an instant and lost it just as fast. The first time, Lodovico's own forces were enough to throw him out: the very people who had opened the gates, finding the future they had hoped for had not come, would not stomach the abuses of their new ruler. It is quite true that when a prince retakes a rebellious province a second time, he does not lose it so easily, because he uses the rebellion as a pretext to punish the guilty, expose the suspect, and shore up his weak points without much restraint. The first time, all it took to make France lose Milan was Duke Lodovico rattling the borders; the second time, it took the whole world combining against the king, his armies broken and chased out of Italy — and that followed from the causes already named.

Nevertheless, Milan was taken from France both the first time and the second. The general reasons for the first have been given; it remains to give the reasons for the second, and to see what remedies Louis had — what remedies anyone in his place would have — to hold a new acquisition more firmly than the King of France held his.

Even so, Milan was wrested from France both times. The general reasons for the first loss have been given; it remains to set out the reasons for the second, and to ask what resources the king had — what anyone in his position would have had — to hold his conquest more securely than he did.

Now I say that the dominions a conqueror gains and joins to an older state of his own either belong to the same country and language, or they do not. When they do, holding them is very easy, especially when they are not used to living free; to possess them securely, it is enough to have extinguished the line of the prince who ruled them. For the rest, leave the old conditions alone; where customs match, men live quietly together — as they have in Brittany, Burgundy, Gascony, and Normandy, so long bound to France. There may be some difference of language, but the customs are alike, and people manage easily among themselves. Whoever acquires such lands and means to keep them must see to just two things: that the old prince's bloodline is extinguished, and that neither laws nor taxes are altered. In a very short time the new territory and the old principality become one body.

Now, the territories a ruler annexes to his existing state are either of the same country and language as his own, or they are not. When they are, holding them is easy, especially if they are not used to governing themselves. To make your grip secure it is enough to wipe out the line of the prince who ruled them, because, with everything else in their old life left untouched and their customs much like yours, the two peoples will settle down together quietly — as we have seen in Brittany, Burgundy, Gascony, and Normandy, bound to France for so long. There may be some difference of language, but the customs are alike, and the peoples get along easily. Whoever annexes such lands and means to keep them has only two things to watch: that the family of the former lord is extinguished, and that he changes neither their laws nor their taxes. Then in a very short time the new territory fuses into one body with the old.

But when states are acquired in a province that differs in language, in customs, and in institutions, here the difficulties begin, and here you need great fortune and great industry to keep hold. One of the best and most immediate remedies is for the conqueror to go and live there in person. That makes the possession more secure and more lasting — as it has for the Turk in Greece, who, with every other measure he took for holding that state, could not have kept it without settling in it. On the spot, you see disorders as they are born, and you can put them down at once; from a distance, you hear of them only when they are full grown, and past curing. Besides this, the province is not stripped bare by your officials; the subjects are satisfied by quick access to their prince, which gives them more cause to love him if they mean to be good, and more cause to fear him if they do not. Any foreign power thinking of attacking the state hesitates; a prince who lives in it is dispossessed only with the greatest difficulty.

But when you acquire states in a region that differs in language, customs, and laws, the difficulties are real, and it takes good luck and great skill to hold them. One of the best remedies, and one of the most solid, is for the man who has taken them to go and live there himself. That makes his hold steadier and more lasting — as it has for the Turk in Greece, who, for all the other measures he took to keep that country, could never have held it had he not settled there. Living on the spot, you see disorders the moment they sprout and can deal with them at once; living far off, you hear of them only once they are large, and by then there is no cure. On top of that, your officials cannot strip the country bare; the people are content, because the prince is close at hand to appeal to; so those inclined to be loyal have more reason to love him, and those inclined otherwise more reason to fear him. Anyone planning to attack such a state from outside will think twice: as long as the prince lives there, it can only be torn from him with the greatest difficulty.

The other and better remedy is to plant colonies in one or two places that will serve as shackles on that state; either you do this, or you must keep large numbers of cavalry and infantry there instead. Colonies cost little. At little or no expense of his own, the prince sends them out and keeps them there, and he injures only those he strips of fields and houses to give to the new settlers — a minority of that state, and one left poor and scattered, which can never do him harm. All the rest remain uninjured on one side, and therefore easily quieted, and frightened on the other, in case what happened to the despoiled should happen next to them. I conclude: colonies cost nothing, are more loyal, and give less offense; and the offended, poor and scattered, cannot hurt you, as I have said. For here is a thing to note: men should be either treated well or snuffed out. They can avenge a light injury; a fatal one they cannot. So the injury done to a man must be of the kind that leaves no revenge to fear.

The next best course is to plant colonies in one or two places that serve as keys to the country. You must do this, or else keep a large force of cavalry and infantry stationed there. Colonies cost a prince little or nothing: he sends them out and maintains them cheaply, and the only people he injures are the few whose fields and houses he takes to give the newcomers — a small minority. Those he injures, left poor and scattered, can never harm him, while everyone else, untouched, stays quiet, and is careful besides not to step out of line, for fear of being dispossessed like the others. In short, colonies are cheap, more loyal, and do less harm; and the few who are harmed, being poor and scattered, can do nothing about it. On which note, men ought either to be caressed or crushed, for they will avenge small injuries but cannot avenge grave ones; so the harm you do a man should be such that you need never fear his revenge.

But keep armed men there instead of colonies and the cost multiplies: the whole revenue of the state goes to feed its garrison, until the acquisition runs at a loss. And it gives far more offense, since the whole state feels the injury as the garrison shifts its quarters from place to place. Everyone tastes the hardship; everyone becomes an enemy — and they are enemies who can still hurt you, beaten but still at home. On every count, then, a garrison is as useless as a colony is useful.

Holding the country with soldiers instead of colonies costs far more, since the whole revenue of the state is eaten up keeping the garrison, so that the gain turns into a loss; and it gives far more offense, since billeting the troops up and down inflicts hardship on the whole population, until everyone is your enemy — enemies who, beaten in their own homes, can still do you harm. By every measure, then, a garrison is as useless as a colony is useful.

Again, a prince holding a province unlike his own, as I have said, should make himself the head and protector of the smaller powers around him, work to weaken the strong ones, and take care that no foreigner as powerful as himself finds a way in by any accident. For such a one will always be called in by the discontented, out of too much ambition or out of fear — as the Ætolians once brought the Romans into Greece; indeed, into every province the Romans entered, they were brought by its own inhabitants. And the order of things is this: the moment a powerful foreigner enters a province, all its lesser powers attach themselves to him, driven by envy of the power that has stood over them — so that as regards these lesser powers he need not lift a finger to win them, since all together they immediately and willingly make one mass with the state he has taken there. He has only to see that they do not lay hands on too much strength and too much authority; then, with his own forces and their goodwill, he can easily bring down the powerful and remain, in everything, the arbiter of that province. And whoever fails to manage this part well will quickly lose what he has gained — and while he holds it, will find in it infinite difficulties and vexations.

Again, a prince who takes over a country unlike his own in these respects should make himself the head and protector of his weaker neighbors, work to weaken the stronger ones, and above all see to it that no foreigner as powerful as himself ever gets a foothold there by any mishap. For such a foreigner will always be let in by the discontented within, whether out of excessive ambition or out of fear — as we have already seen. It was the Aetolians who brought the Romans into Greece; and in every other country the Romans entered, it was the inhabitants who brought them. The way of things is that the moment a powerful outsider sets foot in a land, all the lesser states there rally to him, driven by their hatred of the power that ruled them. So with these lesser states he need take no trouble at all to win them over — they flock of their own accord to the position he has taken. He has only to see that they do not gain too much strength and authority; and then, with his own forces and their goodwill, he can easily hold down the stronger powers and remain complete master of the country. The ruler who mismanages this will quickly lose what he has won, and for as long as he keeps it will be plagued by endless troubles.

In the provinces they seized, the Romans kept these rules exactly: they planted colonies; they humored the lesser powers without increasing their strength; they beat down the strong; and they never let a powerful foreigner win credit there. The province of Greece will do as the one example. The Romans kept the Achaeans and the Ætolians as friends; the kingdom of Macedonia was humbled; Antiochus was driven out. Yet no merit of the Achaeans or the Ætolians ever bought them leave to enlarge a state of theirs; no persuasion from Philip ever induced the Romans to be his friends until they had brought him low; and all the power of Antiochus never made them consent to his keeping any state in that province. For the Romans did in these cases what every wise prince must do: attend not only to present disorders but to future ones, and ward those off with every kind of effort. Seen from far off, they are easily remedied; wait until they are on top of you, and the medicine is too late — the disease has become incurable. It is as the physicians say of the wasting fever: early on, it is easy to cure and hard to detect; with time, neither detected nor treated, it becomes easy to detect and impossible to cure. So it goes in matters of state. Recognize evils while they are still forming — a gift given only to the prudent — and they are cured quickly. Fail to recognize them, let them grow until anyone can see them, and no remedy remains. So the Romans, seeing troubles while they were still distant, always dealt with them then, and never let one run on merely to escape a war; they knew that a war is not escaped — only postponed, to the advantage of others. So they chose to fight Philip and Antiochus in Greece rather than have to fight them in Italy. They could, at the time, have avoided both. They chose not to. And they never cared for the saying that is forever in the mouths of the wise men of our day — enjoy the benefit of time. They preferred the benefit of their own virtù and prudence. For time drives everything before it, and can bring good as easily as evil, evil as easily as good.

In the countries they annexed, the Romans observed these rules to the letter: they sent colonies, kept the minor powers friendly without letting them grow, held down the great ones, and would not let any strong foreign power gain authority. Greece alone is example enough. The Romans kept the Achaeans and Aetolians as friends; they humbled the kingdom of Macedon; they drove out Antiochus. Yet for all the services of the Achaeans and Aetolians, the Romans never let them enlarge their power; no persuasion of Philip's ever won them his friendship without first humbling him; and all the weight of Antiochus could not make them grant him so much as a single holding in the country. For in these cases the Romans did what every wise prince must do: look not only to present troubles but to future ones, and guard against those with all their energy. Trouble foreseen is easily cured; let it come close before you act, and the medicine arrives too late, for the disease has grown incurable. It is here as the doctors say of consumption: early on it is easy to cure and hard to detect, but with time, left undetected and untreated, it becomes easy to detect and hard to cure. So it is in affairs of state. Foresee the evils brewing — which only a wise man can do — and they are quickly set right; let them go unseen until they have grown so plain that everyone sees them, and there is no longer any remedy. The Romans, then, saw their troubles coming and dealt with them at once. They would not let a danger run on merely to dodge a war, because they knew that war is never avoided, only postponed to another man's advantage. So they chose to fight Philip and Antiochus in Greece, rather than have to fight them later in Italy. They could have ducked both wars at the time, but they chose not to. They never trusted that maxim forever on the lips of the wise men of our own day — "enjoy the benefits of time" — but trusted instead the benefits of their own skill and foresight. For time sweeps everything before it, and can bring good as easily as ill, and ill as easily as good.

But let us return to France and consider whether she did any of the things I have named. I will speak of Louis and not of Charles, since Louis held possessions in Italy longer, and his course is the easier to read; and you will see that he did the contrary of everything that must be done to hold a state unlike one's own.

But let us turn back to France and ask whether she did any of these things. I will speak of Louis, not Charles, since Louis held ground in Italy longer and his conduct is the clearer to read; and you will see he did the very opposite of what must be done to hold a state of differing parts.

King Louis was brought into Italy by the ambition of the Venetians, who meant his coming to win them half the state of Lombardy. I will not blame the king for the part he took: wanting a first foothold in Italy, and having no friends in the province — every door barred to him, indeed, by the conduct of Charles — he had to take whatever friendships he could get; and the plan would have succeeded quickly enough had he made no errors elsewhere. With Lombardy taken, the king at once won back the standing Charles had thrown away: Genoa yielded; the Florentines became his friends; the Marquess of Mantua, the Duke of Ferrara, the Bentivogli, my lady of Forli, the lords of Faenza, of Pesaro, of Rimini, of Camerino, of Piombino, the Lucchese, the Pisans, the Sienese — all came forward to offer him their friendship. Then the Venetians had leisure to consider the rashness of what they had done: to gain themselves two towns in Lombardy, they had made the king master of two-thirds of Italy.

King Louis was brought into Italy by the ambition of the Venetians, who meant to seize half of Lombardy through his coming. I do not blame the king for the move: wanting a foothold in Italy and having no friends there — every door shut to him, in fact, by Charles's earlier conduct — he was forced to take whatever friendships he could get, and his design would have succeeded fast had he not blundered elsewhere. Having taken Lombardy, the king at once recovered the standing Charles had thrown away: Genoa gave in; the Florentines became his friends; the Marquess of Mantua, the Duke of Ferrara, the Bentivogli, the Lady of Forli, the Lords of Faenza, Pesaro, Rimini, Camerino, and Piombino, the Lucchese, the Pisans, the Sienese — all came forward to be his friend. Only then could the Venetians grasp the recklessness of their gamble: to gain two towns in Lombardy, they had made the king master of two-thirds of Italy.

Consider now how little trouble the king would have had in holding his standing in Italy if he had observed the rules set down above and kept all those friends of his secure and defended. They were many, they were weak, they were afraid — some of the Church, some of the Venetians — and so they were bound always to stand with him; and through them he could easily have secured himself against the powers that remained great. But he was no sooner in Milan than he did the reverse, lending Pope Alexander a hand to seize the Romagna. And it did not occur to him that with this decision he was weakening himself — casting off his friends, and the people who had thrown themselves into his lap — while making the Church great, stacking so much temporal power onto the spiritual power that already gives it such authority. Having made the first error, he was dragged into the rest, until finally, to check Alexander's ambition and keep him from becoming master of Tuscany, he was forced to come into Italy himself.

Consider how little trouble it would have cost the king to hold his position in Italy, had he kept to the rules laid out above and kept all those friends safe and protected. They were many, but weak and timid — some afraid of the Church, some of the Venetians — and so they would always have been bound to stand with him, and through them he could easily have secured himself against the powers that remained strong. But no sooner was he in Milan than he did the opposite: he helped Pope Alexander seize the Romagna. It never crossed his mind that by this he was weakening himself, throwing away his friends and the very men who had thrown themselves into his lap, while he built up the Church, adding great temporal power to its spiritual authority and so making it stronger still. Having made this first error, he was dragged into others: to check Alexander's ambition and keep him from making himself master of Tuscany, Louis was forced to come into Italy himself.

And as if it were not enough to have made the Church great and stripped himself of his friends, he then wanted the kingdom of Naples — and divided it with the King of Spain. Where he had been sole arbiter of Italy he installed a partner, so that the ambitious men of that province, and the malcontents of his own party, would have somewhere to turn; and where he could have left in that kingdom a king who was his pensioner, dependent on him, he removed him — and put in his place a man capable of driving out Louis himself.

And as if it were not enough to have built up the Church and stripped himself of friends, Louis — coveting the kingdom of Naples — split it with the King of Spain. So where he had been the chief arbiter of Italy, he brought in a partner, giving the ambitious and the malcontents of that country a refuge to run to; and where he could have left a king of his own there, beholden to him, he drove that man out and installed one strong enough to drive out Louis himself.

The wish to acquire is a thing truly natural and ordinary; when men who can, acquire, they will be praised for it, or at least not blamed. The error, and the blame, come when men who cannot are set on acquiring anyway. If France could have taken Naples with her own forces, she should have taken it; since she could not, she should not have split it. The split she made of Lombardy with the Venetians had an excuse: it bought her entry into Italy. This one had no such necessity behind it, and so it stands condemned.

The desire to acquire is a thoroughly natural and ordinary thing, and when men can do it, they will, and be praised for it rather than blamed. But when they cannot, and try anyway by any means, that is the folly that earns blame. If France could have struck at Naples with her own forces, she should have; if she could not, she should never have divided it. And if the partition of Lombardy with the Venetians could be excused on the ground that it bought her a foothold in Italy, this partition of Naples deserves blame, for it had no such necessity to excuse it.

Louis, then, had made five errors: he destroyed the lesser powers; he increased the power of one already great in Italy; he brought into Italy a foreign power of the first rank; he did not come to live there; he did not plant colonies. And even these five, in his lifetime, might not have hurt him had he not made a sixth: taking their dominions from the Venetians. Had he never made the Church great, never brought Spain into Italy, then cutting the Venetians down would have been reasonable, even necessary. But having taken those first steps, he should never have consented to their ruin: while the Venetians were strong, they would have kept everyone else clear of any venture against Lombardy — partly because the Venetians would allow no such venture unless it ended with Lombardy theirs, partly because the others had no wish to take it from France only to hand it to the Venetians, and no nerve to take on both together.

So Louis made these five mistakes: he destroyed the lesser powers; he built up the strength of one of the greater powers in Italy; he brought in a powerful foreigner; he did not settle in the country; and he planted no colonies. These errors, while he lived, might still not have ruined him, had he not made a sixth — stripping the Venetians of their lands. For had he not aggrandized the Church or brought Spain into Italy, it would have been entirely reasonable, even necessary, to humble Venice; but once he had taken those other steps, he should never have agreed to her ruin. As long as the Venetians were strong, they would always have kept others off any designs on Lombardy — partly because Venice would never have allowed it unless she could be mistress there herself, and partly because no one else would want to take Lombardy from France only to hand it to Venice, and would lack the nerve to defy them both.

And if anyone says that King Louis ceded the Romagna to Alexander, and the kingdom to Spain, to avoid a war — I answer with the reasons given above: a disorder should never be allowed to run on for the sake of avoiding a war, because the war is not avoided; it is deferred, to your own disadvantage. And if others cite the pledge the king had given the Pope — this campaign in exchange for the dissolution of his marriage and a cardinal's hat for Rouen — I answer with what I will say further on about the word of princes, and how far it should be kept.

And should someone object, "King Louis ceded the Romagna to Alexander and Naples to Spain to avoid a war," I answer, for the reasons already given, that you should never let a disorder run on to avoid a war, because the war is not avoided — only deferred to your disadvantage. And should someone else plead the promise the king had given the Pope, to back his enterprise in exchange for the annulment of his marriage and the cardinal's cap for Rouen, I refer him to what I shall say later about the faith of princes and how it ought to be kept.

So King Louis lost Lombardy by keeping none of the conditions kept by others who have taken provinces and meant to hold them. Nor is there any miracle in this — it is ordinary, and entirely reasonable. I said as much at Nantes to the Cardinal of Rouen, when Valentino — as Cesare Borgia, Pope Alexander's son, was commonly called — was occupying the Romagna. When the Cardinal of Rouen told me that the Italians understood nothing of war, I answered that the French understood nothing of statecraft; for if they did, they would not be letting the Church grow so great. And experience has borne it out: the greatness of the Church and of Spain in Italy was made by France, and France's ruin was made by them. From which a general rule can be drawn that never fails, or rarely: whoever makes another man powerful ruins himself. He builds that power with either cunning or force — and cunning and force are exactly what the man he raised will never trust.

So King Louis lost Lombardy for failing to observe a single one of the rules kept by those who have taken countries and meant to hold them. There is no miracle in this — it is reasonable and entirely natural. I spoke of these very matters at Nantes with the Cardinal of Rouen, at the time Valentino — as Cesare Borgia, Pope Alexander's son, was commonly called — was occupying the Romagna. When the Cardinal of Rouen remarked to me that the Italians did not understand war, I replied that the French did not understand statecraft, for had they understood it they would never have let the Church grow so great. And indeed it has proven true: France was the cause of the greatness of both the Church and Spain in Italy, and those two were the cause of France's ruin. From this we draw a rule that rarely if ever fails: whoever makes another powerful ruins himself, because he builds that power up by cunning or by force, and both of these are suspect to the very man he has raised.

sections.label: Chapter IV
sections.title: Why Darius's Kingdom Did Not Rebel
Why the Kingdom of Darius, Conquered by Alexander, Did Not Rebel Against Alexander's Successors at His Death

segments.text: Considering how hard it is to hold a newly acquired state, one might wonder at this: Alexander the Great made himself master of Asia in a few years and died when he had barely settled it — the very moment, it would seem, for the whole empire to rebel. Yet Alexander's successors held it, and the only difficulty they had in keeping it was the one their own ambition bred among themselves.

Given how much trouble men have in holding a newly won state, one might wonder at this: Alexander the Great made himself master of Asia in a few years, and died before it was scarcely settled. It would seem natural for the whole empire to have risen in revolt. Yet his successors held on, and met no difficulty in keeping it beyond what their own ambitions stirred up among themselves.

I answer that all the principalities on record have been governed in one of two ways: either by one prince, with everyone else his servant, some of them helping him govern the kingdom as ministers, by his grace and license; or by a prince and by barons, who hold their rank not by their master's favor but by ancient blood. Such barons have states and subjects of their own — subjects who recognize them as lords and bear them a natural affection. In states governed by a prince and his servants, the prince stands higher in men's eyes, for in the whole province no one is acknowledged superior but him; if people obey anyone else, they obey a minister and an official, and feel no particular love for him.

My answer is that all the principalities we have any record of are governed in one of two ways. Either by a prince and a body of servants who, by his favor and leave, help him govern the kingdom as his ministers; or by a prince and barons, who hold their rank not by the prince's grace but by antiquity of blood. Barons of this kind have states and subjects of their own, who acknowledge them as lords and bear them a natural affection. In the states ruled by a prince and his servants, the prince holds far greater authority, for in all his country there is no one recognized as a superior above him; and if the people obey anyone else, they do it as toward a minister and official, and feel no particular loyalty to him.

The living examples of these two kinds of government are the Turk and the King of France. The whole monarchy of the Turk is governed by one lord; the rest are his servants. He divides his kingdom into sanjaks, sends out administrators, and moves and replaces them as he pleases. The King of France, by contrast, sits in the midst of an ancient multitude of lords, each acknowledged and loved by subjects of his own; they have their privileges, and the king cannot touch them without danger to himself. Consider these two states, then, and you will find the difficulty is in conquering the Turk's — but once conquered, it is held with great ease. The reasons his kingdom is hard to seize are these: an invader cannot be called in by the princes of the realm, and cannot hope for a revolt in the ruler's own circle to ease his enterprise. That follows from what was said above: the ruler's ministers, being all slaves, and bound men, are corrupted only with great effort, and even corrupted they are worth little, since they cannot pull the people after them, for the reasons given. So whoever attacks the Turk must expect to find him united, and had better count on his own strength rather than on the other side's disorders. But once the Turk is beaten — broken in the field past raising new armies — there is nothing left to fear but the prince's bloodline. Extinguish that, and no one remains to be feared, for none of the others has any credit with the people; and just as the conqueror could expect nothing from them before his victory, he need fear nothing from them after it.

The clearest examples of these two kinds of government in our own day are the Turk and the King of France. The whole monarchy of the Turk is governed by one lord, and all the rest are his servants. He divides his kingdom into districts and sends out different administrators to govern them, shifting and replacing them as he pleases. The King of France, by contrast, stands in the midst of a great body of ancient lords, each acknowledged by subjects of his own and beloved by them. These lords have their hereditary prerogatives, which the king cannot strip away without danger to himself. So whoever weighs these two states will see that the Turk's is hard to seize but, once taken, easy to hold; while the opposite is true of France. The difficulty of seizing the Turk's state lies in this: an invader cannot be invited in by princes of the kingdom, nor hope that those around the lord will revolt and help his cause. The reasons are the ones already given. Since they are all slaves and bondmen, they are corrupted only with great difficulty, and even once corrupted they are of little use, for they cannot carry the people with them. So anyone who attacks the Turk must reckon on finding him united, and must rely on his own strength rather than on disorder among the enemy. But once the Turk is beaten and routed in the field so thoroughly that he cannot raise his armies again, there is nothing left to fear but the prince's own family; and once that line is wiped out, no one remains to be feared, since the others have no standing with the people. Just as the conqueror could expect nothing from them before his victory, so he has nothing to fear from them after it.

The opposite holds in kingdoms governed like France. There you can enter with ease by winning over some baron of the realm, for malcontents are always to be found, and men who want things changed. Such men, for the reasons given, can open the road into the state and hand you the victory. But keeping it afterward brings infinite trouble, from those who helped you and from those you crushed alike. Nor is it enough to have extinguished the prince's line, because the lords remain, ready to make themselves heads of new movements; and being able neither to satisfy them nor to snuff them out, you lose the state the first time the occasion offers.

The reverse holds in kingdoms governed like that of France. There you can easily get in by winning over some baron of the realm, for there are always malcontents and men hungry for change. For the reasons given, such men can open the way into the state and make the victory easy. But holding it afterward brings endless difficulties, from those who helped you and from those you crushed alike. It is not enough to have wiped out the prince's line, because the lords who remain put themselves at the head of fresh risings; and since you can neither satisfy them nor destroy them, you lose that state the moment the chance presents itself.

Now consider what kind of government Darius had, and you will find it like the kingdom of the Turk. So Alexander had first to smash him in the field and sweep him from open country; and after that victory, with Darius dead, the state stayed securely in Alexander's hands, for the reasons argued above. Had his successors stayed united, they could have enjoyed it at their leisure — no tumults arose in that kingdom but the ones they raised themselves.

Now, if you consider what kind of government Darius had, you will find it resembled the Turk's. So Alexander had first to beat him outright in the field and drive him from the country. After that victory, with Darius dead, the state was secure to Alexander for the reasons set out above. Had his successors held together, they could have enjoyed it in ease, for the only upheavals raised in that kingdom were the ones they stirred up themselves.

But states ordered like France cannot be possessed so quietly. Hence the repeated rebellions of Spain, of France, and of Greece against the Romans — all because of the many principalities those provinces contained. As long as the memory of them lasted, Rome's hold was never sure; when that memory was extinguished by the power and long duration of the empire, the hold became secure. And later, when the Romans fought among themselves, each commander could carry with him the part of those provinces where his own authority had taken root; the bloodlines of the old lords being extinguished, the provinces acknowledged no one but Romans.

But states built like France cannot be held with any such calm. This is why the Romans faced those repeated revolts in Spain, France, and Greece — because of the many principalities in those lands. So long as the memory of them lasted, Rome's hold was never secure; but once the power and long endurance of the empire had blotted that memory out, the Romans became settled masters. And when they later fell to fighting among themselves, each could draw to his side the part of the country where his authority ran; and with the line of the former lords extinguished, those peoples acknowledged no masters but the Romans.

Keep all this in mind, and no one will wonder at the ease with which Alexander kept his hold on the empire of Asia, or at the trouble others — Pyrrhus among many — have had in keeping what they won. It comes not from the little or great virtù of the conqueror, but from the difference in what was conquered.

Weigh all this, and no one will marvel at the ease with which Alexander held the empire of Asia, or at the difficulties others have had in keeping what they took — Pyrrhus and many more. This turns not on the conqueror's having more skill or less, but on the difference in the states he takes.

sections.label: Chapter V
sections.title: Cities That Lived Free
How to Govern Cities or Principalities That Lived Under Their Own Laws Before They Were Annexed

segments.text: When states acquired in the way I have described are accustomed to living free under their own laws, there are three ways to hold them: the first is to ruin them; the second is to go and live there in person; the third is to let them live on under their own laws, taking a tribute from them and setting up inside a government of a few men who will keep the state friendly to you. For such a government, being the prince's creature, knows it cannot stand without his friendship and his power, and will do everything to keep him standing. And a city used to living free, if you mean to preserve it at all, is held more easily through its own citizens than by any other means.

When the states you acquire have been used to living under their own laws and in freedom, there are three ways to hold them. The first is to ruin them. The second is to go and live there yourself. The third is to let them keep their own laws, exact a tribute, and set up inside the state an oligarchy that will keep it friendly to you. Such a government, knowing it owes its existence to the prince, knows too that it cannot stand without his backing and his power, and so it will do everything to uphold him. A city used to its freedom is held more easily through its own citizens, when you mean to keep it, than by any other means.

Take the Spartans and the Romans. The Spartans held Athens and Thebes by setting up governments of a few men in them; they lost them anyway. The Romans, to hold Capua, Carthage, and Numantia, demolished them, and did not lose them. They tried to hold Greece more or less as the Spartans had held it — leaving it free, leaving it its laws — and it failed; to keep the province they were forced to demolish many of its cities. For the truth is that there is no secure way to possess such cities except to ruin them.
