And whoever becomes master of a city accustomed to living free, and does not destroy it, should expect to be destroyed by it; for in rebellion it will always find its rallying cry in the name of liberty and in its own old order, which neither the length of years nor any amount of good treatment ever makes it forget. Do what you like, provide what you like: unless the inhabitants are split apart or scattered, they never forget that name or that order, and at every accident they run straight back to both — as Pisa did after a hundred years in bondage to the Florentines.

Take the Spartans and the Romans. The Spartans held Athens and Thebes by planting an oligarchy in each — and lost them both anyway. The Romans, to hold Capua, Carthage, and Numantia, dismantled them, and did not lose them. They tried to hold Greece much as the Spartans had held their cities, leaving it free under its own laws, and failed; so in the end, to keep it, they were forced to raze many of its cities. For the truth is there is no sure way to hold such places except to lay them in ruins. Whoever becomes master of a city used to living free, and does not destroy it, may expect to be destroyed by it. For in rebellion it always has a refuge in the name of liberty and its ancient privileges, which neither the passing of time nor any favor will ever make it forget. Whatever you do, whatever provision you make, unless its people are scattered and broken apart they never forget that name or those privileges, but reach for them the moment a chance appears — as Pisa did after the hundred years she had been held in bondage by the Florentines.

But when cities or provinces are used to living under a prince and his bloodline is extinguished, then — trained to obey, their old prince gone — they can neither agree on a new prince from among themselves nor manage to live free. They are slower to take up arms, and a prince can win them more easily and hold them more securely. In republics there is more life, more hatred, more appetite for revenge. The memory of their old liberty gives them no rest — it cannot. So the safest way is to snuff them out — or to go and live there.

But when cities or provinces have been used to living under a prince, and his line is wiped out, then — schooled on the one hand to obey, and left on the other without their old master — they cannot agree on raising one of their own to the throne, and they do not know how to govern themselves. So they are slow to take up arms, and a prince can win them over and make himself secure far more easily. In republics, though, there is more life, more hatred, more hunger for revenge; the memory of their former liberty gives them no rest and never will. The safest course with them is to wipe them out, or to go and live there.

sections.label: Chapter VI
sections.title: By Your Own Arms and Virtù
Concerning New Principalities Acquired by One's Own Arms and Skill

segments.text: No one should be surprised if, in speaking of principalities entirely new, I bring in the greatest examples of prince and of state. Men almost always walk in paths beaten by others, and conduct their affairs by imitation; but the paths of others cannot be followed exactly, and you cannot reach the virtù of the man you imitate. So a prudent man should always enter by paths beaten by great men, and imitate those who have been most excellent — so that if his own virtù does not reach theirs, at least it carries some scent of it. He should do as the clever archers do when the target looks too far off: knowing how far their bow will carry, they aim well above the mark — not to drive the arrow to that height, but to hit, by so high an aim, the mark they intend.

Let no one be surprised if, in speaking of principalities that are wholly new — both the prince and the state new — I reach for the very greatest examples. Men nearly always walk in paths beaten by others, shaping their own conduct by imitation; and though they can never keep entirely to another man's road, or match the skill of the men they imitate, a prudent man will still always set his feet in the paths trodden by the great and model himself on those who have been supreme, so that even if his own ability does not reach theirs, it may at least catch something of their scent. He should do as the skilled archers do: judging the mark too far off, and knowing just how far the strength of their bow will carry, they aim well above it — not to drive the arrow that high, but so that, aiming high, they may strike the mark they actually mean to hit.

I say, then, that in principalities entirely new, where there is a new prince, holding on is more or less difficult according to the virtù of the man who acquires them. And since becoming prince from private citizen presupposes either virtù or fortune, one or the other of these, it seems, must ease many of the difficulties. Even so, the man who has leaned less on fortune has held on longer. It also helps when the prince, having no other state, is forced to come and live in this one in person.

I say, then, that in principalities entirely new, where there is a new prince, the difficulty of holding them is greater or less in proportion to the skill of the man who has acquired them. And since rising from private citizen to prince presupposes either skill or luck, it is plain that one or the other of these will smooth away many of the difficulties. Even so, the man who has leaned least on luck has held on the longest. It also helps that the prince, having no other state, is forced to come and live there in person.

But to come to those who became princes by their own virtù and not by fortune: the most excellent, I say, are Moses, Cyrus, Romulus, Theseus, and their like. And though Moses should hardly be discussed, being a mere executor of things ordered by God, still he deserves admiration, if only for the grace that made him worthy to speak with God. But consider Cyrus and the others who acquired or founded kingdoms: you will find them all admirable; and if you weigh their particular actions and arrangements, they will not look much different from those of Moses, who had so great a teacher. Examine their actions and their lives, and you will find they owed nothing to fortune but opportunity — the raw material they shaped into whatever form seemed best to them. Without that opportunity the virtù of their minds would have gone out; without that virtù, the opportunity would have come in vain.

But to come to those who became princes by their own skill and not by luck, I say that the most outstanding are Moses, Cyrus, Romulus, Theseus, and men like them. And though Moses ought not perhaps to be discussed, since he was merely carrying out what God commanded, still he deserves our admiration if only for the grace that made him worthy to speak with God. But take Cyrus and the others who won or founded kingdoms: you will find them all admirable; and if you weigh their particular deeds and methods, they will not look inferior to those of Moses, for all that he had so great a teacher. Examining their actions and their lives, you see that they owed nothing to luck except the opportunity, which handed them the raw material they could then mold into whatever shape they pleased. Without that opportunity their force of mind would have been wasted; without that force the opportunity would have come in vain.

It was necessary, then, that Moses find the people of Israel in Egypt, enslaved and ground down by the Egyptians, so that to escape their servitude they would be ready to follow him. It was necessary that Romulus not stay in Alba, and that he be exposed at birth, if he was to become King of Rome and founder of that fatherland. It was necessary that Cyrus find the Persians sick of the empire of the Medes, and the Medes gone soft from long peace. Theseus could not have shown his virtù had he not found the Athenians scattered. These opportunities made these men fortunate, then, and their surpassing virtù made them recognize the opportunity; and by it their countries were ennobled and made supremely happy.

It was necessary, then, that Moses should find the people of Israel in Egypt, enslaved and oppressed by the Egyptians, so that they would be willing to follow him to escape their bondage. It was necessary that Romulus should have no place in Alba, and be cast out at birth, if he was to become King of Rome and founder of his country. It was necessary that Cyrus should find the Persians chafing under the rule of the Medes, and the Medes gone soft and slack from a long peace. Theseus could never have shown his skill had he not found the Athenians scattered. These opportunities, then, made these men's fortune, and their own high skill let them seize the opportunity; by which their countries were ennobled and made famous.

Men like these, who become princes by paths of virtù, acquire their principality with difficulty but hold it with ease. The difficulties in acquiring come partly from the new orders and methods they are forced to introduce to found their state and secure it. And it should be kept in mind that nothing is harder to take in hand, more doubtful of success, or more dangerous to manage than making yourself the leader in introducing a new order of things. The innovator has enemies in everyone who did well under the old order, and lukewarm defenders in everyone who might do well under the new. The lukewarmness comes partly from fear of the opponents, who have the laws on their side, and partly from the incredulity of men — who never truly believe in anything new until solid experience has shown it to them. So whenever the enemies of the new order get their chance to attack, they attack like partisans, and the others defend half-heartedly; and between them the prince is put at risk.

Those who come to power by such paths of skill acquire their principality with difficulty but hold it with ease. The difficulties they meet in acquiring it spring in part from the new orders and methods they are forced to bring in to found their rule and make it secure. And it must be borne in mind that there is nothing harder to undertake, nothing more perilous to manage, nor more uncertain of success, than to set oneself up as the leader in introducing a new order of things. For the innovator makes enemies of all who did well under the old order, and finds only lukewarm defenders in those who might do well under the new. This lukewarmness comes partly from fear of their adversaries, who have the law on their side, and partly from the skepticism of men, who do not truly believe in anything new until they have had solid experience of it. So it happens that whenever those hostile to the change get the chance to attack, they do so with the fury of partisans, while the others defend so half-heartedly that the prince is endangered along with them.

If we want to examine this part thoroughly, we must ask whether these innovators stand on their own or depend on others — that is, whether they must beg to carry their work through, or whether they can force it. When they must beg, they always end badly and accomplish nothing. But when they depend on their own strength and can use force, they are rarely in danger. This is why all armed prophets have conquered, and the unarmed have been destroyed. For besides everything said already, the nature of peoples is fickle: it is easy to persuade them of a thing, and hard to hold them to the persuasion. So matters must be ordered in such a way that when they no longer believe, they can be made to believe by force.

It is necessary, therefore, if we mean to examine this matter properly, to ask whether these innovators stand on their own feet or depend on others — that is, whether to carry their work through they must beg, or whether they can compel. In the first case they always come to grief and accomplish nothing; but when they depend on themselves and can use force, then they are rarely in danger. This is why all armed prophets have conquered, and the unarmed ones have been destroyed. For besides what I have already said, the temper of the people is fickle: it is easy to convince them of a thing, but hard to hold them to that conviction. So matters must be so arranged that when they no longer believe, they can be made to believe by force.

Moses, Cyrus, Theseus, and Romulus could not have made their orders obeyed for long had they been unarmed — as happened in our own time to Fra Girolamo Savonarola, who was ruined along with his new order the moment the crowd began not to believe him; and he had no way to hold firm the ones who had believed, or to make the unbelievers believe. Men like these, then, face great difficulty in carrying the work through: all their dangers lie on the way up, and virtù must get them past. But once they are past — once they are held in reverence, and have wiped out the men who envied them their standing — they remain powerful, secure, honored, and happy.

Had Moses, Cyrus, Theseus, and Romulus been unarmed, they could not have made their constitutions hold for long — as happened in our own day to Fra Girolamo Savonarola, who was ruined along with his new order the moment the crowd stopped believing in him, since he had no way to keep the believers steadfast or to force the doubters to believe. Men like these, then, have great trouble carrying their work through, for all their dangers lie in the climb; but with skill they overcome them, and once they are past, and those who envied their success have been wiped out, they begin to be respected, and go on powerful, secure, honored, and content.

To such lofty examples I want to add a lesser one; but it keeps some proportion with them, and I mean it to stand for every other case of its kind: Hiero the Syracusan. From private citizen, he became Prince of Syracuse — and he owed nothing to fortune but opportunity. The Syracusans, being oppressed, elected him their captain; from there he earned his promotion to prince. And he was of such virtù even in private life that the man who wrote of him said he lacked nothing of a king but the kingdom. He abolished the old militia and raised a new one; he dropped the old friendships and made new ones; and once the friendships and the soldiers were his own, he could build any building on that foundation — so that what cost him great effort to acquire cost him little to keep.

To these great examples I will add a lesser one, though it bears some likeness to them and can stand for all of its kind: Hiero of Syracuse. This man rose from private citizen to Prince of Syracuse, and he too owed nothing to luck but the opportunity; for the Syracusans, hard pressed, chose him as their captain, and afterward judged him worthy to be made their prince. Even as a private man his skill was so great that one who wrote of him said he lacked nothing to be a king but a kingdom. He did away with the old army and organized a new one; he dropped his old alliances and made new ones; and once he had soldiers and allies of his own, on such a foundation he could raise whatever building he liked — so that he had endured much trouble in the winning and had little in the keeping.

sections.label: Chapter VII
sections.title: By Others' Arms and Fortune
Concerning New Principalities Acquired by the Arms of Others or by Fortune

segments.text: Those who rise from private citizen to prince by fortune alone rise with little effort but hold on with a great deal. They have no trouble on the way up, because they fly there; all the trouble begins once they land. Such are the men who are handed a state, either for money or as a favor from whoever grants it — as happened to many in Greece, in the cities of Ionia and the Hellespont, where Darius made princes so they would hold the cities for his security and his glory; and as happened to those emperors who rose from private citizens to the throne by bribing the soldiers. Men like this stand simply on the goodwill and the fortune of whoever raised them — two utterly fickle and unstable things — and they neither know how to hold the position nor can they. They do not know how, because unless a man has great intelligence and virtù, it is not reasonable that he should know how to command after a lifetime as a private citizen; and they cannot, because they have no forces of their own that they can count on to be loyal and faithful.

Men who rise from private citizen to prince by sheer luck have little trouble getting there, but a great deal staying there. They meet no obstacles on the way up, because they fly; the trouble comes the moment they land. Such are the men handed a state for money, or by the favor of whoever bestows it — as happened to many in Greece, in the cities of Ionia and the Hellespont, where Darius made men princes so that they would hold those cities for his security and his glory; and as happened, too, with those emperors who climbed from private station to the empire by bribing the soldiers. Men like these rest on nothing but the goodwill and the fortune of whoever raised them — two things as inconstant and unstable as any in the world. They lack both the knowledge and the means to hold their place: the knowledge, because unless a man is of great ability and force of character, it is unreasonable to expect that one who has always lived as a private citizen should suddenly know how to command; and the means, because they have no forces of their own that they can keep loyal and devoted.

Besides, states that spring up overnight, like everything else in nature that is born and grows too fast, cannot have put down roots and connections deep enough to survive the first storm — unless, as I said, the men who become princes overnight have so much virtù that they know at once how to hold what fortune has dropped in their laps, and can lay afterward the foundations that others lay before they become princes.

States that spring up overnight, then, are like everything else in nature that is born and grows in haste: they cannot put down the roots and form the connections they need, and the first spell of bad weather destroys them. Unless, as I said, the men who become princes so suddenly are of such ability that they know at once how to hold what fortune has dropped in their laps — laying afterward the foundations that other princes lay before they rise.

For these two ways of becoming prince — by virtù or by fortune — I want to offer two examples from within living memory: Francesco Sforza and Cesare Borgia. Francesco, by the right means and by great virtù of his own, rose from private citizen to Duke of Milan, and what he had acquired with a thousand pains he kept with little effort. Cesare Borgia, on the other hand — called Duke Valentino by the people — acquired his state by his father's fortune and lost it the same way, even though he did everything and used every means a prudent and capable man should use to sink his roots into the states that the arms and fortune of others had given him.

On these two ways of becoming a prince — by skill or by luck — I want to set down two examples from our own time: Francesco Sforza and Cesare Borgia. Francesco, by the right means and with great skill, rose from private citizen to Duke of Milan, and what he won with a thousand hardships he kept with little trouble. Cesare Borgia, on the other hand — Duke Valentino, as the people called him — won his state through the fortunes of his father, and lost it when those fortunes failed, even though he had taken every measure and done everything a shrewd and able man should do to sink his roots into the states that the arms and fortune of others had handed him.

Because, as was said above, whoever does not lay his foundations in advance might, with great virtù, lay them later — though it costs the architect trouble and puts the building at risk. If you consider all the steps the duke took, you will see that he laid great foundations for his future power; and I do not think it beside the point to go through them, because I would not know what better lessons to give a new prince than the example of his actions. And if his arrangements came to nothing in the end, it was not his fault: it was an extraordinary and extreme malice of fortune.

For, as I said above, the man who has not laid his foundations first may with great skill lay them afterward, but only at much trouble to the builder and much risk to the building. Look at every step the duke took, and you will see he laid solid foundations for his future power. I think it worth setting them out, for I know no better lesson to give a new prince than the example of his actions. And if in the end his measures failed him, that was no fault of his, but the extraordinary and extreme malignity of fortune.

Alexander the Sixth, wanting to make his son the duke great, faced plenty of difficulties, present and future. First, he saw no way to make him master of any state that was not a state of the Church; and he knew that if he moved to take from the Church, the Duke of Milan and the Venetians would not stand for it — Faenza and Rimini were already under Venetian protection. Beyond that, he saw the arms of Italy, especially the ones he might have used, in the hands of men with every reason to fear a greater Pope — the Orsini, the Colonnesi, and their followers. It was necessary, then, to upset this arrangement and throw their states into disorder, so as to make himself securely master of part of them. That proved easy, because he found the Venetians, for reasons of their own, already working to bring the French back into Italy; he not only did not oppose it, he smoothed the way by annulling King Louis's old marriage. So the king came into Italy with the help of the Venetians and the consent of Alexander; and no sooner was he in Milan than the Pope had troops from him for the campaign in the Romagna, which was surrendered to him on the king's reputation. Having taken the Romagna, then, and beaten the Colonnesi, the duke wanted to hold what he had and push further, but two things stood in his way: his own forces, which did not look loyal to him, and the will of France. He feared that the Orsini arms he had been using would fail under him — that they would not only block further gains but take from him what he had already gained — and that the king would do the same. He got his proof about the Orsini when, after taking Faenza, he attacked Bologna and watched them go cold on the assault; and he learned the king's mind when, after seizing the Duchy of Urbino, he moved on Tuscany and the king made him back off. At that point the duke resolved to depend no longer on the arms and fortune of others.

When Pope Alexander VI set out to make his son the duke a great man, he faced no end of difficulties, both immediate and to come. First, he saw no way to make him master of any state that was not the Church's; and he knew that if he tried to carve one out of Church lands, the Duke of Milan and the Venetians would never stand for it, since Faenza and Rimini were already under Venetian protection. On top of that, he saw that the arms of Italy — especially the ones he might have leaned on — were in the hands of men who had every reason to dread the growth of papal power: namely the Orsini, the Colonna, and their following. He had to upset this whole arrangement, then, and throw the Italian powers into confusion, so as to make himself safe master of part of their lands. This proved easy, for he found the Venetians, moved by reasons of their own, bent on bringing the French back into Italy. Not only did he not oppose this — he made it easier still by dissolving King Louis's former marriage. So the king came into Italy with Venetian help and Alexander's blessing, and was no sooner in Milan than the Pope had troops from him for the campaign on the Romagna, which surrendered to the duke on the king's reputation alone. So the duke took the Romagna and beat the Colonna. But when he wanted to hold what he had and push further, two things stood in his way. One was that his own forces did not look loyal; the other was the goodwill of France. He feared, that is, that the Orsini troops he was using would fail him — that they might not only block him from winning more, but even seize what he had already won — and that the king might do the same. He had his warning about the Orsini when, after the capture of Faenza, he attacked Bologna and saw how grudgingly they went into that assault. And he learned the king's mind when, after taking the duchy of Urbino, he moved on Tuscany and the king made him pull back. After that, the duke resolved to depend no longer on the arms and the luck of others.

His first move was to weaken the Orsini and Colonna factions in Rome. He won over all their gentlemen adherents by making them his own gentlemen — paying them well and honoring them, according to their rank, with commands and offices — so that within a few months their old party loyalties died out and the whole allegiance turned to the duke. After that, having already scattered the men of the Colonna house, he waited for his chance to crush the Orsini, and when it came he used it well. The Orsini, realizing too late that the greatness of the duke and the Church meant their ruin, called a meeting at Magione, in Perugian territory. Out of that came the revolt of Urbino, the uprisings in the Romagna, and endless dangers for the duke — all of which he overcame with the help of the French. Then, his reputation restored, and trusting neither France nor any other outside force enough to put them to the test, he turned to deception. And he knew so well how to disguise his mind that the Orsini themselves — through Signor Pagolo, whom the duke took care to reassure with every courtesy, giving him money, clothes, and horses — were reconciled to him; and their simplicity delivered them into his hands at Sinigalia. So with the leaders wiped out and their partisans turned into his friends, the duke had laid quite good foundations for his power: he held all the Romagna along with the Duchy of Urbino, and above all he had won the Romagna itself, whose people had begun to taste prosperity under him. And because this part deserves notice, and imitation by others, I do not want to pass over it.

His first step was to weaken the Orsini and Colonna parties in Rome. He won over all their gentleman adherents, taking them into his own household, putting them on good pay, and honoring them — each according to his rank — with offices and commands, so that within a few months their old loyalty to the factions melted away and fastened entirely on the duke. Then he waited for a chance to crush the Orsini, the Colonna following having already been scattered. The chance came soon, and he used it well. For the Orsini, realizing at last that the rise of the duke and the Church meant their own ruin, called a council at Magione, in the country near Perugia. Out of that came the revolt at Urbino and the uprisings in the Romagna, and no end of danger to the duke — all of which he overcame with French help. With his authority restored, and unwilling to leave it at the mercy of the French or any other outside force, he turned to cunning. He concealed his intentions so well that, through the mediation of Signor Paolo — whom he was careful to secure with every attention, lavishing money, fine clothes, and horses on him — the Orsini were reconciled to him; and their own gullibility delivered them into his hands at Senigallia. Having wiped out the leaders and turned their followers into his friends, the duke had laid more than adequate foundations for his power, holding all the Romagna along with the duchy of Urbino — and with the people now beginning to taste the good of his rule, he won them over entirely. This last point deserves notice and is worth imitating, so I will not pass it by.

When the duke took the Romagna, he found it had been run by weak lords, quicker to strip their subjects than to govern them, who had given the province more cause for division than for unity, so that it was rife with theft, feuds, and every sort of outrage. He judged that to make it peaceful and obedient to the ruler's arm, it needed good government; so he set over it Messer Ramiro d'Orco, a cruel and efficient man, and gave him the fullest power. In a short time Ramiro made the province peaceful and united, and won an enormous reputation doing it. Then the duke judged that such excessive authority was no longer wanted, fearing it would breed hatred; and he set up a civil court in the middle of the province, under an excellent president, where every city had its advocate. And because he knew the past severities had bred some hatred against himself, he wanted to purge the minds of the people and win them over completely — to show that whatever cruelty had been done had come not from him but from the harsh nature of his minister. So, having found his moment, one morning at Cesena he had Ramiro laid out in two pieces on the piazza, with a block of wood and a bloody knife beside him. The ferocity of that spectacle left the people at once satisfied and stunned.

When the duke took the Romagna, he found it had been governed by feeble masters who plundered their subjects rather than ruled them, and gave them more cause for discord than for unity, so that the whole province was rife with robbery, feuds, and every kind of violence. He judged that to restore it to peace and obedience he would have to give it a good governor. So he set over it Messer Remirro de Orco, a swift and brutal man, and gave him absolute power. In short order this man brought the country to peace and unity, and won great renown by it. Then the duke decided that such unchecked authority was no longer wise, fearing it would breed hatred; so he set up a civil court in the heart of the province, under a most able president, where every city had its own advocate. And because he knew that the late severities had earned him some hatred, he wanted — to purge men's minds and win the people over completely — to show that whatever cruelty had been done sprang not from him but from the harsh nature of his minister. Seizing on this pretext, one morning he had Remirro laid out in the piazza at Cesena in two pieces, with a block of wood and a bloody knife beside him. The ferocity of that spectacle left the people at once satisfied and stupefied.

But let us return to where we left off. I say that the duke now found himself powerful enough, and partly insured against present dangers — armed his own way, and having largely destroyed the neighboring forces that could hurt him — and what remained, if he meant to go on conquering, was France; because he knew the king, who had seen his mistake too late, would not tolerate it. So he began to look for new alliances and to stall France over the expedition she was making toward the kingdom of Naples, against the Spaniards besieging Gaeta. His intention was to secure himself against them, and he would soon have managed it if Alexander had lived.

But let me return to where I began. With the duke now strong enough, and largely secured against immediate dangers — having armed himself in his own way and broken most of the neighboring forces that could have harmed him — what remained, if he meant to keep pressing his conquest, was France. He knew the king, awake too late to his blunder, would no longer back him. So from this point he began to look for new alliances, and to hold France at arm's length over the campaign she was then waging toward the kingdom of Naples against the Spaniards besieging Gaeta. His aim was to secure himself against the French; and he would have managed it quickly, had Alexander lived.

That was how he handled things present. As for things to come, he had to fear, first, that a new head of the Church would be no friend to him and would try to take back what Alexander had given him. He thought to secure himself against that in four ways. First, by wiping out the bloodlines of the lords he had despoiled, to strip the Pope of that pretext. Second, by winning over all the gentlemen of Rome, as I have said, so as to hold the Pope in check through them. Third, by making the College of Cardinals his, as far as he could. Fourth, by acquiring so much power before the Pope died that he could withstand a first attack on his own. Of these four things, by the time Alexander died, he had accomplished three. Of the despoiled lords he had killed as many as he could reach, and very few escaped; the Roman gentlemen were won; and in the College he had the largest party. As for new acquisitions, he had designs on Tuscany; he already possessed Perugia and Piombino, and had taken Pisa under his protection. And since he no longer had to defer to France — the French had already been stripped of the kingdom of Naples by the Spaniards, so that each side now had to buy his friendship — he pounced on Pisa. After that, Lucca and Siena would fold at once, partly out of spite toward the Florentines and partly out of fear; and the Florentines would have had no remedy. Had he brought this off — and he was bringing it off the very year Alexander died — he would have gathered such force and such reputation that he would have stood on his own, no longer depending on the fortune and forces of another, but on his own power and virtù.

So much for how he handled the present. As for the future, his first fear was that a new head of the Church might not be his friend, and might try to take back what Alexander had given him. Against this he resolved to guard four ways. First, by exterminating the families of all the lords he had stripped of their lands, so as to deny the Pope that pretext. Second, by winning over all the gentlemen of Rome, so as to hold the Pope in check through them, as already noted. Third, by bringing the College of Cardinals as far as he could onto his side. Fourth, by gaining so much power before the Pope's death that he could withstand the first shock on his own. By the time Alexander died, he had achieved three of these four. He had killed as many of the dispossessed lords as he could lay hands on, and few had slipped away; he had won over the Roman gentlemen; and he had the largest party in the College. As for fresh conquests, he meant to make himself master of Tuscany; he already held Perugia and Piombino, and had taken Pisa under his protection. And since he no longer had to mind France — the French having by now been driven out of the kingdom of Naples by the Spaniards, so that both sides had to court his goodwill — he pounced on Pisa. After that, Lucca and Siena gave in at once, partly out of hatred of the Florentines and partly out of fear of them; and the Florentines would have had no defense left. Had he gone on prospering as he was prospering the year Alexander died, he would have built up such power and standing that he could have stood on his own feet, no longer leaning on the luck and the forces of others but solely on his own power and skill.

But Alexander died five years after the duke first drew his sword. He left him with only the state of Romagna consolidated, everything else in the air, caught between two very powerful enemy armies, and deathly ill. Yet there was such ferocity and such virtù in the duke — he understood so well how men are won or lost, and the foundations he had laid in so short a time were so sound — that if he had not had those armies on his back, or if he had been healthy, he would have ridden out every difficulty. And that his foundations were good, you could see: the Romagna waited for him more than a month; in Rome, half dead, he was safe; and though the Baglioni, the Vitelli, and the Orsini came to Rome, they could raise nothing against him. If he could not make Pope the man he wanted, he could at least keep out the man he did not want. Had he been healthy when Alexander died, everything would have gone easily for him. He told me himself, on the day Julius the Second was elected, that he had thought through everything that could happen when his father died, and had found a remedy for all of it — except that he never imagined that when the day came, he too would be at the point of death.

But Alexander died five years after the duke first drew his sword. He left him with only the state of the Romagna firmly consolidated and everything else up in the air, caught between two of the most powerful hostile armies, and himself sick to death. Yet there was in the duke such boldness and such ability, and he understood so well how men are to be won or lost, and so firm were the foundations he had laid in so short a time, that had he not had those armies at his back, or had he simply been in good health, he would have come through every difficulty. And the proof that his foundations were sound is that the Romagna held for him more than a month. In Rome, though barely half alive, he stayed secure; and though the Baglioni, the Vitelli, and the Orsini came to Rome, they could do nothing against him. If he could not make whomever he wished pope, at least he could keep out anyone he did not want. Had he only been in sound health when Alexander died, everything would have gone easily for him. He told me himself, the day Julius II was elected, that he had foreseen everything that might happen at his father's death and had a remedy ready for all of it — except that he had never imagined that, when the death came, he too would be at the point of death.

Gathering up all the duke's actions, then, I would not know how to fault him. On the contrary, it seems right to hold him up, as I have done, as a model for all those who rise to rule by fortune and the arms of others. With his great spirit and his high aims, he could not have conducted himself otherwise; only the shortness of Alexander's life and his own sickness stood against his designs. So whoever judges it necessary, in a new principality, to secure himself against enemies; to win friends; to conquer by force or by fraud; to make himself loved and feared by the people, followed and respected by the soldiers; to wipe out those who can or must hurt him; to replace the old order with new; to be severe and gracious, magnanimous and open-handed; to destroy a disloyal army and build a new one; to keep the friendship of kings and princes on such terms that they help him gladly and cross him carefully — such a man can find no fresher example than this man's actions.

Weighing up all the duke's actions, I cannot find it in me to fault him. On the contrary, I think — as I have said — that he should be held up as a model for everyone who comes to power by the fortune or the arms of others. For with his great spirit and his far-reaching aims, he could not have conducted himself otherwise, and it was only the shortness of Alexander's life and his own sickness that wrecked his designs. So a man who finds it necessary, in a new principality, to make himself safe against his enemies, to win friends, to conquer by force or by fraud, to make himself loved and feared by the people, to be followed and revered by his soldiers, to wipe out those who have the power or the reason to harm him, to replace the old order with a new one, to be at once severe and gracious, generous and openhanded, to disband a disloyal army and raise his own, to keep on such terms with kings and princes that they must either help him gladly or strike at him with caution — such a man can find no fresher example than the actions of this one.

The one thing he can be blamed for is the election of Julius as Pope: there he chose badly. Because, as I said, if he could not make a Pope of his own, he could keep the papacy from anyone he chose — and he should never have consented to the elevation of any cardinal he had injured, or any who, once Pope, would have reason to fear him. For men do injury out of fear or out of hatred. Those he had injured included San Pietro ad Vincula, Colonna, San Giorgio, and Ascanio; all the rest, on becoming Pope, would have had cause to fear him — except Rouen and the Spaniards: the Spaniards through kinship and obligation, Rouen through power, having the kingdom of France behind him. So the duke's first choice should have been a Spanish Pope; failing that, he should have consented to Rouen, not San Pietro ad Vincula. Whoever believes that with great men new favors erase old injuries is deceiving himself. The duke erred in this election, and it was the cause of his final ruin.

The one thing he can be blamed for is the election of Julius II, where his choice was a bad one. As I said, though he could not make a pope to his own liking, he had it in his power to block anyone he did not want; and he should never have let any cardinal reach the papacy who had been injured by him, or who, once pope, would have reason to fear him — for men strike out of fear as readily as out of hatred. Among those he had injured were San Pietro in Vincoli, Colonna, San Giorgio, and Ascanio. All the rest, on becoming pope, would have had cause to fear him, except Rouen and the Spaniards — the Spaniards by ties of blood and obligation, Rouen by his strength, being backed by the kingdom of France. So above all the duke should have made a Spaniard pope; failing that, he should have agreed to Rouen and never to San Pietro in Vincoli. Whoever thinks that new favors make great men forget old injuries deceives himself. The duke, then, erred in this election, and it was the cause of his final ruin.

sections.label: Chapter VIII
sections.title: Rising by Crime
Concerning Those Who Have Obtained a Principality by Wickedness

segments.text: But since there are two more ways a private citizen can become a prince, neither of which can be put down entirely to fortune or to virtù, I cannot leave them out — though one of them could be treated at more length where republics are discussed. These are: when a man rises to the principality by some criminal and wicked path, and when a private citizen becomes prince of his native city by the favor of his fellow citizens. Speaking of the first way, I will show it by two examples, one ancient and one recent, without otherwise weighing the merits of this course — because for anyone who needs it, I judge these two are enough to imitate.

A private citizen can rise to be prince in two more ways, neither of which can be put down wholly to luck or to skill, and I do not mean to pass them over in silence — though one of them might be treated more fully where I discuss republics. These are: coming to power by some wicked and criminal path, or being raised to the rule of one's country by the favor of one's fellow-citizens. I will illustrate the first by two examples, one ancient and one modern, without going further into its merits; for I judge these two enough for anyone forced to follow such methods.

Agathocles the Sicilian became King of Syracuse not merely from private life but from the bottom — from a low and abject start. The son of a potter, he lived a criminal life at every stage of his career. Yet he joined his crimes to such virtù of mind and body that, after entering the militia, he rose through its ranks to be Praetor of Syracuse. Once settled in that rank, he decided to become prince — to hold by violence, and owing nothing to anyone, what had been granted him by consent. He reached an understanding about his plan with Amilcar the Carthaginian, who was campaigning with his armies in Sicily; then one morning he assembled the people and the senate of Syracuse as if he had business of the Republic to discuss, and at a prearranged signal his soldiers killed all the senators and the richest of the people. With them dead, he seized and held the rule of that city without any civil strife. And though the Carthaginians twice defeated him and finally besieged him, he not only defended his city: leaving part of his forces to hold off the siege, he attacked Africa with the rest, lifted the siege of Syracuse in short order, and drove the Carthaginians to such extremity that they were forced to come to terms with him — to content themselves with Africa and leave Sicily to Agathocles.

Agathocles the Sicilian became King of Syracuse not just from private life but from a low and abject station. The son of a potter, he led a disgraceful life at every turn of his fortunes. Yet he matched his disgraces with such force of mind and body that, taking up soldiering, he climbed through the ranks to become Praetor of Syracuse. Set in that office, he resolved to make himself prince — to hold by violence, and beholden to no one, what had been granted him by consent. He came to an understanding on this with Hamilcar the Carthaginian, who was then campaigning with his army in Sicily. One morning he assembled the people and senate of Syracuse, as though he had matters of state to lay before them, and at a prearranged signal his soldiers killed every senator and the richest of the citizens. With them dead, he seized and held the rule of the city, and no one stirred against him. And though the Carthaginians twice routed him and at last laid siege to him, he not only defended his city but, leaving part of his men to hold it, crossed with the rest into Africa, and in short order lifted the siege of Syracuse. The Carthaginians, driven to extremity, were forced to come to terms with him: they left Sicily to him and contented themselves with Africa.

Whoever weighs this man's actions and virtù, then, will find little or nothing that can be credited to fortune. As I said, he came to the principality not by anyone's favor but up through the ranks of the militia, earning every step with a thousand hardships and dangers, and afterward held his place by many bold and risky decisions. And yet it cannot be called virtù to kill your fellow citizens, betray your friends, and be without faith, without pity, without religion. Such methods can win empire, but not glory. If you consider Agathocles' virtù in walking into dangers and walking out of them, and his greatness of spirit in bearing and beating adversity, there is no reason to rank him below the most celebrated captains. All the same, his savage cruelty and inhumanity, and his countless crimes, do not allow him to be honored among the truly excellent men. So what he achieved cannot be credited to fortune — and it cannot be credited to virtù.

Anyone who weighs the actions and the gifts of this man will see little or nothing he owed to fortune, since he came to the top, as I have said, not by anyone's favor but step by step through the army, winning each step through a thousand hardships and dangers, and then holding power by many bold and hazardous strokes. Yet it cannot be called skill to slaughter your fellow-citizens, to betray your friends, to be without faith, without mercy, without religion. Such methods may win you power, but not glory. For if you weigh his courage in walking into danger and out again, and his greatness of spirit in bearing and beating down hardship, there is no reason to rank him below the finest captain who ever lived. All the same, his savage cruelty and inhumanity, and his measureless crimes, forbid us to count him among the greatest men. What he achieved, then, cannot be put down to either fortune or skill.

In our own times, under Alexander the Sixth, there is Oliverotto da Fermo. Left fatherless years before as a small child, he was raised by a maternal uncle, Giovanni Fogliani, and in his early youth sent to soldier under Pagolo Vitelli, so that a training in that discipline might carry him to some high rank in the profession. After Pagolo died he served under his brother Vitellozzo, and in a very short time — being clever, and vigorous in body and mind — he became the first man of his company. But it seemed servile to him to take orders from others, so he resolved to seize Fermo — with the help of certain citizens of Fermo who preferred their city enslaved to their city free, and with the backing of the Vitelleschi. He wrote to Giovanni Fogliani that after so many years away he wanted to come see him and his city, and to have some look at his own inheritance; and since he had labored for nothing but honor, he wished to arrive honorably, escorted by a hundred horsemen of his friends and servants, so that his fellow citizens would see he had not spent his years for nothing; and he begged Giovanni to arrange an honorable reception from the people of Fermo — which would do honor not only to him but to Giovanni himself, who had raised him.

In our own time, under Pope Alexander the Sixth, there was Oliverotto da Fermo. Orphaned years before, he was raised by his maternal uncle, Giovanni Fogliani, and sent young to soldier under Paolo Vitelli, so that, trained in that discipline, he might rise to high rank in the profession. When Paolo died, he served under his brother Vitellozzo, and being quick-witted and vigorous in body and mind, he soon became the foremost man in that service. But finding it a poor thing to serve under others, he resolved to seize Fermo — with the help of certain men of Fermo who held the slavery of their city dearer than its freedom, and with the backing of the Vitelli. So he wrote to Giovanni Fogliani that, having been away from home for many years, he wished to come and see him and his city and to take some look at his own inheritance; and since he had labored for nothing but honor, he wanted his fellow-citizens to see he had not wasted his time, and so meant to come in style, escorted by a hundred horsemen, his friends and retainers. He begged Giovanni to see to it that the people of Fermo received him with honor — which would reflect not only on himself but on Giovanni, who had brought him up.

Giovanni failed in no courtesy owed his nephew. He had him honorably received by the Fermians and lodged him in his own house — where Oliverotto, after a few days spent quietly arranging what his coming crime required, gave a formal banquet and invited Giovanni Fogliani and all the leading men of Fermo. When the food and the usual entertainments of such banquets were done, Oliverotto artfully steered the talk to weighty matters — the greatness of Pope Alexander and his son Cesare, and their undertakings. Giovanni and the others were answering when he rose all at once, saying these were things to discuss in a more private room, and withdrew to a chamber; Giovanni and all the other citizens followed him in. No sooner were they seated than soldiers came out of hiding and killed Giovanni and all the rest. After the slaughter, Oliverotto mounted his horse, rode the town, and besieged the chief magistracy in its palace; so that out of fear the people obeyed him and formed a government, of which he made himself prince. And with everyone dead who, being discontented, could have hurt him, he strengthened himself with new civil and military ordinances — so that within the year he held the principality, he was not only secure inside the city of Fermo but feared by all its neighbors. Rooting him out would have been as hard as rooting out Agathocles, had he not let himself be tricked by Cesare Borgia, when at Sinigalia, as was told above, the duke took the Orsini and the Vitelli and took him with them. There, one year after the parricide he had committed, he was strangled, together with Vitellozzo, who had been his teacher in virtù and in crime.

Giovanni did not stint any courtesy owed his nephew. He had him honorably received by the Fermians and lodged him in his own house. There, after a few days spent making the arrangements his wicked design required, Oliverotto gave a grand banquet and invited Giovanni Fogliani and the leading men of Fermo. When the food and all the other entertainments customary at such banquets were done, Oliverotto cunningly turned to weighty matters, speaking of the greatness of Pope Alexander and his son Cesare and their undertakings. Giovanni and the others took up the talk, but Oliverotto suddenly rose, saying such things ought to be discussed somewhere more private, and withdrew to an inner room, with Giovanni and the rest of the citizens following him in. No sooner were they seated than soldiers burst from hidden places and butchered Giovanni and all the rest. After the killings Oliverotto mounted his horse and rode through the town, and laid siege to the chief magistrate in the palace, until the people, in fear, were forced to obey him and to set up a government with himself as prince. He put to death everyone who, being discontented, might have harmed him, and shored up his position with new ordinances, civil and military, so that within the single year he held the principality he was not only secure in Fermo but a terror to all his neighbors. He would have been as hard to dislodge as Agathocles, had he not let himself be outwitted by Cesare Borgia, who took him along with the Orsini and the Vitelli at Sinigaglia, as I have already told. There, one year after he committed his parricide, he was strangled, together with Vitellozzo, the man who had been his master in prowess and in crime.

Some may wonder how it could happen that Agathocles and men like him, after countless betrayals and cruelties, could live long and secure in their own country, defend themselves against foreign enemies, and never face a conspiracy from their own citizens — while many others, using cruelty, could not hold their states even in peacetime, let alone in the uncertain times of war. I believe it comes down to cruelties badly used or well used. Well used we may call those — if it is permissible to speak well of evil — that are done at a single stroke, out of the necessity of securing oneself, and then not persisted in, but converted into the greatest usefulness to the subjects that they can be. Badly used are those which, though few at the start, grow with time instead of dying out. Those who take the first way can, with God and with men, find some remedy for their position, as Agathocles did; for the others, it is impossible to hold on.

Some may wonder how it can be that Agathocles, and others like him, after endless treachery and cruelty, can live long and secure in their own country, defend themselves against outside enemies, and never be conspired against by their own citizens — while many others, for all their cruelty, have failed to hold their state even in settled times, let alone in the doubtful times of war. I believe this turns on whether cruelty is badly or well used. Cruelties may be called well used — if of evil one may speak well at all — when they are committed all at once, out of the need to make yourself secure, and then are not kept up, but turned to the good of your subjects. They are badly used when, few though they may be at the start, they grow with time instead of dying away. Those who take the first course can, with God's help or man's, find some way to soften their rule, as Agathocles did. Those who take the second cannot possibly keep their footing.

So it should be noted that in seizing a state, the man who takes it should run through all the injuries he will need to commit, and commit them all at once, so as not to have to renew them every day — and then, by not renewing them, reassure men and win them over with benefits. Whoever does otherwise, out of timidity or bad advice, has to keep the knife in his hand forever; and he can never lean on his subjects, since their fresh and continual injuries keep them from ever trusting him. For injuries should be done all together, so that, being tasted less, they offend less; benefits should be handed out little by little, so that they are savored longer.

From this it is to be noted that in seizing a state, a man should reckon up all the injuries he must inflict, and do them all at one stroke, so as not to be repeating them day after day; for then, by not unsettling men, he can reassure them and win them over with benefits. Whoever does otherwise, whether out of timidity or bad advice, must always keep the knife in his hand; he can never rely on his subjects, nor they trust themselves to him, because of the fresh and ceaseless wrongs he does them. For injuries should be done all at once, so that, being tasted less, they offend less; benefits should be handed out little by little, so that their flavor lasts longer.

And above all, a prince should live with his subjects in such a way that no accident, good or bad, forces him to change course; because when hard times bring the necessity, you are too late for the evil, and the good you do buys you nothing — it is judged forced, and earns you no thanks at all.

And above all, a prince should live among his people in such a way that no turn of events, good or bad, can force him to change course. For if the need comes upon you in troubled times, you are too late for harsh measures; and any kindness you show will do you no good, since it will be seen as wrung out of you, and no one will thank you for it.

sections.label: Chapter IX
sections.title: The Civil Principality
Concerning a Civil Principality

segments.text: But coming to the other case — when a leading private citizen becomes prince of his native city not by crime or any intolerable violence but by the favor of his fellow citizens — this can be called a civil principality. Reaching it does not take pure virtù or pure fortune; it takes, rather, a kind of lucky cunning. I say a man rises to this principality by the favor of the people or by the favor of the nobles. For these two opposed humors are found in every city, and they arise from this: the people do not want to be ruled or oppressed by the nobles, and the nobles want to rule and oppress the people. From these two appetites, one of three effects follows in a city: principality, liberty, or license.

Now for the other way up. A leading citizen becomes the prince of his country not by crime, nor by any unbearable show of force, but by the favor of his fellow citizens. This may be called a civil principality, and reaching it takes neither great skill nor great luck, but rather a shrewdness that knows its moment. Such a principality is won either by the favor of the people or by the favor of the nobles. For in every city these two opposed parties are found, and the source of the split is this: the people do not want to be commanded or oppressed by the nobles, and the nobles want to command and oppress the people. Out of these two contrary appetites one of three things comes about in a city — a principality, a free government, or anarchy.

A principality is set up either by the people or by the nobles, depending on which of the two gets its chance. When the nobles see they cannot hold out against the people, they begin building up the reputation of one of their own and make him prince, so that under his shadow they can satisfy their appetite. The people likewise, seeing they cannot hold out against the nobles, build up the reputation of one man and make him prince, to be defended by his authority. The man who comes to the principality with the nobles' help holds it with more difficulty than the one who comes to it with the people's, because he finds himself prince surrounded by many who think themselves his equals — and for that reason he can neither command them nor manage them his own way. But the man who reaches the principality by popular favor finds himself alone at the top, with no one around him, or almost no one, who is not ready to obey.

Whether the principality comes from the people or from the nobles depends on which of them gets the opening. When the nobles see they cannot hold out against the people, they begin to talk up the standing of one of their own and make him prince, so that under his cover they can satisfy their own ambitions. The people, when they find they cannot resist the nobles, likewise talk up the standing of one of their own and make him prince, to have his authority for their shield. A man who reaches power with the help of the nobles holds it with more difficulty than one who reaches it by the help of the people, because he finds himself surrounded by many who count themselves his equals, and so he can neither command them nor manage them as he likes. But the man who reaches power by the people's favor stands there alone, with no one around him, or next to no one, unwilling to obey.

Beyond that, you cannot satisfy the nobles honestly and without wronging others, but you can satisfy the people that way — because the people's aim is more decent than the nobles': the nobles want to oppress, and the people only want not to be oppressed. Add to this that against a hostile people a prince can never make himself safe, because there are too many of them; against the nobles he can, because they are few. The worst a prince can expect from a hostile people is to be abandoned by them. From hostile nobles he must fear not only abandonment but attack; for the nobles see further and move earlier, they always act in time to save themselves, and they court favor with whichever side they expect to win. And besides, the prince has to live with the same people always, but he can do perfectly well without the same nobles, since he can make them and unmake them every day, and give or take away their standing as he pleases.

Beyond that, you cannot in fairness, and without wronging others, satisfy the nobles — but you can satisfy the people, because their aim is more honest than the nobles': the nobles want to oppress, the people want only not to be oppressed. And there is this too: a prince can never make himself safe against a hostile people, since they are too many, whereas against the nobles he can, since they are few. The worst a prince has to fear from a hostile people is to be abandoned by them; but from hostile nobles he has to fear not only abandonment but their turning against him — for being shrewder and more far-sighted in these matters, they always move in time to save themselves, and to court the favor of the man they expect to win. And there is more: a prince is forced to go on living always with the same people, but he can do well enough without the same nobles, since he can make them and unmake them day by day, granting and stripping their standing whenever he pleases.

To make this part clearer, I say the nobles should be considered in two main ways: either they run their course so as to bind themselves entirely to your fortune, or they do not. Those who bind themselves, and are not greedy, should be honored and loved. Those who do not bind themselves come in two kinds. If they hold back out of faint-heartedness — a natural shortage of spine — then make use of them, especially the ones with good counsel in them; in prosperity they do you honor, and in adversity you have nothing to fear from them. But when they keep clear of you deliberately, for reasons of ambition, it is a sign they are thinking more of themselves than of you; and against those a prince must guard himself, and fear them as if they were declared enemies, because in adversity they will always help bring him down.

To make this point clearer: the nobles are to be looked at chiefly in two ways. Either they so bind themselves to your fortune that their whole course is tied to yours, or they do not. Those who bind themselves to you, and are not greedy, should be honored and loved. Those who do not bind themselves split into two kinds. Some hold back out of timidity, a natural want of nerve; these you should put to use, especially the ones who give good counsel, since in good times they bring you honor and in bad times you have nothing to fear from them. But those who hold off out of calculation, for their own ambitious ends, are showing that they think more of themselves than of you; and a prince should be on his guard against these and fear them as if they were declared enemies, because when things turn against him they will always help to bring him down.

Therefore, one who becomes prince by the favor of the people must keep the people his friend — which is easy, since all they ask is not to be oppressed. But one who becomes prince against the people, by the favor of the nobles, must before anything else try to win the people over — also easy, once he takes them under his protection. And because men, when they receive good from someone they expected only harm from, bind themselves all the more tightly to their benefactor, the people become better disposed toward him at once than if he had been raised by their own favor. A prince can win them in many ways, but the ways vary so much with circumstance that no fixed rule can be given, and I will leave them out. I will conclude only this: a prince must have the people friendly — otherwise, in adversity, he has no remedy.

So a man who becomes prince by the favor of the people should keep them friendly, which is easily done, since all they ask is not to be oppressed. But a man who becomes prince by the favor of the nobles, against the people, should before anything else work to win the people over to himself — which is also easily done, if he takes them under his protection. For when men receive good from someone they had braced for harm, they bind themselves to their benefactor all the more tightly; and so the people will turn more devoted to him than if he had been raised to power by their own favor in the first place. A prince can win the people in many ways, but since these change with the circumstances no fixed rule can be laid down, so I leave them aside. The conclusion stands: a prince must have the people friendly, or in hard times he has nothing to fall back on.

Nabis, Prince of the Spartans, withstood the siege of all Greece and of a triumphant Roman army, and against them defended his country and his own rule; and when the danger came, all he needed was to secure himself against a few — which would not have been enough if the people had been his enemy. And let no one counter this opinion of mine with the worn proverb that 'he who builds on the people builds on mud.' That is true when a private citizen lays his foundation there and lets himself believe the people will rescue him when his enemies or the magistrates come for him; in that case a man will often find himself deceived, as the Gracchi were in Rome and Messer Giorgio Scali was in Florence. But if it is a prince who builds on the people — one who can command, a man of spirit, unshaken in adversity, who does not neglect his other preparations, and who keeps the whole city's nerve up by his own courage and his own orders — he will never find himself betrayed by them, and he will find he has built on solid ground.

Nabis, prince of the Spartans, withstood the assault of all Greece and of a Roman army flush with victory, and against them defended his country and his state; and to ride out that danger he had only to make himself secure against a few — though that would not have been enough had the people been against him. And let no one throw the worn-out proverb at this opinion of mine, that "he who builds on the people builds on mud." That holds when a private citizen makes the people his foundation and lets himself believe they will come to his rescue when his enemies or the magistrates bear down on him — in which case he will often find himself deceived, as the Gracchi were in Rome and Messer Giorgio Scali in Florence. But take a prince who has established himself as I have described, who can command, who is a man of nerve, not thrown by adversity, who does not fall short in the other qualities, and who by his resolve and his energy keeps the whole people heartened — such a prince will never be deceived by them, and will be shown to have laid his foundations well.

These principalities usually come into danger at the moment they are climbing from the civil order to the absolute one. For these princes rule either in their own person or through magistrates. In the second case their position is weaker and more dangerous, because it rests entirely on the will of the citizens who hold the magistracies — and they, especially in hard times, can take the state from him with great ease, either by moving against him or simply by not obeying. And in the middle of the danger there is no time for the prince to seize absolute authority: citizens and subjects who are used to taking their orders from the magistrates are not about to obey his in that crisis, and in uncertain times he will always be short of men he can trust. A prince like this cannot build on what he sees in quiet times, when the citizens need the state — then everyone runs to him, everyone promises, and with death nowhere in sight, everyone is ready to die for him. But in hard times, when the state needs its citizens, few are to be found. And this experiment is all the more dangerous because it can only be run once. So a wise prince must think of a way to make his citizens need the state and need him — always, in every kind of weather. Then they will always be faithful.

These principalities are most in danger when they are passing from the civil to the absolute order of rule. For such princes govern either in person or through magistrates. In the second case their position is weaker and less secure, since it rests entirely on the goodwill of those citizens raised to office, who in troubled times can wreck the government with great ease, whether by scheming or by open defiance. And in the thick of such upheavals the prince has no chance to seize absolute authority, because the citizens and subjects, used to taking their orders from the magistrates, are in no mood amid the confusion to take them from him; and in doubtful times he will always be short of men he can trust. A prince of this kind cannot count on what he sees in quiet times, when the citizens need the state — for then they all rush to agree with him, all make promises, and with death far off all swear to die for him; but when trouble comes, when the state has need of its citizens, then he finds very few. And the test is the more dangerous because it can be run only once. So a wise prince must contrive things in such a way that his citizens, in every kind of circumstance whatever, always have need of the state and of him; and then they will always be faithful to him.

sections.label: Chapter X
sections.title: Measuring a State's Strength
How the Strength of All Principalities Should Be Measured

segments.text: In examining the qualities of these principalities, there is one more question to consider: whether a prince has a state strong enough to stand on its own at need, or whether he will always need someone else's protection. To make the point clearer, I say that in my judgment those princes can stand on their own who have enough men or enough money to put together a proper army and meet in the field whoever comes to attack them; and those always need others who cannot take the field against the enemy, but are forced to fall back behind their walls and defend them. The first case has been discussed, and later I will say whatever more it needs. In the second case there is nothing to say except to urge such princes to fortify and provision their own town, and to take no account of the countryside. Whoever has fortified his town well, and has handled his subjects in the way described above and to be described again, will never be attacked except with great hesitation; for men are always wary of ventures where the difficulty is plain to see, and no one sees an easy target in a prince whose town is strong and whose people do not hate him.

There is one more point to weigh when examining the character of these principalities: whether a prince has power enough to stand on his own at need, or whether he must always lean on the help of others. To make this plain, I count as able to stand on their own those who, by abundance of men or money, can raise an army strong enough to take the field against anyone who comes to attack them; and I count as always needing others those who cannot face the enemy in the open but are forced to shelter behind their walls and defend those. The first case I have already discussed, and will return to as occasion requires. To those in the second case there is nothing to say except to urge them to provision and fortify their towns, and never on any account to defend the open country. Whoever fortifies his town well, and has handled his subjects' affairs as I described above and will describe again, will never be attacked without great caution; for men are always loath to take on enterprises that look difficult, and there is no easy prize in attacking a prince whose town is well fortified and who is not hated by his people.

The cities of Germany are completely free, they have little surrounding territory, and they obey the emperor when they choose to; they fear neither him nor any other power near them, because they are fortified in such a way that everyone reckons taking them would be slow, grinding work. They all have proper moats and walls; they have artillery enough; they keep enough in the public stores to eat, drink, and burn for a year. Beyond that — to keep the common people fed without cost to the public — they always hold in common a year's worth of work to give out in the trades that are the nerve and life of the city, the industries the people live by. They keep military exercises in good repute, and have many ordinances besides to maintain them.

The cities of Germany are wholly free; they own little of the country around them, and they obey the emperor only when it suits them, fearing neither him nor any other power they have near them, because they are fortified in such a way that everyone reckons the taking of them by assault would be slow and hard. They all have proper ditches and walls; they have artillery enough; and they always keep stored in public depots enough to eat, drink, and burn for a year. On top of this, to keep the common people content without cost to the state, they always have the means to set them to work for a year at the labors that are the life and strength of the city, the trades by which the people live. They hold military exercises in honor besides, and have many ordinances to keep them up.

So a prince who has a strong city and does not make himself hated cannot be attacked; and even if someone did attack him, the attacker would leave in disgrace — because the affairs of this world are so changeable that it is next to impossible to sit idle with an army for a whole year while you besiege him. And to whoever answers that if the people have their property outside the walls and watch it burn, they will lose patience, and the long siege and their own self-interest will make them forget the prince — I reply that a powerful and spirited prince will always get past those difficulties: now giving his subjects hope that the evil will not last long, now stoking fear of the enemy's cruelty, now deftly securing himself against the ones who seem too bold.

So a prince who has a strong city and has not made himself hated cannot be attacked; and if anyone should attack him, he will be driven off in disgrace, for the affairs of this world shift so much that it is all but impossible for a man to keep an army idle in the field for a whole year, laying siege. And should someone object that, if the people have property outside the walls and see it burned, they will lose patience, and the long siege and their own self-interest will make them forget their prince — to this I answer that a powerful and spirited prince will master every such difficulty: now giving his subjects hope that the trouble will not last long, now turning their minds to fear of the enemy's cruelty, now dealing shrewdly with those who seem too bold.

Besides, the enemy will naturally burn and wreck the countryside on arrival, while the defenders' blood is still hot and willing; so the prince has all the less reason to worry, because after a few days, when tempers have cooled, the damage is already done, the losses already taken, and there is no undoing them. And then the people close ranks with their prince all the more, feeling he is now obliged to them, their houses burned and their lands ruined in his defense. For it is the nature of men to be bound by the benefits they give as much as by the benefits they receive. So all things considered, it will not be hard for a prudent prince to keep his citizens' minds firm through a siege, from first day to last — so long as they lack neither food nor the means to fight.

Besides, the enemy will naturally burn and lay waste the country the moment he arrives, while the people's spirits are still hot and set on the defense; and so the prince has all the less reason to hesitate, because a few days on, when those spirits have cooled, the damage is already done, the harm is already taken, and there is no remedy left. By then the people only bind themselves more closely to their prince, judging that he stands in their debt now that their houses have been burned and their lands ruined in his defense. For it is the nature of men to feel as much bound by the good they do as by the good they receive. So weigh it all up, and a wise prince will find it no hard thing to keep his citizens' spirits firm through a siege from first to last, so long as he does not fail to feed them and to defend them.

sections.label: Chapter XI
sections.title: Ecclesiastical Principalities
Concerning Ecclesiastical Principalities

segments.text: It remains now only to speak of ecclesiastical principalities. With these, every difficulty comes before you possess them: they are acquired by virtù or by fortune, and kept without either, because they are sustained by the ancient institutions of religion, which have grown so powerful, and are of such a kind, that they keep their princes in power however those princes act and live. These princes alone have states and do not defend them, subjects and do not govern them; and the states, though undefended, are not taken from them, and the subjects, though ungoverned, do not care — they neither think of breaking away, nor could they. Only these principalities, then, are secure and happy. But since they are upheld by a higher cause, which the human mind cannot reach, I will say no more about them; they are raised up and maintained by God, and it would be the work of a presumptuous and reckless man to pass judgment on them.

It remains only to speak of ecclesiastical principalities. With these, all the difficulty lies in getting hold of them, for they are won either by skill or by fortune, and held by neither. They are sustained instead by the ancient institutions of religion, which are so powerful, and of such a kind, that they keep their princes in power no matter how those princes act or live. These princes alone have states and do not defend them; they have subjects and do not govern them; and yet their states, undefended, are not taken from them, and their subjects, ungoverned, do not mind, and have neither the wish nor the means to break away. Such principalities alone are secure and content. But since they are upheld by powers the human mind cannot reach, I will say no more about them: being exalted and maintained by God, it would be the act of a presumptuous and rash man to discuss them.

Still, someone might ask me how it happens that the Church has risen to such greatness in temporal power — given that until Alexander the Italian powers, and not only the ones called powers but every baron and lord down to the smallest, held that temporal power cheap, and now a king of France trembles before it, and it has been able to throw him out of Italy and to ruin the Venetians.
