Well known as this is, I do not think it wasted effort to call some part of it back to mind.

Still, someone might ask how it comes about that the Church has grown so great in temporal power. Before Alexander, the Italian powers — and not just those properly called powers, but every baron and lord, down to the very smallest — counted that temporal power for very little; yet now a king of France trembles before it, and it has been able to drive him out of Italy and to ruin the Venetians. The thing may be plain enough, but I think it worth recalling to mind.

Before Charles, King of France, came down into Italy, this country was under the rule of the Pope, the Venetians, the King of Naples, the Duke of Milan, and the Florentines. These powers had two chief anxieties: that no foreigner should enter Italy in arms, and that none of their own number should seize more territory. The two watched most closely were the Pope and the Venetians. To hold back the Venetians it took a league of all the rest, as in the defense of Ferrara; and to hold down the Pope they used the barons of Rome. Divided into two factions, Orsini and Colonnesi, the barons never lacked a pretext for disorder; standing with weapons in hand under the Pontiff's own eyes, they kept the papacy weak and sickly. Now and then a spirited pope arose — a Sixtus — but neither fortune nor wisdom could ever rid him of this nuisance. The shortness of papal lives was the cause. In the ten years an average pope reigns, he could barely beat down one of the factions; and if one pope, so to speak, had all but wiped out the Colonnesi, up came a successor who was enemy to the Orsini — which raised the Colonnesi again — and there was no time left to wipe out the Orsini. This is why the Pope's temporal powers were held in little esteem in Italy.

Before Charles, King of France, came down into Italy, this country lay under the dominion of the Pope, the Venetians, the King of Naples, the Duke of Milan, and the Florentines. These powers had two chief anxieties: first, that no foreigner should enter Italy under arms; second, that none of their own number should seize more territory. The two watched most closely were the Pope and the Venetians. To hold the Venetians in check, all the others had to combine, as they did in the defense of Ferrara; and to keep the Pope down, they made use of the barons of Rome, who, split into two factions, the Orsini and the Colonna, always had some pretext for disorder, and, standing with arms in hand under the very eyes of the pontiff, kept the papacy weak and helpless. And though now and again a bold pope would arise, a Sixtus for instance, neither his fortune nor his wisdom could ever rid him of these troubles. The short life of a pope was a cause of weakness too: in the ten years that is a pope's average reign, he could barely beat down one of the factions, and if, say, one pope had nearly destroyed the Colonna, another would come up hostile to the Orsini, who would revive the Colonna again — and yet would not live long enough to crush the Orsini in his turn. This is why the temporal power of the pope counted for so little in Italy.

Then came Alexander the Sixth, who showed better than any pontiff who ever lived what a pope with money and arms could do. Using Duke Valentino as his instrument and the French invasion as his occasion, he brought about everything I described above in discussing the duke's actions. His intention was to make the duke great, not the Church; but what he did made the Church great anyway, and after his death, and the duke's ruin, the Church inherited his labors.

Then came Alexander VI, who, of all the popes there have ever been, showed how far a pope could prevail with money and with arms. Using Duke Valentino as his instrument, and seizing on the entry of the French, he brought about all those things I described above in recounting the duke's actions. And although his aim was not to make the Church great but the duke, what he did told all the same to the Church's greatness — for after his death and the duke's ruin, the Church fell heir to all his labors.

Then came Pope Julius, and he found the Church strong: mistress of all the Romagna, the barons of Rome crushed, the factions beaten flat under Alexander's blows — and the road open to piling up money by methods never used before Alexander's time. Julius not only continued all this but improved on it. He set out to take Bologna, to snuff out the Venetians, and to drive the French from Italy; and every one of these enterprises succeeded, with the more credit to him because he did it all to strengthen the Church and no private man. He also kept the Orsini and Colonnesi factions within the bounds in which he found them; and though there were heads among them itching to make trouble, two things held them still: the greatness of the Church, which cowed them, and the fact that they were allowed no cardinals of their own — the origin of all their disorders. These factions will never be quiet while they have cardinals, because cardinals feed the factions, in Rome and beyond, and the barons are forced to defend them: from the ambitions of prelates come the discords and tumults of the barons. So His Holiness Pope Leo has found the papacy at the height of its power; and if others made it great with arms, one may hope that he, by his goodness and his infinite other virtues, will make it greater still, and revered.

Pope Julius came next, and found the Church strong: master of all the Romagna, with the barons of Rome reduced to impotence and their factions wiped out by Alexander's chastisements, and with the way open, as never before Alexander's time, to heap up money. Julius not only carried on what he found but improved upon it. He set out to take Bologna, to ruin the Venetians, and to drive the French out of Italy; and in all these enterprises he succeeded, and to his greater credit, since he did everything to strengthen the Church and no private man. He kept the Orsini and Colonna factions within the bounds in which he found them; and though there was still some appetite for trouble among them, two things held firm. One was the greatness of the Church, with which he overawed them; the other was his refusal to let them have cardinals of their own, for cardinals are the root of the disorders among them. Whenever these factions have their cardinals, they will not stay quiet for long, since cardinals foster the factions in Rome and outside it, and the barons are forced to back them — and so out of the ambitions of prelates spring the quarrels and tumults of the barons. For these reasons His Holiness Pope Leo has found the papacy at the height of its power; and it is to be hoped that, if his predecessors made it great by arms, he will make it greater still, and more revered, by his goodness and his countless other virtues.

sections.label: Chapter XII
sections.title: The Kinds of Troops, and Mercenaries
How Many Kinds of Soldiery There Are, and Concerning Mercenaries

segments.text: Having discussed one by one the kinds of principality I proposed at the outset, having considered in some measure why they do well or badly, and having shown the methods by which so many men have tried to win and hold them, it remains for me now to speak generally of the offense and defense that each of them may require.

Having dealt one by one with the kinds of principality I set out at the start to examine, and having weighed in some measure why one fares well and another badly, and shown the methods by which men have sought to win them and to hold them, it remains for me to discuss in general the means of attack and defense that belong to each.

I said above that a prince must have solid foundations under him, or he necessarily comes to ruin. The principal foundations of all states — new, old, or mixed — are good laws and good arms. And since there cannot be good laws where there are not good arms, and where there are good arms there are bound to be good laws, I will leave the laws aside and speak of arms.

We have seen already how necessary it is for a prince to have his foundations well laid; otherwise he is bound to come to ruin. The chief foundations of every state — new, old, or mixed — are good laws and good arms. And since there cannot be good laws where there are not good arms, and where there are good arms there are bound to be good laws, I will set the laws aside and speak of the arms.

I say, then, that the arms with which a prince defends his state are either his own, or they are mercenary, auxiliary, or mixed. Mercenaries and auxiliaries are useless and dangerous. If a man rests his state on mercenary arms, he will never stand firm or safe; for they are disunited, ambitious, undisciplined, disloyal — swaggering among friends, cowardly before the enemy; no fear of God, no faith with men. Your ruin is put off only as long as the assault is put off: in peace you are stripped by them, in war by the enemy. The reason is that they have no love for you, and no cause to keep them in the field beyond a little pay — which is not enough to make them want to die for you. They are delighted to be your soldiers while you are not making war; when war comes, they desert or run. It should cost me little effort to prove this, since the ruin of Italy has been caused by nothing else than her resting all her hopes, for so many years, on mercenary arms. They did once make headway for certain men, and they looked brave enough against one another; but when the foreigner came, they showed what they were. So it was that Charles, King of France, was allowed to take Italy with a piece of chalk; and the man who said our sins were the cause of it told the truth — only they were not the sins he meant, but the ones I have described. And since they were the sins of princes, it is the princes who have paid the penalty.

I say, then, that the arms with which a prince defends his state are either his own, or mercenary, or auxiliary, or a mixture of these. Mercenary and auxiliary arms are useless and dangerous; and any man who rests his state on mercenaries will never stand firm or safe. For they are disunited, ambitious, undisciplined, and faithless; brave among friends, cowardly among enemies; with no fear of God and no good faith toward men. Ruin is put off only for as long as the assault is put off; in peace you are robbed by them, in war by the enemy. The reason is that they have no love and no motive to keep the field beyond their scrap of pay, which is not enough to make them willing to die for you. They are glad to be your soldiers while you wage no war, but when war comes they either bolt or run from the foe. I should have little trouble proving this, for the ruin of Italy has been caused by nothing but her resting, for so many years, all her hopes on mercenaries. They did, it is true, make some showing for a time and looked brave enough among themselves; but when the foreigners came they showed what they were. So it was that Charles, King of France, was let seize Italy with chalk in hand. The man who said our sins were the cause of it spoke the truth — only they were not the sins he had in mind, but the ones I have described; and since they were the sins of princes, the princes too have paid the penalty.

I want to show the wretchedness of these arms more fully. Mercenary captains are either excellent soldiers or they are not. If they are, you cannot trust them: they will always be working toward greatness of their own, either by crushing you, their master, or by crushing others against your intent. And if the captain is no good, he ruins you in the ordinary way — by losing.

I want to show further how wretched these arms are. The mercenary captains are either able men or they are not. If they are, you cannot trust them, because they will always be reaching for their own greatness, either by crushing you, their own master, or by crushing others against your will. And if the captain is no soldier, he ruins you in the ordinary way.

If the answer is that anyone with arms in hand will act this way, mercenary or not, I reply: arms are wielded either by a prince or by a republic. The prince should go in person, and do the captain's job himself. The republic must send its own citizens; when it sends a man who proves worthless, it must replace him, and when it sends a good one, it must bind him with laws so that he does not overstep the mark. Experience shows princes acting alone, and republics armed with their own arms, making enormous progress, and mercenary arms doing nothing but damage. And a republic armed with its own arms is far harder to bring under the rule of one of its citizens than a republic armed with foreign arms. Rome and Sparta stood armed and free for centuries. The Swiss are the best-armed people alive, and the freest.

And if it is objected that any man under arms, mercenary or not, will do the same, I answer this: arms have to be wielded either by a prince or by a republic. The prince ought to go in person and serve as his own captain. The republic must send its own citizens; and when it sends one who does not prove himself, it should recall him, and when it sends a worthy one, it should bind him by the laws so that he cannot overstep his command. Experience shows that princes who stand alone, and republics under their own arms, make the greatest headway, while mercenary arms do nothing but harm; and a republic armed with its own arms is far harder to bring under the rule of one of its citizens than a republic armed with foreign arms. Rome and Sparta stood for ages armed and free. The Swiss are fully armed and entirely free.

As for ancient examples of mercenaries, there are the Carthaginians, who at the end of the first war with Rome were nearly crushed by their own mercenary soldiers, though the Carthaginians had their own citizens for captains. After the death of Epaminondas, the Thebans made Philip of Macedon captain of their forces; and after he had won, he took away their liberty.

For an example of mercenaries in ancient times, take the Carthaginians, who were nearly overthrown by their own hired soldiers after the first war with Rome, even though the Carthaginians had men of their own for captains. After the death of Epaminondas, the Thebans made Philip of Macedon captain of their army, and after the victory he stripped them of their freedom.

When Duke Filippo died, the Milanese hired Francesco Sforza against the Venetians. He beat the enemy at Caravaggio — and then joined with the enemy to crush the Milanese, his employers. Sforza his father, in the pay of Queen Johanna of Naples, abandoned her defenseless in a stroke, so that to save her kingdom she had to throw herself into the arms of the King of Aragon. And if the Venetians and the Florentines did once enlarge their dominions with such arms, and their captains did not make themselves princes but defended them, I answer that in this the Florentines were favored by chance. Of the able captains they had cause to fear, some did not win, some met opposition, and some turned their ambition elsewhere. The one who did not win was Giovanni Acuto; and since he did not win, his loyalty was never put to the proof — but everyone will grant that had he won, the Florentines stood at his discretion. Sforza always had the Bracceschi against him, and each kept watch on the other; Francesco turned his ambition on Lombardy, Braccio against the Church and the kingdom of Naples. But come to what happened only yesterday. The Florentines made Pagolo Vitelli their captain, a very shrewd man who from private life had risen to great renown. If he had taken Pisa, no one can deny that the Florentines would have been bound to him: had he gone over to their enemies, they had no defense, and so long as they kept him, they had to obey him. As for the Venetians, look at their record, and you will see that they acted safely and gloriously so long as they made war with their own men — this was before they turned to enterprises on land — when gentlemen and armed commoners together fought with the greatest virtù. The moment they began to fight on land, they abandoned this virtù and took up the customs of Italy. In the early days of their expansion on land, having little territory there and a great reputation, they had little to fear from their captains; but as they expanded — under Carmignuola — they got a taste of the mistake. They had seen how supremely able he was; under his command they had beaten the Duke of Milan. But they also saw how cold he had grown toward the war, and they judged that with him they could win no longer, because he had no wish to win; yet they could not dismiss him, or they would lose again what they had gained. So, to secure themselves against him, they were forced to murder him. Since then they have had for captains Bartolomeo da Bergamo, Roberto da San Severino, the count of Pitigliano, and the like — men under whom the fear was of loss, not the hope of gain; as happened later at Vaila, where in one day's battle they lost what eight hundred years of hard labor had won them. From these arms come conquests that are slow, late, and feeble; and losses that are sudden and astonishing.

When Duke Filippo died, the Milanese hired Francesco Sforza against the Venetians; and once he had beaten the enemy at Caravaggio, he joined with them to crush the Milanese, his own employers. His father, the elder Sforza, in the pay of Queen Giovanna of Naples, abandoned her without warning, so that to save her kingdom she was forced to throw herself into the arms of the King of Aragon. And if it is said that the Venetians and Florentines did once enlarge their dominions with such arms, and yet their captains did not make themselves princes but defended them faithfully, I answer that the Florentines in this were favored by luck. Of the able captains they might have had reason to fear, some did not win their wars, some met opposition, and others turned their ambition elsewhere. One who did not win was Giovanni Acuto — Sir John Hawkwood — and since he did not win, his loyalty was never put to the test; but everyone will admit that, had he won, the Florentines would have lain at his mercy. Sforza always had the Bracceschi against him, so the two watched each other in check: Francesco turned his ambition toward Lombardy, Braccio against the Church and the kingdom of Naples. But let us come to what happened only a little while ago. The Florentines made Paolo Vitelli their captain, a most shrewd man who had risen from private life to the highest renown. Had he taken Pisa, no one can deny the Florentines would have been bound to keep on his good side, for if he had gone over to their enemies they would have had no way to resist him, and if they held on to him they would have had to obey him. As for the Venetians, look at their record and you will see they acted safely and gloriously so long as they sent their own men to war — when, with their armed gentlemen and commoners, they fought bravely. This was before they turned to campaigns on land; once they began fighting on land, they abandoned that virtue and fell in with the custom of Italy. In the early stage of their expansion on land, having little territory and a great reputation, they had not much to fear from their captains. But as they expanded, under Carmagnola, they got a taste of their mistake. They had found him a most able commander — under him they had beaten the Duke of Milan — yet they also saw how lukewarm he had grown in the war, and they judged they would win no more under him. They were unwilling to let him go, and unable to, for fear of losing back what they had gained; so, to make themselves safe, they were driven to murder him. After him they had for captains Bartolomeo da Bergamo, Roberto da San Severino, the Count of Pitigliano, and the like — men under whom they had loss to dread and no gain to hope for, as duly happened later at Vailà, where in a single battle they lost what it had cost them eight hundred years of toil to win. For from such arms come only conquests that are slow, late, and slight, but losses that are sudden and staggering.

And since these examples have brought me to Italy, ruled now for many years by mercenary arms, I want to trace them from further back, so that once their origin and course are in view they can be better corrected. You must understand, then, how in recent times, as soon as the Empire began to be pushed out of Italy and the Pope gained more standing in temporal affairs, Italy broke up into more states. Many of the great cities took up arms against their nobles, who, favored by the emperor, had held them down, while the Church favored the cities to build its temporal power; and in many other cities, citizens rose to be princes. So Italy fell largely into the hands of the Church and of certain republics; and the Church being priests and the republics being citizens unaccustomed to arms, both began to hire foreigners.

And since these examples have brought me to Italy, which has been ruled for so many years by mercenaries, I want to take them up more seriously, so that, having traced their rise and progress, one may be better placed to set them right. You must understand that in recent times the empire has come to be cast off in Italy, that the Pope has gained more temporal power, and that Italy has been carved up into more states. The reason is that many of the great cities took up arms against their own nobles, who, once favored by the emperor, had been oppressing them, while the Church backed the cities to build up its own temporal authority; and in many others, private citizens became princes. So Italy fell largely into the hands of the Church and of republics; and since the Church is made up of priests and the republic of citizens unused to arms, both began to hire foreigners.

The first to give this soldiery a reputation was Alberigo da Conio, of the Romagna. From his school came, among others, Braccio and Sforza, who in their day were the arbiters of Italy. After them came all the other captains who down to our own times have commanded the arms of Italy — and the sum of all their virtù is that Italy has been overrun by Charles, plundered by Louis, violated by Ferdinand, and insulted by the Swiss. Their method was this: first, to raise their own standing, they destroyed the standing of the infantry. They did it because, having no state of their own and living off their trade, a few foot soldiers gave them no reputation and many were more than they could feed; so they kept to cavalry, where a manageable number could be both fed and honored. Matters came to the point where in an army of twenty thousand soldiers you would not find two thousand foot. Beyond this, they had used every device to spare themselves and their soldiers hardship and fear: in the skirmishes they did not kill one another, but took prisoners and freed them without ransom; they made no assault on towns by night, and the men in the towns made none on the camps; they built neither stockade nor ditch around their quarters; they did not campaign in winter. All of this their military code permitted, and all of it, as I have said, they invented to escape hardship and danger — until they had brought Italy to slavery and contempt.

The first to give this kind of soldiery a name was Alberigo da Conio, the Romagnol. Out of his school came, among others, Braccio and Sforza, who in their day were the arbiters of Italy. After them came all the other captains who down to our own time have directed the arms of Italy; and the upshot of all their prowess has been that she has been overrun by Charles, plundered by Louis, ravaged by Ferdinand, and disgraced by the Swiss. The first principle these captains followed was to take all credit from the infantry, to raise their own. They did this because, living on their pay and holding no territory of their own, they could not keep many men, and a handful of foot soldiers gave them no standing; so they took to cavalry, of which a manageable number kept them maintained and honored. Things came to such a pass that in an army of twenty thousand men there were not two thousand on foot. Beyond this, they had used every device to spare themselves and their soldiers hardship and danger, not killing one another in the fray but taking prisoners and releasing them without ransom. They would not attack towns by night, nor would the garrisons of the towns attack their camps by night; they ringed their camp with neither stockade nor ditch; they did not take the field in winter. All this their military rules allowed, and all of it was contrived, as I have said, to dodge effort and danger — and so they have led Italy into slavery and contempt.

sections.label: Chapter XIII
sections.title: Auxiliaries, Mixed Troops, and One's Own
Concerning Auxiliaries, Mixed Soldiery, and One's Own

segments.text: Auxiliaries — the other useless kind of arms — are what you have when you call in a powerful outsider to come with his forces to aid you and defend you, as Pope Julius did in recent memory. Having seen in the Ferrara campaign what a sorry showing his mercenaries made, he turned to auxiliaries, and arranged with Ferdinand, King of Spain, to help him with his men and armies. These arms can be useful and good in themselves, but for the man who calls them in they are almost always ruinous: if they lose, you are undone; if they win, you are their prisoner.

Auxiliaries are the other useless kind of arms. You take them on when you call in some power to come with its own forces to aid and defend you, as Pope Julius did not long ago: having had poor proof of his mercenaries in the campaign against Ferrara, he turned to auxiliaries and struck a bargain with Ferdinand, King of Spain, for help in men and arms. Such arms may be useful and good in themselves, but for the man who calls them in they are always a danger. For if you lose, you are undone; and if you win, you are their prisoner.

Ancient histories are full of such examples, but I will stay with this fresh one of Pope Julius the Second, whose choice could hardly have been less considered: to get Ferrara, he put himself entirely into a foreigner's hands. Only his good fortune brought forth a third outcome, so that he did not reap the fruit of his bad choice. His auxiliaries were routed at Ravenna; then the Swiss rose up and — against every expectation, his own and everyone else's — chased out the victors. So he ended prisoner neither of his enemies, who had fled, nor of his auxiliaries, since the winning had been done by arms other than theirs.

Ancient history is full of examples, but I will not pass over this recent one of Pope Julius II, whose recklessness could not be plainer. In his eagerness to get Ferrara, he threw himself wholly into the hands of a foreigner. But his good luck brought on a third turn of events, so that he did not reap the fruit of his rash choice. For when his auxiliaries were routed at Ravenna, and the Swiss then rose up and drove out the victors — against all expectation, his and everyone else's — it came about that he fell prisoner neither to his enemies, who had fled, nor to his auxiliaries, since he had won by other arms than theirs.
The Florentines, having no arms at all of their own, brought ten thousand Frenchmen to take Pisa; and by that policy they ran more danger than at any other moment of their troubles.
The Florentines, entirely without arms of their own, sent ten thousand Frenchmen to take Pisa, and by doing so ran more danger than at any other point in all their troubles.

The Emperor of Constantinople, to oppose his neighbors, put ten thousand Turks into Greece; and when the war was over, they would not leave. That was the beginning of Greece's servitude to the infidel.

The Emperor of Constantinople, to stand against his neighbors, sent ten thousand Turks into Greece, who, once the war was over, would not leave; and that was the beginning of the enslavement of Greece to the infidels.

So: the man who wants to make sure he cannot win should use these arms. They are far more dangerous than mercenaries, because with them the ruin comes ready-made: they are all one body, and all obedient to someone other than you. Mercenaries, even once they have won, need more time and a better opening to hurt you: they are not one body, and you raised them and you pay them; the outsider you set at their head cannot at once take enough authority to do you damage. In short — with mercenaries the deadliest thing is their cowardice; with auxiliaries, their virtù. Wise princes have therefore always shunned these arms and turned to their own, and have preferred to lose with their own men rather than win with another's, judging no victory real that is won with borrowed arms.

So let the man who has no wish to conquer make use of these arms, for they are far more hazardous than mercenaries. With auxiliaries the ruin is ready-made: they are all united, and all trained to obey someone else. With mercenaries, even after they have won, more time and a better opening are needed before they can do you harm, since they are not all of one body, and they are found and paid by you — and a man you have set at their head cannot, all at once, take on enough authority to injure you. In short, with mercenaries the danger is their cowardice; with auxiliaries, their courage. So the wise prince has always shunned these arms and turned to his own, choosing rather to lose with his own men than to win with the others, since he counts no true victory one that is won with the arms of others.

I will never hesitate to cite Cesare Borgia and his actions. This duke entered the Romagna with auxiliary arms, bringing in nothing but French soldiers, and with them he took Imola and Forli. When those arms then struck him as unsafe, he turned to mercenaries, judging the danger there smaller, and hired the Orsini and the Vitelli. Finding these, in the handling, doubtful, disloyal, and dangerous, he destroyed them, and turned to his own men. And the difference between these kinds of arms is easily seen by considering the difference in the duke's reputation when he had the French, when he had the Orsini and Vitelli, and when he stood on his own soldiers and on himself. His reputation grew at every step; and he was never rated so high as when everyone saw that he was complete master of his own forces.

I will never hold back from citing Cesare Borgia and what he did. This duke entered the Romagna with auxiliaries, bringing nothing but French soldiers, and with them he took Imola and Forlì. But when those forces came to seem unreliable to him, he turned to mercenaries, judging them less of a risk, and hired the Orsini and the Vitelli. Then, finding these doubtful, faithless, and dangerous as he handled them, he destroyed them and fell back on his own men. And the difference between one kind of force and the other is easily seen if you weigh how the duke's standing differed when he had only the French, when he had the Orsini and Vitelli, and when he relied on his own soldiers and his own strength: his reputation always rose, and he was never held in higher esteem than when everyone saw that he was complete master of his own forces.

I meant not to go beyond Italian and recent examples, but I am unwilling to leave out Hiero the Syracusan, since he is one of those I named above. Made head of the army by the Syracusans, as I said, he saw at once that mercenary soldiery was useless — its captains were built just like our Italian condottieri. And concluding that he could neither keep them nor let them go, he had them all cut to pieces; after which he made war with his own arms, and not with anyone else's.

I meant to keep to Italian and recent examples, but I will not leave out Hiero of Syracuse, since he is one of those I named earlier. This man, as I have said, was made head of the army by the Syracusans, and soon found that mercenary soldiery — made up the way our Italian condottieri are — was good for nothing. Judging that he could neither keep them nor safely let them go, he had them all cut to pieces, and afterward made war with his own forces and not with hired men.

I want to recall, too, a figure from the Old Testament made for this subject. When David offered himself to Saul to go and fight Goliath, the Philistine champion, Saul, to give him heart, dressed him in his own armor — and David, once he had it on, refused it, saying he could not give a true account of himself in it: he would meet the enemy with his sling and his knife. In the end, the armor of others falls off your back, or weighs you down, or binds you tight.

I want to call to mind, too, an instance from the Old Testament that bears on this. When David offered himself to Saul to fight Goliath, the Philistine champion, Saul, to give him heart, armed him with his own armor. But David, once he had it on his back, refused it, saying he could make no use of it, and that he would rather meet the enemy with his sling and his knife. In short, another man's armor either slips off your back, or weighs you down, or binds you fast.

Charles the Seventh, father of King Louis the Eleventh, having freed France from the English by his fortune and his virtù, understood this necessity of arming himself with his own arms, and set up in his kingdom the ordinances of the men-at-arms and the infantry. Then his son King Louis abolished the infantry and began to hire the Swiss — a mistake which, followed by others, is now plainly seen to be the source of that kingdom's dangers. For by raising the reputation of the Swiss, he degraded all his own arms: the infantry he wiped out altogether, and his men-at-arms he made dependent on the arms of others, since, being accustomed to fight alongside the Swiss, they no longer believe they can win without them. Hence the French are not enough against the Swiss, and without the Swiss they do not attempt much against anyone else. The armies of France, then, have been mixed — part mercenary, part her own; arms which, taken together, are much better than pure auxiliaries or pure mercenaries, and much inferior to one's own. The example already given is enough: the kingdom of France would be unbeatable today if the ordinance of Charles had been enlarged, or even kept.

Charles the Seventh, father of King Louis the Eleventh, having by good luck and skill freed France from the English, saw the necessity of arming himself with forces of his own, and set up in his kingdom ordinances for men-at-arms and infantry. Afterward his son, King Louis, did away with the infantry and began hiring the Swiss — a blunder that, followed by others, is now plainly a source of peril to that kingdom. For by raising the standing of the Swiss he has wholly lowered the worth of his own arms: he scrapped the infantry altogether, and tied his men-at-arms to others, since, being so used to fighting alongside the Swiss, they no longer think they can win without them. And so the French cannot hold their ground against the Swiss, and without the Swiss they come off badly against anyone else. The armies of France have thus become mixed, part mercenary and part their own — a combination far better than mercenaries alone or auxiliaries alone, but far worse than forces wholly one's own. And this example proves it: France would be unconquerable if the ordinance of Charles had been built upon and kept up.

But the small wisdom of men will begin a thing that tastes good at the time and never notice the poison underneath — as I said earlier about wasting fevers. The ruler of a principality who does not recognize evils at their birth is not truly wise; and that is given to few. And if you look for the first cause of the ruin of the Roman Empire, you will find it was nothing but the hiring of the Goths: from that beginning the strength of the Roman Empire started to slacken, and all the virtù that drained out of it was handed to them.

But man's scant wisdom, going into a thing that looks well at first, cannot make out the poison hidden in it — as I said before of wasting fevers. So the man who rules a principality and cannot recognize troubles until they are upon him is not truly wise; and this insight is given to few. And if you trace the first disaster of the Roman Empire, you will find it began precisely with the hiring of the Goths; for from that point the vigor of the Roman Empire started to fail, and all the prowess that had built it up drained away to others.

I conclude, then, that no principality is secure without arms of its own; it is instead wholly dependent on fortune, having no virtù to defend it faithfully in adversity. And it was ever the opinion and verdict of wise men that nothing is so weak or so unstable as a reputation for power that does not rest on strength of one's own. And one's own arms are those composed of subjects, or of citizens, or of dependents of yours: all others are mercenary or auxiliary. The way to organize your own arms is easily found if you go back over the arrangements of the four men I have named, and if you see how Philip, father of Alexander the Great, and how many republics and princes have armed and ordered themselves. To their methods I defer entirely.

I conclude, then, that no principality is secure without its own arms — on the contrary, it rests wholly on fortune, having no prowess of its own to defend it in adversity. It has always been the opinion and judgment of wise men that nothing is so weak and unstable as a reputation for power that is not founded on a power of one's own. And one's own arms are those made up of subjects, citizens, or your own dependents; all the rest are mercenary or auxiliary. The way to make ready arms of one's own will be easily found if you reflect on the rules I have set down, and consider how Philip, the father of Alexander the Great, and many republics and princes have armed and organized themselves — to which rules I wholly commit myself.

sections.label: Chapter XIV
sections.title: The Prince and the Art of War
A Prince's Duty Concerning Military Affairs

segments.text: A prince, then, should have no other object, no other thought, and take nothing else for his craft, but war, its rules, and its discipline; for that is the only art expected of the man who commands. And it is an art of such virtù that it not only keeps in place those who were born princes, but many times lifts men from private station to that rank — while the reverse is also on record: princes who thought more of luxury than of arms have lost their states. The first thing that loses you your state is neglect of this art; the thing that wins you a state is mastery of it. Francesco Sforza, because he was armed, rose from private citizen to Duke of Milan; his sons, because they fled the hardships of arms, sank from dukes to private citizens. For among the other evils that being unarmed brings you, it makes you despised — one of those disgraces, as will be said below, that a prince must guard against. Between an armed man and an unarmed man there is no proportion at all; and it is not reasonable that the armed should obey the unarmed willingly, or that the unarmed should be safe among armed servants. With disdain on one side and suspicion on the other, they cannot work well together. So a prince who understands nothing of war, beyond the other miseries already mentioned, cannot be respected by his soldiers, and cannot trust them. He should never, therefore, lift his thoughts from the exercise of war; and he should exercise it harder in peace than in war. He can do this in two ways: with action, and with the mind.

A prince should have no other aim or thought, nor take up anything else for his study, but war and its organization and discipline; for this is the one art expected of a man who rules. It is of such force that it not only keeps in power those born princes, but often raises men from private station to that rank. And the reverse is just as plainly seen: when princes have given more thought to their comfort than to arms, they have lost their states. The first cause of losing a state is neglecting this art; and the thing that wins you one is being its master. Francesco Sforza, because he was armed, rose from a private man to Duke of Milan; his sons, because they shirked the hardships of arms, sank from dukes to private men. For among the other evils that being unarmed brings you, it makes you despised — and contempt is one of those disgraces a prince must guard himself against, as I will show further on. Between an armed man and an unarmed one there is no proportion whatever; it stands to no reason that the armed man should willingly obey the unarmed, or that the unarmed should be safe among armed servants. There is scorn on the one side and suspicion on the other, and the two can never work well together. So a prince who knows nothing of war, on top of the other misfortunes already named, cannot be respected by his soldiers, nor can he trust them. He should therefore never let this subject of war out of his thoughts, and in peace he should train at it harder than in war itself. This he can do in two ways: by action and by study.

As for action: besides keeping his men well ordered and well drilled, he should live in the hunt, hardening his body to exertion and learning the nature of ground as he goes — how the mountains rise, how the valleys open, how the plains lie; what the rivers and marshes are like — and in this he should take the greatest care. The knowledge pays twice. First, he learns to know his own country, and can better see how to defend it. Second, by knowing that terrain and having it under his feet, he grasps with ease any new terrain he must scout; for the hills, valleys, plains, rivers, and marshes of Tuscany, say, bear a certain resemblance to those of other provinces, so that from knowing the ground of one province you come easily to know the ground of others. And the prince who lacks this skill lacks the first quality a captain must have; for it is what teaches you to find your enemy, choose your quarters, lead armies, order a battle, and lay siege to towns with the advantage on your side.

As for action, above all he should keep his men well organized and drilled, and never stop hunting, by which he hardens his body to hardship and at the same time learns the lie of the land — how the mountains rise, how the valleys open out, how the plains lie — and comes to understand the nature of rivers and marshes, giving all of this his closest attention. This knowledge is useful two ways. First, he comes to know his own country, and is the better able to defend it. Then, through the knowledge and observation he has of one place, he grasps any other he may need to study with ease; for the hills, valleys, plains, rivers, and marshes of Tuscany, say, have a certain likeness to those of other regions, so that from knowing the terrain of one country one passes easily to knowing others. The prince who lacks this skill lacks the first thing a commander needs, for it is what teaches him to surprise the enemy, choose his ground, lead his army, draw up the line of battle, and lay siege to towns to his advantage.

Philopoemen, prince of the Achaeans, among the praises writers have given him, is praised for this: that in peacetime he never thought about anything but the ways of war. When he was in the country with friends, he would often stop and reason with them: "If the enemy were on that hill and we stood here with our army, which of us would have the advantage? How could we go at them, keeping formation? If we wanted to retreat, how would we manage it? If they retreated, how should we pursue?" And as he went he would set before them every chance that can befall an army; he heard their opinions, gave his own, and backed it with reasons — so that, through this endless rehearsal, no accident could ever arise, with his armies in the field, for which he did not have the remedy.

Philopoemen, prince of the Achaeans, among the other praises writers have heaped on him, is commended for this: that in time of peace he thought of nothing but the conduct of war. When he was out in the country with friends he would often stop and reason with them — "If the enemy were on that hill, and we stood here with our army, which of us would have the advantage? How could we advance on him in good order? If we wanted to retreat, how should we go about it? If he retreated, how should we give chase?" And as they went along he would put to them every contingency that can befall an army; he would hear their view and give his own, backing it with reasons. So from this constant turning of cases over, no situation could ever arise in war that he had not already met and could not handle.

As for exercising the mind, the prince should read histories, and study in them the actions of excellent men: see how they carried themselves in war; examine the causes of their victories and their defeats, so as to flee the one and imitate the other; and above all, do as some excellent man before him has done — take as his model some earlier man who was praised and glorified, and keep that man's deeds and actions always by him, as Alexander the Great is said to have imitated Achilles; Caesar, Alexander; Scipio, Cyrus. And whoever reads the life of Cyrus written by Xenophon will then recognize, in the life of Scipio, how much glory that imitation earned him, and how closely, in chastity, affability, humanity, and generosity, Scipio kept to what Xenophon wrote of Cyrus. Such are the ways a wise prince must observe; and he should never stand idle in peaceful times, but work in them industriously to build up capital he can draw on in adversity — so that when fortune turns, she finds him ready to resist her.

But as for the exercise of the mind, the prince should read histories, and there study the deeds of great men: see how they bore themselves in their wars, examine the causes of their victories and defeats, so as to avoid the one and copy the other. Above all he should do as some great man has done before him, who took as his model one who had been praised and held glorious before his own time, and kept that man's bearing and conduct always before him — as it is said Alexander the Great imitated Achilles, Caesar imitated Alexander, and Scipio imitated Cyrus. And anyone who reads the life of Cyrus written by Xenophon will see, in the life of Scipio, how much that imitation made his glory, and how closely in self-command, courtesy, humanity, and generosity Scipio kept to the things Xenophon wrote of Cyrus. A wise prince should hold to ways like these, and never sit idle in times of peace, but make capital of them by his own diligence, so that he may draw on it in adversity — so that when fortune turns, it finds him ready to withstand her.

sections.label: Chapter XV
sections.title: What Princes Are Praised or Blamed For
Concerning Things for Which Men, and Especially Princes, Are Praised or Blamed

segments.text: It remains now to see what the conduct and bearing of a prince ought to be toward his subjects and his friends. And because I know that many have written on this, I fear that in writing on it too I will be thought presumptuous — the more so because in treating the matter I depart from the paths laid down by others. But since my intention is to write something useful to whoever understands it, it has seemed to me more fitting to go straight after the effectual truth of the thing than after the imagination of it. Many have imagined republics and principalities that no one has ever seen or known to exist in the world as it is; for the way men live is so far from the way men ought to live that whoever lets go of what is done for what ought to be done learns his ruin sooner than his preservation. A man who insists on being good in everything must come to ruin among so many who are not good.

It remains now to see how a prince ought to conduct himself toward his subjects and his friends. And since I know that many have written on this, I am afraid that in writing of it again I shall be thought presumptuous, the more so because I depart, in discussing it, from the methods of the others. But as my intention is to write something useful to anyone who grasps it, it has seemed to me more to the point to go after the effectual truth of the matter than the imagination of it. For many have pictured republics and principalities that were never seen or known to exist in fact; because how one lives is so far removed from how one ought to live, that the man who lets go of what is done for what ought to be done sooner learns his ruin than his preservation. For a man who sets out to act the good man in every way must come to grief among so many who are not good.

So it is necessary for a prince who wants to keep his state to learn how not to be good, and to use that knowledge, or not use it, as necessity requires. Setting aside, then, the things imagined about a prince, and speaking of the things that are true, I say that all men, whenever they are spoken of — and princes most of all, being set so high — are marked with some one of those qualities that draw blame or praise. One is held generous, another a miser — I use the Tuscan word, since in our tongue an avaricious man is still one who craves to get by plunder, while we call a miser the man who holds back too hard from using what is his own; one is a giver, another grasping; one cruel, another merciful; one a breaker of faith, another a keeper of it; one effeminate and cowardly, another fierce and full of spirit; one humane, another haughty; one lecherous, another chaste; one straightforward, another sly; one hard, another easygoing; one grave, another frivolous; one religious, another unbelieving; and so on. And I know that everyone will admit it would be a most praiseworthy thing for a prince to possess, of all the qualities named above, the ones held to be good. But since they cannot all be had, nor all wholly practiced — the conditions of human life do not allow it — a prince must be prudent enough to know how to escape the infamy of those vices that would take his state from him, and to guard, if he can, against the vices that would not; and if he cannot, he may let those go with less concern. And further, he must not care about incurring infamy for vices without which the state can hardly be saved; because, when everything is weighed, he will find some things that look like virtue and would be his ruin if he followed them, and others that look like vice and bring him, if he follows them, his security and his well-being.

And so a prince who means to hold his own must learn how not to be good, and to use this or not use it according to necessity. Setting aside, then, the imaginary things said of a prince, and speaking of those that are true, I say that all men, when they are talked of — and princes most of all, being set higher — are noted for some of those qualities that earn them either blame or praise. One is held to be liberal, another miserly (to use a Tuscan term, since in our language an avaricious man is one who wants to get hold of things by plunder, while we call a man miserly who holds back too much from the use of his own); one is reckoned a giver, another grasping; one cruel, another merciful; one a breaker of faith, another faithful; one soft and cowardly, another fierce and bold; one humane, another proud; one lecherous, another chaste; one straight, another sly; one hard, another easy; one grave, another frivolous; one religious, another unbelieving, and so on.

And I know that everyone will admit it would be a most praiseworthy thing for a prince to be found possessed of all the qualities reckoned good in the list above. But because they cannot all be had, nor wholly kept to, since the human condition does not allow it, he must be prudent enough to know how to escape the disgrace of those vices that would lose him his state, and to guard himself, if he can, against those that would not; and where he cannot, he may give himself up to them with less scruple. And further, he need not trouble himself about incurring the disgrace of those vices without which he could scarcely save his state; for if the whole thing is weighed carefully, something will be found that looks like virtue, and following it would be his ruin, while something else that looks like vice, followed, brings him security and well-being.

sections.label: Chapter XVI
sections.title: Generosity and Miserliness
Concerning Liberality and Meanness

segments.text: Beginning, then, with the first of the qualities named above, I say that it would be good to be thought generous. Nevertheless, generosity practiced in such a way that you get the name for it does you harm; for if it is practiced virtuously, and as it ought to be practiced, it will not be known, and you will not escape the infamy of its opposite. And so a man who wants to keep up the name of generous among men cannot leave out any kind of lavish display; a prince of that sort will consume his whole substance in such displays, and in the end, if he wants to keep the name of generous, he will be forced to burden his people beyond measure, to squeeze them with taxes, and to do everything that can be done to raise money. This will begin to make him hateful to his subjects and, as he grows poor, little regarded by anyone; so that, having offended the many with this generosity of his and rewarded the few, he feels the first pinch of trouble and totters at the first real danger; and when he recognizes this and tries to pull back, he runs at once into the infamy of a miser.

Beginning, then, with the first of the qualities named above, I say that it would be a fine thing to be reckoned generous. Yet generosity practiced in a way that wins you no name for it does you harm; for if you practice it honestly, as it ought to be practiced, it goes unseen, and you will not escape the reproach of its opposite. And so anyone who wants to keep up a name for generosity among men is forced to spare no extravagance of display — until a prince of this bent has poured out his whole fortune on such things, and is driven in the end, if he means to hold on to the name, to grind his people with heavy taxes, to squeeze them, and to do everything possible to lay his hands on money. This quickly makes him hateful to his subjects, and as he grows poor he is held cheap by everyone. So that, having with his generosity injured the many and rewarded the few, he feels the first trouble that comes, and is endangered by the first hazard. And when he sees this and tries to draw back, he runs at once into the reproach of being mean.

A prince, then, since he cannot practice this virtue of generosity in a way that is recognized without hurting himself, ought, if he is prudent, not to mind being called a miser. With time he will be thought more and more generous, once men see that his thrift makes his revenues sufficient, that he can defend himself against whoever makes war on him, and that he can undertake campaigns without burdening his people — so that he ends up practicing generosity toward all those from whom he takes nothing, who are countless, and miserliness toward all those to whom he gives nothing, who are few.

Since, then, a prince cannot practice this generosity in a way that gets him the name for it without harming himself, he ought, if he is wise, not to mind being called mean. For with time he will come to be reckoned the more generous, once it is seen that through his thrift his revenues are enough, that he can defend himself against any who make war on him, and that he can undertake campaigns without burdening his people. In this way he comes to be generous toward all those from whom he takes nothing, who are countless, and mean toward all those to whom he gives nothing, who are few.

In our times we have not seen great things done except by those who were held miserly; the rest were wiped out. Pope Julius the Second, though he made use of a name for generosity to reach the papacy, did not try to keep it afterward, because he wanted to be able to make war on the King of France; and he waged all his wars without laying any extraordinary tax on his subjects, because his long thrift covered the extra expense. The present King of Spain, if he had been held generous, would not have undertaken or won so many campaigns. A prince, then, so long as he does not have to rob his subjects, can defend himself, is not forced into poverty and contempt, and is not driven to become rapacious, ought to count the name of miser for little, since it is one of the vices that make his rule possible.

In our own day we have seen great things done only by those who were reckoned mean; the rest have come to nothing. Pope Julius the Second made use of a name for generosity to reach the papacy, but once there he made no effort to keep it up, since he meant to make war on the King of France; and he waged many wars without laying a single extra tax on his people, because his long thrift met the added cost. The present King of Spain could never have undertaken so many enterprises, nor carried them through, had he been reckoned generous. A prince, therefore, so long as it spares him from robbing his subjects, lets him defend himself, keeps him from poverty and contempt, and saves him from turning rapacious, ought to think little of incurring the name of mean; for this is one of the vices that let him rule.

And if someone says: Caesar rose to empire through his generosity, and many others have reached the highest ranks because they were generous and were held to be so — I answer: either you are already a prince, or you are on the way to becoming one. In the first case this generosity is harmful; in the second it is quite necessary to be thought generous. And Caesar was one of those trying to reach the rule of Rome; but if, after reaching it, he had lived on and had not moderated his spending, he would have destroyed that empire. And if someone replies: many who were held most generous have been princes and have done great things with their armies — I answer: a prince spends either what is his own and his subjects', or what belongs to others. In the first case he ought to be sparing; in the second he ought not to leave out any part of generosity. For the prince who marches with his armies, living on plunder, sack, and ransom, is handling other men's property, and there this openhandedness is necessary — without it his soldiers would not follow him. With what is not yours or your subjects' you can be a freer giver, as Cyrus, Caesar, and Alexander were; for spending what belongs to others takes away none of your reputation but adds to it; only spending your own hurts you.

And if anyone should say: Caesar came to power by generosity, and many others, by being generous and reckoned so, have risen to the highest places — I answer: either you are already a prince, or you are on the way to becoming one. In the first case this generosity is harmful; in the second it is quite necessary to be reckoned generous. And Caesar was one of those who meant to reach the height of power in Rome; but had he lived on after reaching it, and not reined in his spending, he would have ruined his rule. And should anyone reply that there have been many princes, reckoned most generous, who have done great things with their armies — I answer: a prince spends either what is his own and his subjects', or what belongs to others. In the first case he should be sparing; in the second he should let no chance for generosity go by. For the prince who marches out with his army, living off plunder, sacking, and ransom, handling what belongs to others, must be generous, or his soldiers will not follow him. With what is neither yours nor your subjects' you can be a free giver, as Cyrus, Caesar, and Alexander were; for squandering what belongs to others takes nothing from your good name but adds to it — it is only squandering your own that does you harm.

And there is nothing that consumes itself the way generosity does: while you practice it, you lose the power to practice it, and you become either poor and despised or, to escape poverty, rapacious and hated. And among all the things a prince must guard against is being despised and hated — and generosity leads you to both. So it is wiser to keep the name of miser, which breeds an infamy without hatred, than, by straining after the name of generous, to be forced into the name of rapacious, which breeds an infamy with hatred.

And there is nothing that consumes itself like generosity: even as you practice it you lose the means to practice it, and you become either poor and despised, or, to escape poverty, rapacious and hated. And of all things a prince must guard against being despised and hated; generosity leads you to both. So there is more wisdom in accepting a name for meanness, which breeds reproach without hatred, than in courting a name for generosity and being driven into a name for rapacity, which breeds reproach with hatred.

sections.label: Chapter XVII
sections.title: Cruelty and Mercy: Loved or Feared
Concerning Cruelty and Mercy, and Whether It Is Better to Be Loved Than Feared

segments.text: Coming now to the other qualities named before, I say that every prince ought to want to be held merciful and not cruel; nevertheless, he must take care not to use this mercy badly. Cesare Borgia was held cruel; and yet that cruelty of his mended the Romagna, united it, and brought it back to peace and loyalty. Looked at closely, he will be seen to have been far more merciful than the Florentine people, who, to escape a name for cruelty, let Pistoia be destroyed. A prince, then, ought not to mind the infamy of cruelty when it keeps his subjects united and loyal; for with a very few exemplary punishments he will be more merciful than those who, out of too much mercy, let disorders run on until they end in killings and plunder — for these hurt a whole community, while the executions that come from a prince hurt only a single man.

Coming now to the other qualities I named above, I say that every prince ought to wish to be thought merciful and not cruel. Yet he must take care not to misuse that mercy. Cesare Borgia was reckoned cruel; all the same, his cruelty set the Romagna in order, united it, and brought it back to peace and obedience. Weigh that rightly, and he will be seen to have been far more merciful than the Florentine people, who, to escape the name of cruelty, let Pistoia be torn apart. A prince, then, so long as he keeps his subjects united and loyal, should not mind the reproach of cruelty; for with a very few exemplary punishments he will prove more merciful than those who, out of too much mercy, let disorders run on, and so let murder and robbery follow — for these injure the whole people, while the executions that come from the prince fall only on one man at a time.

And of all princes, it is the new prince who cannot escape the name of cruel, since new states are full of dangers. Hence Virgil, through Dido's mouth, excuses the inhumanity of her rule by the fact that it was new, saying:

And of all princes, the new prince can least of all escape the name of cruel, since new states are full of dangers. So Virgil, through the mouth of Dido, excuses the harshness of her rule on the ground that it is new: "Hard circumstance, and the newness of my reign, force me to do such things, and to guard my borders far and wide." Even so, the prince should not be quick to believe a charge or to act on it, nor go in fear of his own shadow; he should move with measure, prudence, and humanity, so that too much trust does not make him careless and too much suspicion does not make him unbearable.
Res dura, et regni novitas me talia cogunt moliri, et late fines custode tueri.

From this a question arises: whether it is better to be loved than feared, or feared than loved. The answer is that one would wish to be both; but since it is hard to join the two in one man, it is much safer to be feared than loved, if one of the two must be given up. For this can be said of men in general: that they are ungrateful, fickle, false, cowards in the face of danger, and greedy for gain. While you serve their turn they are wholly yours — they will offer you their blood, their goods, their lives, and their children, as I said before, when the need is far off; but when it draws near, they turn against you. And the prince who has built entirely on their word, and made no other preparation, is ruined; for friendships bought with money, and not won by greatness and nobility of spirit, are earned but never owned, and in the hour of need there is no spending them. Men have less hesitation in wronging one who makes himself loved than one who makes himself feared, because love is held by a bond of obligation, which, men being the wretched creatures they are, is broken the moment it serves their own advantage; but fear is held by a dread of punishment that never lets go.
Hard necessity, and the newness of my kingdom, force me to such measures — to guard my borders far and wide with sentries.

Still, the prince should make himself feared in such a way that, if he wins no love, he at least escapes hatred; for to be feared and not hated go very well together, and he will always manage it so long as he keeps his hands off the property of his citizens and subjects, and off their women. And if he must shed someone's blood, let him do it only where there is fitting justification and a plain cause; but above all let him keep his hands off other men's property, for men sooner forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony. Besides, pretexts for seizing a man's goods are never lacking, and one who begins to live by plunder will always find excuses to take what belongs to others; whereas reasons for taking life are rarer, and run out sooner.

Nevertheless, he should be slow to believe and slow to act, and should not conjure fears for himself; he should proceed in a temperate way, with prudence and humanity, so that too much confidence does not make him incautious and too much distrust does not make him unbearable.

But when the prince is at the head of his army, with a great mass of soldiers under his command, then it is altogether necessary that he not mind the name of cruel; for without that name no army was ever kept united or fit for its work. Among the marvels told of Hannibal is this: that having led an enormous army, made up of countless different races, to fight in foreign lands, no quarrel ever broke out among them, nor any against their commander, in his bad fortune or his good. This came from nothing but his inhuman cruelty, which, together with his boundless prowess, made him at once revered and dreaded in his soldiers' eyes; and without that cruelty, his other qualities would not have sufficed to do it. Writers who see only one side admire his deeds and then condemn the very thing that made them possible.

From this a dispute arises: whether it is better to be loved than feared, or the reverse. The answer is that one would want to be both; but since it is hard to combine them, it is much safer to be feared than loved, if one of the two must be given up. For this can be said of men generally: they are ungrateful, fickle, pretenders and dissemblers, quick to run from danger, greedy for gain; and while you are doing them good they are entirely yours — they offer you their blood, their property, their lives, their children, as I said above, so long as the need is far off; but when it comes near, they turn away. And the prince who has rested entirely on their words, and finds himself bare of other preparations, is ruined; for friendships bought at a price, and not with greatness and nobility of spirit, are paid for but not owned, and at the moment of need they cannot be spent. And men have less hesitation about harming one who makes himself loved than one who makes himself feared; for love is held by a chain of obligation which, men being wretched, is broken at every turn of their own advantage; but fear is held by a dread of punishment that never lets you go.

That his other qualities would not have been enough is proven by the case of Scipio — a man without equal not only in his own age but in all recorded memory — whose armies in Spain nevertheless rebelled against him. The whole cause was his too great leniency, which gave his soldiers more license than military discipline allows. Fabius Maximus rebuked him for it in the Senate, and called him the corrupter of the Roman soldiery. The people of Locri had been laid waste by one of Scipio's lieutenants, and he neither avenged them nor punished the man's insolence — all out of that easy nature of his; so that someone in the Senate, seeking to excuse him, said there were many men who knew better how to avoid faults of their own than to correct them in others. Given time and a free hand, this temper would have stained Scipio's fame and glory; but living under the control of the Senate, the flaw was not only hidden but turned to his honor.

Nevertheless, a prince should make himself feared in such a way that, if he does not win love, he escapes hatred; for being feared and not being hated go together very well. And he will always manage this if he keeps his hands off the property of his citizens and his subjects, and off their women. And when he does have to proceed against someone's life, he should do it where there is proper justification and manifest cause; but above all he must keep off other men's property, for men forget the death of a father more quickly than the loss of a patrimony. Besides, pretexts for taking property are never lacking: a man who begins to live by plunder will always find a reason to seize what belongs to someone else; whereas reasons for taking a life are rarer, and give out sooner. But when a prince is with his armies and has a multitude of soldiers under his command, then it is absolutely necessary not to care about the name of cruel, for without that name no army was ever kept united or fit for any action.

Among Hannibal's admirable actions this one is counted: that though he led an enormous army, a mixture of countless races of men, to fight in foreign lands, no dissension ever arose in it — not among the men, and not against their leader — in bad fortune or in good. This could come from nothing but his inhuman cruelty, which, together with his boundless virtù, made him always revered and terrible in his soldiers' eyes; and without it, his other virtù would not have been enough to produce that effect. Writers who have thought about this too little admire his achievement on the one hand and condemn its chief cause on the other. And that his other virtù would not have sufficed can be seen in Scipio — a man of the rarest kind, not only in his own times but in the whole memory of human affairs — whose armies mutinied against him in Spain. That came from nothing but his excessive leniency, which had given his soldiers more license than fits military discipline. Fabius Maximus threw it in his face in the Senate and called him the corrupter of the Roman soldiery. The Locrians, after one of Scipio's legates had wrecked them, went unavenged by him, and the legate's insolence went uncorrected — all of it born of that easy nature of his; so that when someone in the Senate wanted to excuse him, he said there were many men who knew better how to avoid erring themselves than how to correct the errors of others. In time that nature would have stained Scipio's fame and glory, had he kept command long enough; but living under the government of the Senate, this damaging quality of his not only stayed hidden but brought him glory.

I conclude, then, returning to being feared and loved: since men love at their own pleasure and fear at the pleasure of the prince, a wise prince should build on what is his own, not on what belongs to others; he must only contrive to escape hatred, as was said.

To return, then, to the question of being feared or loved, I conclude that, since men love at their own pleasure but fear at the prince's, a wise prince should build on what is his own and not on what belongs to others — taking care only, as I have said, to avoid being hated.

sections.label: Chapter XVIII
sections.title: How Princes Should Keep Their Word
How Princes Should Keep Faith

segments.text: Everyone understands how praiseworthy it is in a prince to keep his word and to live with integrity and not by cunning. Nevertheless, experience in our own times shows that the princes who have done great things are the ones who have held their word cheap, who have known how to run rings around men's wits with cunning — and in the end they have beaten the ones who founded themselves on honesty. You must know, then, that there are two ways of fighting: one with laws, the other with force. The first is proper to man, the second to beasts; but because the first is often not enough, one must have recourse to the second. So a prince needs to know how to use both the beast and the man well. This point was taught to princes under cover by the ancient writers, who tell how Achilles and many other princes of antiquity were given to Chiron the centaur to be raised and brought up under his discipline. Having a half-beast, half-man for a teacher means nothing else than this: a prince needs to know how to use both natures, and the one does not last without the other. Since a prince is forced, then, to know how to use the beast well, he should pick from among the beasts the fox and the lion; for the lion cannot defend himself from snares, and the fox cannot defend himself from wolves. So one must be a fox to recognize the snares, and a lion to frighten off the wolves. Those who stand simply on the lion do not understand their business. A prudent lord, therefore, cannot keep his word — and should not — when keeping it works against him and when the reasons that made him promise are gone. If men were all good, this precept would not be good; but because they are wretched, and would not keep their word to you, you need not keep yours to them. Nor has a prince ever lacked legitimate grounds with which to color over his breach of faith. Of this one could give countless modern examples, and show how many peace treaties and how many promises have been made void and empty by the faithlessness of princes; and the one who has known best how to use the fox has come out best.

Everyone understands how praiseworthy it is for a prince to keep faith and to live with integrity rather than by cunning. Yet experience in our own time shows that the princes who have done great things have made little account of keeping faith, and have known how to twist men's minds by craft; and in the end they have got the better of those who built on honest dealing.

But this nature has to be painted over well: one must be a great pretender and dissembler. And men are so simple, and so obedient to the necessities of the moment, that the deceiver will always find someone willing to be deceived. Of recent examples I will not keep silent about one. Alexander the Sixth never did anything else, never thought about anything else, than deceiving men, and he always found subjects it could be done to. Never was there a man with greater force in asserting a thing, or who affirmed it with heavier oaths and kept it less; and yet his deceptions always came off exactly as he wished, because he knew this side of the world so well.

You must understand, then, that there are two ways of fighting: one by law, the other by force. The first is the way proper to men, the second to beasts; but since the first is often not enough, a prince must know how to fall back on the second. So a prince must know how to make use of both the beast and the man. The ancient writers taught this to princes in a veiled way, when they told how Achilles and many other princes of old were given over to the centaur Chiron to be raised and schooled in his discipline. To have for a tutor one who was half beast and half man means simply this: that a prince must know how to use both natures, and that the one without the other does not last.

A prince, then, need not actually have all the qualities listed above, but he very much needs to appear to have them. Indeed, I will dare to say this: that having them and observing them always is harmful, and appearing to have them is useful — to appear merciful, faithful, humane, upright, religious, and to be so; but with your mind so built that, if you need not to be so, you can and do know how to change into the contrary.

Since a prince is forced, then, to know how to use the beast, he should take as his models the fox and the lion; for the lion cannot defend itself against traps, and the fox cannot defend itself against wolves. So one must be a fox to recognize the traps, and a lion to frighten off the wolves. Those who rely simply on the lion do not understand their business. A wise lord, therefore, cannot and should not keep faith when keeping it works against him, and when the reasons that made him give his word are gone. If all men were good, this rule would be bad; but since they are wicked, and would not keep faith with you, you are not bound to keep it with them. Nor will a prince ever lack legitimate reasons to dress up his broken word. Of this one could give countless modern examples, showing how many treaties and promises have been made void and empty by the bad faith of princes — and the man who has best known how to play the fox has come off best.

And this has to be understood: a prince, and especially a new prince, cannot observe all the things for which men are called good, since to maintain his state he is often forced to act against faith, against charity, against humanity, against religion. So he needs a mind ready to turn as the winds of fortune and the shifting of things command him; and, as I said above, not to depart from good while he can, but to know how to enter into evil when he has to.

But you must know how to disguise this nature well, and to be a great pretender and dissembler. Men are so simple, and so bound by the needs of the moment, that anyone who sets out to deceive will always find someone willing to be deceived. I will not pass over one recent example. Alexander VI did nothing else, thought of nothing else, but how to deceive men, and he always found someone to take in; for no man ever affirmed a thing with stronger assurances, or swore to it with greater oaths, and kept it less. Yet his deceptions always came off exactly as he wished, because he understood this side of the world so well.

A prince must therefore take great care that nothing ever falls from his mouth that is not full of the five qualities named above, so that to see him and hear him he seems all mercy, all faith, all integrity, all humanity, all religion. And nothing is more necessary to appear to have than this last quality. Men in general judge more by the eye than by the hand; for everyone gets to see you, few get to touch you. Everyone sees what you appear to be; few feel what you are, and those few do not dare set themselves against the opinion of the many, who have the majesty of the state defending them. And in the actions of all men, and most of all of princes, where there is no court of appeal, one looks to the outcome.

It is unnecessary, then, for a prince to have all the good qualities I have listed, but very necessary that he should seem to have them.
