I will dare to say this too: that to have them and always to observe them is harmful, while to seem to have them is useful — to seem merciful, faithful, humane, upright, and devout, and to be so; yet to keep your mind so disposed that, when the need arises not to be so, you can turn to the opposite and know how to do it.

So let a prince win and hold his state: the means will always be judged honorable, and everyone will praise them; because the crowd is taken by appearances and by the way a thing comes out — and in the world there is no one but the crowd; the few find no footing when the many have something to lean on.

A prince must understand that he cannot observe all the things for which men are accounted good, since to keep his state he is often forced to act against good faith, against charity, against humanity, against religion. He needs a mind ready to shift as the winds of fortune and the changing of circumstances command, and, as I said above, not to depart from the good while he can, but to know how to enter into evil when forced to it.

A certain prince of the present time, whom it is better not to name, never preaches anything but peace and good faith, and he is the bitterest enemy of both; and if he had ever observed either one, it would more than once have cost him his reputation or his state.

A prince should take great care, then, that nothing ever leaves his mouth that is not full of those five qualities, so that to see and hear him he should seem all mercy, all faith, all integrity, all humanity, all religion. And nothing is more necessary to seem to have than this last quality. Men in general judge more by the eye than by the hand, for everyone can see, but few can touch. Everyone sees what you seem to be; few feel what you are; and those few dare not stand against the opinion of the many, who have the majesty of the state to back them. And in the actions of all men, and above all of princes, where there is no court of appeal, one judges by the result.

So let a prince set himself to win and hold his state: the means will always be judged honorable, and praised by everyone. For the common run of men are always taken by appearances and by how things turn out, and the world is made of nothing but the common run; the few find no room there while the many have something to stand on.

A certain prince of our own day, whom it is not well to name, preaches nothing but peace and good faith, and is the bitter enemy of both; and had he kept either one, it would have cost him his reputation or his state, many times over.

sections.label: Chapter XIX
sections.title: Avoiding Contempt and Hatred
That One Should Avoid Being Despised and Hated

segments.text: Now that I have spoken of the most important of the qualities mentioned above, I want to run briefly through the others under this general heading: that the prince should attend, as was partly said above, to avoiding the things that make him hated or held in contempt. Whenever he avoids these, he will have done his part, and he will find no danger at all in his other bad names.

Having now spoken of the most important of the qualities I listed above, I want to run through the rest more briefly, under this single heading: that the prince must take care, as I have partly said already, to avoid whatever would make him hated or despised. As long as he manages that, he has done his part, and need fear no danger from any other failings men may charge him with.

What makes him hated above everything, as I said, is to be rapacious — a usurper of the property and the women of his subjects. From these he must keep away: whenever you take neither property nor honor from the generality of men, they live content, and you have only to contend with the ambition of the few, which can be checked easily, and in many ways.

What makes a prince hated above all is to be rapacious — to lay hands on the property of his subjects and on their women. From both of these he must keep his hands off. So long as you take neither a man's goods nor his honor, the great mass of men live content, and you have only the ambition of a few to contend with, and that can be checked easily enough, in any number of ways.

What makes him contemptible is to be held changeable, frivolous, effeminate, faint-hearted, irresolute. A prince must guard against these as a ship guards against a reef, and contrive that in his actions men recognize greatness, spirit, gravity, and strength; and concerning the private dealings of his subjects, he should insist that his sentence be irrevocable, and keep up such an opinion of himself that no one thinks of deceiving him or getting around him.

What makes a prince despised is to be thought fickle, frivolous, soft, cowardly, or irresolute. From these a prince should guard himself as a sailor guards against a reef, and should so conduct himself that his every action shows greatness, courage, gravity, and strength. In the private business of his subjects he should hold to the rule that his judgments are final, and keep up such a reputation that no one dreams of deceiving him or maneuvering around him.

The prince who gives this impression of himself stands in high repute, and against a man of such repute conspiracy is difficult, and attack is difficult, so long as it is understood that he is excellent and revered by his own people. For a prince must have two fears: one inside, on account of his subjects; one outside, on account of foreign powers. From the outside he defends himself with good arms and good allies — and if he has good arms he will always have good allies. And things inside will always stand firm when things outside stand firm, unless a conspiracy has already disturbed them; and even if the outside does move against him, if he has ordered himself and lived as I have said, and does not lose heart, he will withstand every assault — as I said Nabis the Spartan did.

The prince who projects such a figure of himself stands high in men's regard, and a man held in high regard is hard to conspire against and hard to attack, provided it is known that he is a man of worth and revered by his people. For a prince has two things to fear: one from within, on the part of his subjects; the other from without, on the part of foreign powers. Against the danger from abroad he defends himself with good arms and good allies — and a man with good arms will never lack good allies. And as long as things stand firm abroad, they will stay quiet at home as well, unless they have already been thrown into disorder by some conspiracy; and even if trouble comes from abroad, a prince who has armed and ordered himself as I have said, and does not lose his nerve, will hold out against any assault, just as Nabis the Spartan did.

But as for his subjects, when things outside are quiet, his fear is that they may conspire in secret. From this the prince secures himself well enough by escaping hatred and contempt and keeping the people satisfied with him — which it is necessary to accomplish, as was said above at length. And among the most powerful remedies a prince has against conspiracies is precisely this: not being hated by the people at large. For whoever conspires always believes the prince's death will please the people; when he believes it will offend them, he cannot screw up the courage for such a course, because the difficulties on the conspirators' side are infinite. Experience shows that conspiracies have been many, and few have ended well. For a conspirator cannot act alone, and he can take companions only from those he believes discontented; and the moment you open your mind to a discontented man, you give him the means to content himself, since by informing on you he can hope for every kind of reward. Seeing sure gain on that side, and on the other nothing but doubt and danger, he must be either a rare friend to you, or an utterly implacable enemy of the prince, to keep faith with you.

As for his subjects, when nothing is stirring abroad his only fear is that they will conspire against him in secret. Against this the prince makes himself secure by avoiding being hated and despised and by keeping the people satisfied with him — which, as I argued at length above, he must above all contrive to do. One of the most effective safeguards a prince can have against conspiracies is simply not to be hated by the people at large; for the man who plots against a prince always expects that killing him will please the people. When instead he sees that his act will outrage them, he loses the heart to go through with it, since the obstacles facing a conspirator are endless. Experience shows that conspiracies have been many, but few have come to a good end. For a man cannot conspire alone, and the only confederates he can find are men he believes to be discontented — and the moment you open your mind to a discontented man, you hand him the means to make himself content, since by betraying you he stands to gain everything. Seeing sure profit on the one side, and on the other only danger and doubt, he must be a rare friend indeed, or a stubborn enemy of the prince beyond all reason, to keep faith with you.

And to put the thing briefly, I say that on the conspirator's side there is nothing but fear, jealousy, and the prospect of punishment, which terrifies him; but on the prince's side there is the majesty of the principality, the laws, the protection of friends and of the state, all defending him. Add to these the goodwill of the people, and it is impossible that anyone should be reckless enough to conspire. For where a conspirator ordinarily has cause to fear before the execution of his crime, in this case he must fear afterward as well — having the people for his enemy once the deed is done — and for that reason he can hope for no refuge anywhere.

To put the matter briefly: on the conspirator's side there is nothing but fear, suspicion, and the dread of punishment to hold him back; on the prince's side stand the majesty of his office, the laws, the protection of his friends, and the whole apparatus of the state to defend him. Add to all this the goodwill of the people, and it becomes impossible that any man should be so rash as to conspire. For where a conspirator ordinarily has to fear only up to the moment he strikes, here he has to fear afterward as well — for once the deed is done he has the people for his enemy, and can look for no refuge anywhere.

On this subject one could give endless examples, but I will content myself with one, which happened within the memory of our fathers. Messer Annibale Bentivogli, grandfather of the present Messer Annibale, was prince in Bologna, and the Canneschi, conspiring against him, murdered him; no one of his line remained except Messer Giovanni, then in swaddling clothes. The moment the murder was done, the people rose up and killed all the Canneschi. This came from the goodwill the house of Bentivogli enjoyed among the people in those days — a goodwill so great that, with Annibale dead and no one of the house left in Bologna who could rule the state, the Bolognese, having word that in Florence there was a man of Bentivogli blood who until then had passed for a blacksmith's son, went to Florence to find him and gave him the government of their city; and it was governed by him until Messer Giovanni came of age to rule.

Endless examples could be given on this head, but I will be content with one, brought to pass within the memory of our fathers. Messer Annibale Bentivogli, prince of Bologna and grandfather of the present Annibale, was murdered by the Canneschi, who had conspired against him, leaving no survivor of his house but Messer Giovanni, then still a child. The instant Annibale was assassinated the people rose and slaughtered every one of the Canneschi. This came of the goodwill the house of Bentivogli enjoyed among the Bolognese in those days, a goodwill so great that, although no Bentivogli remained in Bologna who could take up the government after Annibale's death, the people, learning that there was a man of that blood in Florence — until then thought to be the son of a blacksmith — sent for him and put the rule of their city into his hands; and he held it until Messer Giovanni came of age to govern.

I conclude, then, that a prince should take little account of conspiracies when the people are well disposed toward him; but when the people are his enemy and hold him in hatred, he must fear everything and everyone. And well-ordered states and wise princes have taken every care not to drive the great to desperation, and to keep the people satisfied and content: for this is one of the most important matters a prince has.

I conclude, then, that a prince need give little thought to conspiracies so long as the people are well disposed toward him; but when the people are hostile and bear him hatred, he has reason to fear everything and everyone. Well-ordered states and wise princes have always been at great pains not to drive the nobles to despair, and to keep the people satisfied and content — for this is among the most important tasks a prince has.

Among the well-ordered and well-governed kingdoms of our times is France, and in it one finds countless good institutions on which the liberty and security of the king depend. The first of these is the Parlement — the high court — and its authority. For the man who ordered that kingdom, knowing the ambition of the powerful and their insolence, judged that they needed a bit in their mouths to hold them; and knowing on the other side the hatred, rooted in fear, that the people at large bear toward the great, and wanting to reassure them, he did not wish this to be the particular charge of the king — so as to spare him the blame he would get from the great for favoring the people, and from the people for favoring the great. So he set up a third judge, to be the one who, without any burden falling on the king, would beat down the great and favor the small. There could be no better or more prudent arrangement, nor a greater cause of the security of the king and the kingdom. From this one can draw another notable rule: that princes should have unpopular duties administered by others, and hand out the favors themselves. And again I conclude that a prince should value the great, but not make himself hated by the people.

Among the best-ordered and best-governed kingdoms of our day is France, which has within it many good institutions on which the king's freedom and security depend. The first of these is the parlement and its authority. For the man who founded that kingdom, knowing the ambition of the nobles and their insolence, judged that they needed a bit in their mouths to hold them in; and on the other side, knowing the hatred of the people for the nobles, rooted in fear, he wished to protect the people — yet he did not want this to be the particular business of the king. So, to spare the king the resentment he would draw from the nobles for favoring the people, and from the people for favoring the nobles, he set up a third party as arbiter, to beat down the great and uphold the lesser without any blame falling on the king. No arrangement could be wiser or better, none a surer source of safety for the king and his kingdom. From this we can draw another lesson worth noting: that a prince should leave the dealing out of unpopular measures to others, and keep the dispensing of favors in his own hands. And again I conclude that a prince should value the nobles, but never so as to make himself hated by the people.

Perhaps it will seem to some, looking at the lives and deaths of certain Roman emperors, that they are examples contrary to this opinion of mine — men who lived excellently throughout and showed great virtù of spirit, and nevertheless lost the empire, or were killed by their own men conspiring against them. Wishing to answer this objection, I will take up the qualities of some of the emperors, showing that the causes of their ruin were no different from the ones I have set out; and along the way I will put forward the things worth noting for anyone who reads the affairs of those times.

To some, who have studied the lives and deaths of the Roman emperors, it may seem that many of them stand as examples against my argument: for there were emperors who lived nobly and showed great strength of soul, yet lost their empire, or were killed by their own subjects conspiring against them. To answer this objection, I will examine the characters of several of these emperors and show that the causes of their ruin were no different from those I have laid out; and along the way I will draw attention to whatever is worth the notice of anyone who studies the history of those times.

It will be enough to take all the emperors who succeeded to the empire from Marcus the philosopher down to Maximinus: these were Marcus, his son Commodus, Pertinax, Julianus, Severus, his son Antoninus Caracalla, Macrinus, Heliogabalus, Alexander, and Maximinus.

It will be enough to take all the emperors who came to power from Marcus the philosopher down to Maximinus: Marcus and his son Commodus; Pertinax; Julian; Severus and his son Antoninus Caracalla; Macrinus; Heliogabalus; Alexander; and Maximinus.

And first it is to be noted that, where in other principalities one has only to contend with the ambition of the great and the insolence of the people, the Roman emperors had a third difficulty: they had to bear with the cruelty and greed of the soldiers. This was so hard a thing that it caused the ruin of many, since it was difficult to satisfy the soldiers and the people at once. The people loved quiet, and for that reason loved unassuming princes; the soldiers loved a prince of military spirit — insolent, cruel, and rapacious — and wanted him to practice those qualities on the people, so that they could double their pay and vent their own greed and cruelty. The result was that the emperors who did not have, by nature or by art, a reputation great enough to hold both in check always came to ruin; and most of them, especially those who came to the principate as new men, once they recognized the difficulty of these two opposed humors, turned to satisfying the soldiers, counting it a small thing to injure the people. That choice was necessary: since princes cannot avoid being hated by somebody, they are bound first to try not to be hated by any whole class of their subjects; and when they cannot manage that, they must contrive with every effort to escape the hatred of the classes that are most powerful. And so those emperors who, being new men, had need of extraordinary support held to the soldiers rather than to the people — which turned out useful to them or not according to whether the prince knew how to keep his reputation up with the troops.

The first thing to note is this. In other principalities a ruler has only to contend with the ambition of the nobles and the insolence of the people; but the Roman emperors faced a third difficulty — they had to bear with the cruelty and greed of their soldiers. It was so hard a thing to satisfy both the soldiers and the people at once that it was the ruin of many of them. For the people wanted peace, and so loved a quiet, unambitious prince, while the soldiers wanted a prince who was warlike — bold, cruel, and rapacious — and wanted him to be all of these things toward the people, so that they could draw double pay and give free rein to their own greed and cruelty. The result was that any emperor who, whether by his birth or his own nature, lacked the standing to keep both in check was always brought down. Most of them, and especially those who came new to the throne, recognized how hard it was to reconcile these two opposing appetites, and chose to satisfy the soldiers, caring little how much they injured the people. This was a necessary choice. Since a prince cannot help being hated by someone, his first aim must be to avoid being hated by everyone; and when he cannot manage that, he must take all possible care at least to escape the hatred of the most powerful. So the emperors who, being new, had special need of support leaned toward the soldiers rather than the people — though whether this served them well or badly depended on whether the prince knew how to keep his authority over the soldiers.

From these causes it followed that Marcus, Pertinax, and Alexander — all men of modest life, lovers of justice, enemies of cruelty, humane, and kind — all, except Marcus, came to a sad end. Marcus alone lived and died with the highest honor, because he succeeded to the empire by hereditary right and did not have to acknowledge it as a gift of either the soldiers or the people; and then, being furnished with many virtù that made him revered, he held both orders within their bounds as long as he lived, and was never hated or despised.

From these causes it came about that Marcus, Pertinax, and Alexander — all men of modest life, lovers of justice, enemies of cruelty, humane and kindly — all came to a sad end, except Marcus. Marcus alone lived and died honored, because he came to the throne by hereditary right and owed it to neither the soldiers nor the people; and being besides a man of many qualities that won him reverence, he held both orders in their place all his life, and was never either hated or despised.

But Pertinax was made emperor against the will of the soldiers, who, being used to living licentiously under Commodus, could not stand the honest life Pertinax wanted to bring them back to; and having thus made himself hated — and with the hatred came contempt, for he was old — he was ruined at the very start of his administration. And here it must be noted that hatred is earned by good deeds as much as by bad ones; and so, as I said above, a prince who wants to hold his state is often forced not to be good. For when the body you judge you need in order to maintain yourself — the people, the soldiers, or the great — is corrupt, you must follow its humor to satisfy it, and then good deeds are your enemy.

Pertinax, by contrast, was made emperor against the will of the soldiers, who, used to living without restraint under Commodus, could not endure the honest discipline he tried to impose on them. So he made himself hated, and to that hatred was added contempt for his old age, and he was overthrown at the very outset of his reign. Here it is worth noting that hatred is earned by good deeds as readily as by bad ones. This is why a prince who means to keep his state is often forced to be other than good: when the body of men he judges he needs to maintain himself — be it the people, the soldiers, or the nobles — is corrupt, he must humor their appetites and gratify them, and then good deeds are his undoing.

But let us come to Alexander. He was of such goodness that among the praises given him is this: in the fourteen years he held the empire, no one was ever put to death by him without trial. Nevertheless, being held effeminate — a man who let himself be ruled by his mother — he fell into contempt for it, and the army conspired against him and killed him.

But let us come to Alexander, a man of such goodness that, among the other praises given him, this is recorded: in the fourteen years he held the empire he never put a man to death without trial. Yet because he was thought soft and a man who let himself be governed by his mother, he fell into contempt, the army conspired against him, and he was killed.

Turning now to the opposite qualities of Commodus, Severus, Antoninus Caracalla, and Maximinus: you will find them utterly cruel and utterly rapacious — men who, to satisfy their soldiers, spared the people no kind of injury. And all of them, except Severus, came to a bad end. For in Severus there was so much virtù that, by keeping the soldiers his friends, he could always reign happily even while the people were being crushed by him; his virtù made him so remarkable in the eyes of soldiers and people alike that the people stood, in a manner, dazed and stunned before him, and the soldiers reverent and satisfied. And because his actions were great, and notable in a new prince, I want to show briefly how well he knew how to play the fox and the lion — the two natures I said above a prince must imitate.

Turning now to the opposite sort — Commodus, Severus, Antoninus Caracalla, and Maximinus — you will find them all cruel and rapacious, men who, to satisfy their soldiers, spared the people no kind of injury; and all of them came to a bad end except Severus. In Severus there was such prowess that, by keeping the soldiers his friends, he reigned successfully to the end, even though the people were ground down under him; for his prowess made him so admired in the eyes of soldiers and people alike that the people were left in a kind of astonished awe, and the soldiers reverent and content. And because his actions, in a new prince, were great ones, I want to show briefly how well he knew how to play the part of the fox and the lion — the two natures a prince must imitate, as I said above.

Julianus the emperor being known for his slackness, Severus persuaded the army he commanded in Slavonia that it would be right to march on Rome and avenge the death of Pertinax, whom the praetorian soldiers had killed. Under that pretext, and without showing any appetite for the empire, he moved his army against Rome, and was in Italy before his departure was even known. When he reached Rome, the Senate, out of fear, elected him emperor, and Julianus was killed. After this beginning, two obstacles remained if Severus was to master the whole state: one in Asia, where Niger, commander of the Asian armies, had had himself proclaimed emperor; the other in the west, where Albinus also aspired to the empire. And because he judged it dangerous to declare himself the enemy of both, he decided to attack Niger and deceive Albinus. To Albinus he wrote that, having been elected emperor by the Senate, he wished to share that dignity with him; he sent him the title of Caesar and had the Senate take him on as colleague — all of which Albinus accepted as true. But once Severus had defeated and killed Niger and pacified the East, he returned to Rome and complained in the Senate that Albinus, unmindful of the benefits received from him, had treacherously sought to kill him, and that he was therefore obliged to go and punish his ingratitude. He then went to find him in France, and stripped him of his state and his life. Whoever examines this man's actions in detail, then, will find a most ferocious lion and a most cunning fox; will find him feared and revered by everyone, and not hated by his armies; and will not marvel that he, a new man, was able to hold so great an empire — for his enormous reputation defended him always from the hatred the people might have conceived for his plunderings.

Knowing the sloth of the Emperor Julian, Severus persuaded the army he commanded in Slavonia that it would be right to march on Rome and avenge the death of Pertinax, who had been killed by the praetorian guard. Under this pretext, without seeming to reach for the throne, he moved the army on Rome and was in Italy before anyone knew he had set out. On his arrival the Senate, in fear, elected him emperor and put Julian to death. After this Severus, who meant to make himself master of the whole empire, faced two obstacles: one in Asia, where Niger, head of the eastern armies, had had himself proclaimed emperor; the other in the west, where Albinus likewise aspired to the throne. Judging it dangerous to declare himself the enemy of both at once, he resolved to attack Niger and to deceive Albinus. To Albinus he wrote that, having been elected emperor by the Senate, he wished to share that dignity with him; he sent him the title of Caesar, and had the Senate make Albinus his colleague — all of which Albinus took for the truth. But once Severus had beaten and killed Niger and pacified the East, he returned to Rome and complained to the Senate that Albinus, with no gratitude for the favors he had received, had treacherously tried to murder him, and that this ingratitude forced him to punish the man. He then went after him in France, and stripped him of his command and his life. Anyone who studies this man's actions closely will find him a most ferocious lion and a most cunning fox; he will find him feared and revered by everyone and not hated by the armies; and it is no wonder that he, a new man, could hold so great an empire, for his immense reputation always shielded him from the hatred his rapacity might otherwise have stirred in the people.

But his son Antoninus was also a man of the most excellent parts, which made him marvelous in the sight of the people and welcome to the soldiers: he was a military man, able to bear every hardship, contemptuous of every delicate food and every other softness, and this made all the armies love him. Nevertheless, his ferocity and cruelty were so great and so unheard of — after countless individual killings, he had put to death a great part of the people of Rome and all the people of Alexandria — that he became hateful to the whole world and began to be feared even by those he kept around him; and he was killed by a centurion in the middle of his own army. Here it is to be noted that deaths like this one, which follow from the deliberate resolve of an unshakable mind, are impossible for princes to avoid, since anyone who does not care about dying can strike the blow; but a prince may fear them less, because they are very rare. He must only keep from doing grave injury to any of those who serve him and whom he keeps close around him in the service of the state. Antoninus had not: he had shamefully killed a brother of that centurion, and threatened the man himself every day, yet kept him in his bodyguard — a reckless course, fit to ruin him, and so it did.

His son Antoninus was also a man of fine parts, with qualities that made him a marvel in the eyes of the people and welcome to the soldiers: he was a warrior who bore hardship tirelessly and scorned all dainty food and soft living, which made the armies love him. Yet his ferocity and cruelty were so great and so unheard of — after countless single murders he put to death a great part of the people of Rome, and all the people of Alexandria — that he became hated by the whole world, and feared even by those about him, until at last he was killed by a centurion in the midst of his own army. Here it is worth noting that such deaths — dealt by a man of fixed and desperate resolve — cannot be guarded against by any prince, since anyone willing to die himself can carry them out; but a prince need fear them the less because they are very rare. He has only to take care to do no grave wrong to those he employs or keeps about him in the service of his state. Antoninus failed in this: he had put to death, with insult, a brother of that very centurion, and threatened the centurion himself daily, yet kept him on in his bodyguard — a reckless thing to do, as it proved, for it was the ruin of him.

But let us come to Commodus, who could have held the empire with great ease, since as the son of Marcus he had it by inheritance; he had only to walk in his father's footsteps, and he would have satisfied soldiers and people alike. But being of a cruel and bestial spirit, in order to practice his rapacity on the people he set about indulging the armies and making them licentious; and on the other side, by not keeping up his own dignity — going down into the arenas again and again to fight with the gladiators, and doing other things utterly vile and unworthy of the imperial majesty — he became contemptible in the sight of the soldiers. Hated on the one side and despised on the other, he was conspired against and killed.

But let us come to Commodus, who could very easily have held the empire, since, being the son of Marcus, he had it by inheritance, and had only to walk in his father's footsteps to keep both the people and the soldiers content. Yet being by nature cruel and brutal, he set himself to gratify the soldiers and corrupt them, the better to indulge his rapacity upon the people; and on the other hand he threw away his dignity, going down again and again into the arena to fight gladiators and doing other base things, beneath the imperial majesty, until he became contemptible in the eyes of the soldiers. Hated by the one party and despised by the other, he was conspired against and killed.

It remains to tell the qualities of Maximinus. He was a most warlike man; and the armies, disgusted with the softness of Alexander, whom I have discussed above, killed him and elected Maximinus to the empire. He did not keep it long, for two things made him hated and despised: one, that his origin was of the basest — he had once herded sheep in Thrace, a fact known everywhere, which lowered him enormously in every eye; the other, that at the start of his reign he put off going to Rome to take possession of the imperial seat, and meanwhile earned a name for the utmost ferocity, having through his prefects, in Rome and everywhere else in the empire, carried out many cruelties. So the whole world was stirred at once with disdain for the meanness of his blood and with hatred born of fear of his savagery; and first Africa rebelled, then the Senate with the whole people of Rome, and then all Italy conspired against him. His own army joined them: laying siege to Aquileia and finding it hard to take, disgusted with his cruelty, and fearing him less when they saw how many enemies he had, they killed him.

It remains to speak of Maximinus. He was a thoroughly warlike man, and the armies, sick of the softness of Alexander, of whom I have already spoken, killed Alexander and raised Maximinus to the throne. He did not hold it long, for two things made him both hated and despised: the first, the lowness of his origin — he had once kept sheep in Thrace, a thing known to everyone and counted a great disgrace; the second, that on coming to power he put off going to Rome to take possession of the imperial seat. He had also earned a name for extreme ferocity through the many cruelties carried out in his name by his prefects, in Rome and elsewhere in the empire. So the whole world, stirred to scorn at the meanness of his birth and to fear at his savagery, turned against him: first Africa revolted; then the Senate with all the people of Rome; then all Italy conspired against him; and to these was added his own army, which, while besieging Aquileia and finding it hard to take, grew weary of his cruelties and, fearing him the less now that they saw so many ranged against him, murdered him.

Of Heliogabalus, Macrinus, and Julianus I will not speak: being wholly contemptible, they were snuffed out at once. I will come instead to the close of this discourse. The princes of our own times suffer far less from this difficulty of giving the soldiers extraordinary satisfaction in their governments; for though some consideration must still be shown them, the thing is soon settled, since none of these princes keeps standing armies grown old together in the government and administration of provinces, as the armies of the Roman empire were. If it was then necessary to satisfy the soldiers before the people, it was because the soldiers could do more than the people; now it is necessary for all princes, except the Turk and the Sultan of Egypt, to satisfy the people before the soldiers, because the people can do more than they can.

I will not trouble to discuss Heliogabalus, Macrinus, or Julian, who were so utterly contemptible that they were swept away at once. I will instead bring this discourse to a close by saying that the princes of our own day are far less troubled by this need to satisfy their soldiers by extraordinary measures. They must still give them some consideration, but the matter is soon settled, for none of these princes keep standing armies grown old in the government and administration of provinces, as the armies of the Roman empire were. And whereas in those times it was more necessary to satisfy the soldiers than the people, because the soldiers were the more powerful, now the reverse is true: for all princes — except the Turk and the Sultan of Egypt — it is more necessary to satisfy the people than the soldiers, because today the people are the more powerful.

I make an exception of the Turk, because he always keeps about him twelve thousand foot soldiers and fifteen thousand horse, on whom the security and strength of his kingdom depend; and it is necessary for that lord to keep them his friends, setting every other consideration of the people aside. The kingdom of the Sultan of Egypt is similar: being entirely in the hands of the soldiers, he too must keep them his friends, without regard for the people. And note that this state of the Sultan is unlike all other principalities: it resembles the Christian pontificate, which cannot be called a hereditary principality or a new principality. For it is not the sons of the old prince who inherit and remain lords, but the man raised to that rank by those who have the authority to elect him, the sons remaining noblemen only; and since this order is ancient, the state cannot be called a new principality. None of the difficulties of new ones are found in it: for though the prince is new, the orders of the state are old, and arranged to receive him as if he were their hereditary lord.

I except the Turk, who keeps always about him twelve thousand foot and fifteen thousand horse, on whom the security and strength of his kingdom depend; and so he must keep these troops his friends, setting every other consideration aside. The kingdom of the Sultan of Egypt is similar: lying wholly in the hands of soldiers, it too requires its ruler to keep them his friends, with no regard for the people. But note that the Sultan's state is unlike all other principalities, for it resembles the Christian papacy, which can be called neither a hereditary nor a new principality: it is not the dead ruler's sons who inherit, but the man elected to the office by those who have the right to elect, while the sons remain mere noblemen. And since this is an ancient practice, it cannot be called a new principality, for it has none of the difficulties that new ones bring: though the prince is new, the institutions of the state are old, and are framed to receive him as though he were their hereditary lord.

But let us return to our subject. I say that whoever considers the discourse written above will see that either hatred or contempt was the cause of the ruin of the emperors named; and he will also see how it happened that, some proceeding one way and some the contrary way, in each group one man ended happily and the rest unhappily. For Pertinax and Alexander, being new princes, it was useless and harmful to want to imitate Marcus, who stood in the principate by hereditary right; and likewise for Caracalla, Commodus, and Maximinus it was fatal to imitate Severus, since they did not have virtù enough to follow in his footsteps. So a new prince in a new principality cannot imitate the actions of Marcus, and yet has no need to follow those of Severus; rather, he should take from Severus the parts necessary to found his state, and from Marcus the parts fitting and glorious for preserving a state already established and firm.

But to return to my subject, I say that anyone who weighs what I have set out will see that either hatred or contempt was the ruin of the emperors named above, and will understand too why it was that, some of them taking one course and some the opposite, in each group only one came to a happy end and the rest to unhappy ones. For Pertinax and Alexander, being new princes, it was useless and indeed dangerous to imitate Marcus, who held the empire by inheritance; and likewise for Caracalla, Commodus, and Maximinus it was fatal to imitate Severus, since they had not the prowess to follow in his steps. Therefore a new prince, new to his principality, cannot imitate the actions of Marcus, nor again does he need to follow those of Severus. He should take from Severus those things necessary for founding his state, and from Marcus those that are fitting and glorious for preserving a state already settled and secure.

sections.label: Chapter XX
sections.title: Fortresses and Other Expedients
Whether Fortresses and Many Other Things to Which Princes Often Resort Are Useful or Harmful

segments.text: Some princes, in order to hold their states securely, have disarmed their subjects; some have kept their subject towns divided; some have fed enmities against themselves; some have set out to win over the men they suspected at the start of their rule; some have built fortresses; some have torn them down and destroyed them. And though no fixed judgment can be passed on any of this without coming to the particulars of the state where such a decision would have to be taken, nevertheless I will speak in the broad way the matter itself allows.

To hold their state securely, some princes have disarmed their subjects; others have kept their subject towns divided by faction; others have deliberately stirred up enmity against themselves; others have set out to win over the very men they distrusted at the start of their reign; some have built fortresses, and some have torn them down. No final verdict can be passed on any of these measures without knowing the particulars of the state where the decision falls; still, I will speak in the broad terms the subject itself allows.

There has never been a case, then, of a new prince disarming his subjects; on the contrary, whenever he has found them disarmed he has always armed them. For when you arm them, those arms become yours; the men you suspected become faithful, and the ones who were faithful stay so; and from subjects they are made into your partisans. And since all your subjects cannot be armed, when you favor the ones you do arm you can deal more securely with the rest: the difference in treatment that the armed recognize toward themselves puts them in your debt, and the others excuse you, judging it necessary that men who carry more danger and stricter obligation should have more reward. But when you disarm them, you begin to offend them: you show that you distrust them, whether for cowardice or for lack of loyalty, and either of those opinions breeds hatred against you. And because you cannot stay unarmed, you are forced to turn to mercenary soldiery, which is what was said of it above; and even were it good, it cannot be good enough to defend you against powerful enemies and suspect subjects at once. Therefore, as I have said, a new prince in a new principality has always set up arms there; the histories are full of such examples. But when a prince acquires a new state that is joined like a limb to his old one, then that state must be disarmed — except for the men who were your partisans in acquiring it; and those too, with time and occasion, must be made soft and effeminate, and things arranged so that the arms of your whole state are in the hands of your own soldiers, the ones who live close to you in your old state.

There was never a new prince who disarmed his subjects. On the contrary, finding them disarmed, he has always armed them — because, by arming them, those arms become yours, the men you distrusted become loyal, those already loyal stay so, and your subjects become your partisans. You cannot arm them all; but when those you do arm are rewarded, you can deal more freely with the rest. The difference in treatment, which the armed men clearly grasp, binds them to you, while the others forgive you, judging it only right that the men who run the greater danger and bear the greater service should have the greater reward. But disarm them, and you offend them at once: you show that you distrust them, whether for cowardice or for disloyalty, and either suspicion breeds hatred against you. And since you cannot remain unarmed, you are forced to turn to mercenaries — of the worthless kind already described — who, even at their best, could not defend you against powerful enemies and untrustworthy subjects. So, as I have said, a new prince in a new principality has always armed his people; the histories are full of it. But when a prince annexes a new state as a limb grafted onto his old one, then he must disarm the men of that state, except those who helped him take it; and these too, with time and opportunity, should be made soft and pliant. Manage matters so that the only armed men in the whole state are your own soldiers, the men who lived near you in your old dominion.

Our forefathers, and the men who were counted wise, used to say that Pistoia had to be held with factions and Pisa with fortresses; and on that principle they nursed quarrels in some of their subject towns, the more easily to keep hold of them. In those days, when Italy stood in a certain balance, this may have been sound practice; but I do not think it can be given as a precept today, for I do not believe divisions ever did anyone any good. On the contrary: when the enemy approaches, divided cities are inevitably lost at once, because the weaker faction will always attach itself to the outside forces, and the other will not be able to stand. The Venetians, moved, I believe, by the reasons given above, fostered the Guelf and Ghibelline sects in their subject cities; and though they never let them come to blood, they still nursed these differences among the citizens so that, being occupied with their own quarrels, they would not unite against them. Which, as we saw, did not afterward turn out to their purpose: for when they were routed at Vailà, one of the factions immediately took heart and seized their whole dominion. Such methods, besides, argue weakness in the prince; in a vigorous principality such divisions are never permitted, for they profit you only in peacetime, letting you manage your subjects more easily by their means — but when war comes, an order of this kind shows its own falsity.

Our forebears, and those reckoned wise, used to say that Pistoia had to be held by faction and Pisa by fortresses; and so they fed quarrels in some of their subject towns in order to keep them more easily. In those days, when Italy was in a sort of balance, this may have served well enough; but I do not think it can be laid down as a rule for today, since I do not believe faction ever does any good. On the contrary, when the enemy comes upon you, a divided city is lost at once, for the weaker party will always go over to the invader and the other will not be able to hold out. The Venetians, moved (I believe) by this same thinking, nursed the Guelph and Ghibelline factions in their subject cities; and though they never let the quarrels come to bloodshed, they kept them simmering, so that the citizens, taken up with their own divisions, would not unite against Venice. As it turned out, this did them no good: after the rout at Vailà, one faction took heart at once and seized the whole territory. Such methods, then, betray weakness in the prince, for a vigorous principality will never permit these divisions. They serve only in peacetime, as a convenient way to manage subjects; let war come, and the policy is exposed as a fraud.

Without doubt, princes become great when they overcome the difficulties and the opposition put in their way; and so fortune — above all when she wants to make a new prince great, who has more need of winning reputation than a hereditary one — raises up enemies for him and sets them on campaigns against him, so that he may have cause to overcome them and to climb higher up the very ladder his enemies have carried to him. For this reason many judge that a wise prince, when he has the occasion for it, should cunningly feed some enmity against himself, so that by crushing it his greatness rises the higher.

There is no doubt that princes grow great by overcoming the difficulties and the resistance set against them. And so fortune — especially when she wants to make a new prince great, a man who has more need than a hereditary one to earn a name — raises up enemies against him and sets them plotting, precisely so that he may have the chance to crush them and climb higher on the ladder his enemies have built for him. For this reason many hold that a wise prince, when the chance offers, ought cunningly to provoke some hostility against himself, so that by putting it down he may rise the higher.

Princes, and especially new ones, have found more faith and more usefulness in the men they held suspect at the beginning of their rule than in those they trusted at first. Pandolfo Petrucci, prince of Siena, governed his state more with the men he had suspected than with the others. But of this one cannot speak at large, because it varies with the case. I will say only this: men who were enemies of a prince at the beginning of his rule, if they are of the kind that need support to hold their position, can always be won over with the greatest ease; and they are the more tightly bound to serve him faithfully because they know how much they need to cancel, by their deeds, the bad opinion he had formed of them. And so the prince always draws more use from them than from men who, serving him in too much security, neglect his affairs. And since the matter requires it, I will not leave out this reminder to a prince who has newly taken a state by means of inside support from within it: let him weigh well what reason moved the men who supported him to support him. If it was not natural affection for him, but only discontent with the old state, he will keep them friends only with labor and great difficulty, because it will be impossible for him to content them either. Turning over the reason for this in the examples drawn from ancient and modern affairs, he will see that it is far easier to win as friends the men who were content with the old state, and were therefore his enemies, than the men who, being discontent with it, became his friends and helped him seize it.

Princes, and new ones above all, have found more loyalty and more help in men who were distrusted at the start of their rule than in those who were trusted. Pandolfo Petrucci, Prince of Siena, governed his state more through the men he had once distrusted than through any others. But there is no general rule here, for it turns on the particular case. I will say only this: men who were hostile at the beginning of a princedom, if they are of a kind that needs support to keep their footing, can always be won over with the greatest ease, and they will be held fast to serve you faithfully, knowing they must cancel by their deeds the bad opinion you first formed of them. So a prince always draws more profit from such men than from those who serve him in too much security and neglect his affairs. And since the matter calls for it, I must not fail to remind a prince who has gained a new state by the secret favor of men within it to weigh carefully what drove them to favor him. If it is not natural affection for him but mere discontent with the old government, he will keep them as friends only with great toil and trouble, for it will be impossible to satisfy them. Weighing well the reasons for this, with examples drawn from ancient and modern affairs, we find it easier for a prince to win over the men who were content under the former government — and so were his enemies — than those who, being discontented with it, took his side and egged him on to seize it.

It has been the custom of princes, the better to hold their states securely, to build fortresses that serve as bridle and bit to those who might design to move against them, and as a safe refuge from a sudden assault. I praise this way of doing things, because it has been used since antiquity. Nevertheless, in our own times Messer Niccolò Vitelli was seen to raze two fortresses in Città di Castello in order to hold that state; Guidobaldo, Duke of Urbino, returning to the dominion Cesare Borgia had driven him from, tore every fortress in that province down to its foundations, judging that without them the state would be harder to lose a second time; and the Bentivogli, returning to Bologna, took similar measures. Fortresses, then, are useful or not according to the times: if they help you in one quarter, they hurt you in another. The question can be put like this: the prince who fears his own people more than foreigners ought to build fortresses; the one who fears foreigners more than his own people ought to leave them alone. The castle of Milan, which Francesco Sforza built there, has made and will make more wars against the house of Sforza than any other disorder in that state. So the best fortress there is, is not to be hated by the people; for though you hold fortresses, if the people hate you the fortresses will not save you — once the people have taken up arms, they never lack for foreigners ready to come to their aid. In our times no fortress can be seen to have profited any prince, except the Countess of Forlì, when her consort Count Girolamo was killed: her fortress let her escape the popular uprising, wait for help from Milan, and recover her state; and the times then stood so that no foreigner could come to the people's aid. But afterward her fortresses too were worth little, when Cesare Borgia attacked her and the people, hostile to her, joined the foreigner. So then, and earlier too, it would have been safer for her not to be hated by the people than to hold the fortresses. Considering all these things, then, I will praise both the prince who builds fortresses and the one who does not; and I will blame any prince who, trusting in fortresses, counts it a small thing to be hated by his people.

It has long been the custom of princes, to hold their states more securely, to build fortresses — a bridle and bit to any who might plot against them, and a refuge against a sudden first assault. I approve the practice, for it is old. Yet in our own day Messer Niccolò Vitelli was seen to demolish two fortresses at Città di Castello in order to keep that state; Guido Ubaldo, Duke of Urbino, returning to the dominion from which Cesare Borgia had driven him, razed to the ground every fortress in the province, judging that without them he was less likely to lose it again; and the Bentivogli, restored to Bologna, came to the same decision. Fortresses, then, are useful or not according to circumstances; help you in one way, and they harm you in another. The case can be reasoned out thus: a prince who has more to fear from his own people than from foreigners ought to build fortresses; one who has more to fear from foreigners than from his people ought to leave them alone. The castle of Milan, built by Francesco Sforza, has caused, and will cause, the house of Sforza more trouble than any other disorder in that state. So the best fortress there is, is not to be hated by the people; for though you hold your fortresses, they will not save you if the people hate you — once they have taken up arms, foreigners are never lacking to come to their aid. In our times no such fortress has been seen to profit any prince, save the Countess of Forlì, when her consort Count Girolamo was killed; by it she was able to withstand the popular rising and hold out for help from Milan, and so recover her state — and the conditions of the moment were such that no foreigner could come to the people's aid. But the fortresses were of little use to her afterward, when Cesare Borgia attacked her and her people, now her enemies, joined forces with the foreigner. So both then and earlier it would have been safer for her not to have been hated by the people than to have had her fortresses. Weighing all this, I will praise the prince who builds fortresses and the prince who does not, and I will blame any prince who, trusting in fortresses, makes light of being hated by his people.

sections.label: Chapter XXI
sections.title: How a Prince Wins Esteem
How a Prince Should Conduct Himself to Gain Renown

segments.text: Nothing makes a prince so esteemed as great enterprises and rare displays of his own quality. Our own age has Ferdinand of Aragon, the present King of Spain. He can almost be called a new prince, because from a weak king he has become, by fame and glory, the first king in Christendom; and if you examine his deeds you will find them all great, and some of them extraordinary. At the start of his reign he attacked Granada, and that campaign was the foundation of his state. He began it at his leisure and with no fear of interference, for it kept the minds of the barons of Castile fixed on the war and away from any thought of change at home; and meanwhile, without their noticing, he was gaining standing and authority over them. He fed his armies on the money of the Church and of the people, and that long war let him lay a foundation for his own soldiery, which has since brought him honor. Beyond this, always using religion as the pretext for greater designs, he turned to a pious cruelty, hunting the Moors down and clearing them out of his kingdom — no example could be more wretched, or more rare. Under the same cloak he attacked Africa; he made his descent on Italy; he has lately attacked France. So he has never stopped weaving great designs, and they have kept his subjects in suspense and wonder, absorbed in waiting to see how things would come out. And each of his moves has been born out of the last, so that between one and the next, men have never had a quiet stretch in which to work against him.

Nothing wins a prince such standing as great enterprises and rare deeds that set an example. We have in our own day Ferdinand of Aragon, the present King of Spain. He can almost be called a new prince, for from a weak king he has risen by fame and glory to be the foremost ruler in Christendom; and if you weigh his deeds, you will find them all great and some of them extraordinary. At the start of his reign he attacked Granada, and that campaign was the foundation of his power. He set about it at his leisure and without fear of interference, for he kept the minds of the barons of Castile so absorbed in the war that they thought of nothing else and never saw what was being prepared; meanwhile, without their noticing, he was gathering reputation and authority over them. He paid for his armies with the money of the Church and of his people, and through that long war he laid the foundation of the military skill that has since made his name. Then, always using religion as his pretext so as to undertake still greater things, he turned with a kind of pious cruelty to driving the Moors out of his kingdom and clearing them from it altogether — and no enterprise could be more remarkable or more rare. Under the same cloak he struck at Africa, fell upon Italy, and at last attacked France; so his designs have always been great, and have kept his subjects' minds suspended in wonder and fixed on the outcome of them. And his actions have followed one out of another so closely that men have never had the breathing space to work steadily against him.

It also helps a prince a great deal to give rare examples of himself in domestic affairs, like those told of Messer Bernabo da Milano: whenever anyone in civic life did something extraordinary, good or bad, he seized the occasion to reward or punish him in a way that people would talk about for a long time. And above all, a prince must strive in everything he does to earn the name of a great man of exceptional intelligence.

It also helps a prince a great deal to set unusual examples in the government of his own state — like those told of Messer Bernabò of Milan, who, whenever someone in civil life did something out of the ordinary, whether good or bad, would find a way of rewarding or punishing him that set everyone talking. Above all, a prince should so conduct himself in everything he does that he wins the reputation of being a great man, a man of rare ability.

A prince is also esteemed when he is a true friend and a true enemy — when, without hedging, he comes out openly for one side against another. That course is always more useful than standing neutral. For if two of your powerful neighbors come to blows, either the winner will be a threat to you afterward or he will not. In either case it will always be better for you to declare yourself and wage war in earnest. In the first case, if you do not declare yourself, you will be the prize of whoever wins — to the pleasure and satisfaction of whoever loses — and you will have no defense to offer and no reason anyone should give you one, and no one will take you in. The winner does not want doubtful friends who would not stand by him in hard times; the loser will not shelter you, because you would not take up your sword and run his fortune with him.

A prince is also esteemed when he is a true friend or a downright enemy — that is, when he declares himself, without reservation, for one side and against the other. This course is always more useful than staying neutral. For if two powerful neighbors of yours come to blows, either the victor will be one you must fear afterward, or he will not. In either case it is better for you to declare yourself and fight an honest war. If you do not declare yourself, you will always be the prey of the victor, to the delight and satisfaction of the loser; you will have no claim on anyone's protection and no refuge to take. For the winner wants no doubtful friends who would not stand by him in his hour of need; and the loser will not shelter you, since you would not take up arms and share his fortunes.

Antiochus came into Greece, brought in by the Ætolians to drive out the Romans. He sent envoys to the Achaeans, who were friends of the Romans, urging them to stay neutral; the Romans, meanwhile, were urging them to take up arms for their side. The question came before the council of the Achaeans, and when the legate of Antiochus pressed them toward neutrality, the Roman legate answered: “As for the course these men praise as best and most useful for your state — that you keep out of our war — nothing is further from your interest: keep out, and without thanks and without dignity you will be the winner's prize.” So it will always go: the one who is not your friend will ask you for neutrality, and the one who is your friend will ask you to declare yourself with arms. Irresolute princes, trying to escape the danger of the moment, take the neutral road most of the time, and most of the time they are ruined. But when a prince declares himself boldly for one side, then if his ally wins — however powerful the winner, however much you lie at his mercy — he is in your debt; a bond of affection has been formed; and men are never so shameless as to crush you with so flagrant a show of ingratitude. Besides, victories are never so clean that the winner can throw off every restraint, least of all justice. And if your ally loses, he takes you in; while he can, he helps you; and you become companions of a fortune that can rise again.

Antiochus had come into Greece, brought there by the Aetolians to drive out the Romans. He sent envoys to the Achaeans, who were friends of the Romans, urging them to stay neutral; the Romans, for their part, urged them to take up arms on their side. The matter came before the council of the Achaeans, where the envoy of Antiochus pressed them to remain neutral. To this the Roman legate answered: "As for the claim that it is best and most useful for your state to keep out of our war — nothing could be further from the truth; for by keeping out, you will be left without thanks and without honor, the prize of whoever wins." And so it will always be: the one who is not your friend will ask you to stay neutral, and the one who is your friend will ask you to declare yourself with arms. Irresolute princes, to escape the dangers of the moment, usually take the neutral road, and usually come to ruin. But when a prince boldly declares himself for one side, then, if the side he joins wins, even though the victor is powerful and you are left at his mercy, he is in your debt, and a bond of friendship has been formed; and men are never so shameless as to crush you in such black ingratitude. Besides, victories are never so complete that the winner can throw off all restraint, least of all the restraint of justice. And if the side you joined loses, he will shelter you, help you while he can, and make you the companion of a fortune that may yet rise again.

In the second case, when the two who fight are such that you have nothing to fear from whichever of them wins, it is all the more prudent to take a side: you help destroy the one with the aid of the other, who ought to have rescued him if he had been wise; and since with your help he cannot fail to win, he wins and remains at your discretion. And here it should be noted that a prince ought never to make common cause with someone more powerful than himself in order to attack others, unless necessity forces him, as was said above: for if your stronger partner wins, you are his prisoner, and princes should do all they can to avoid lying at anyone's discretion. The Venetians allied themselves with France against the Duke of Milan — a ruinous alliance they could have avoided. But when it cannot be avoided, as it could not be for the Florentines when the Pope and Spain marched their armies into Lombardy, then the prince should commit himself, for the reasons given.

In the second case, when those who fight are such that you have nothing to fear from whoever wins, it is all the more prudent to declare yourself; for you are helping to destroy one power with the aid of another that, had it been wise, would have saved it instead. If your side wins — and with your help it can hardly fail to — it is left at your discretion. Here one thing must be noted: a prince should take care never to join with a power stronger than himself in order to attack another, unless necessity forces him to it, as I said above; for if you win, you are left in the stronger man's hands, and a prince should avoid as far as he can being left at the mercy of others. The Venetians joined with France against the Duke of Milan, and they could have avoided an alliance that proved their ruin. But where it cannot be avoided — as it could not be for the Florentines when the Pope and Spain marched their armies into Lombardy — then, for the reasons given, the prince must take a side.

And let no state ever believe it can choose a safe course; let it expect instead to choose among doubtful ones. For this is in the order of things: you never escape one trouble without walking into another. Prudence consists in knowing how to weigh the troubles against each other, and to take the least bad as good.

And let no state ever imagine that it can always choose a perfectly safe course; rather, it should reckon on having to choose among doubtful ones. For this is the way of things: no sooner do you try to escape one danger than you run into another. Wisdom lies in knowing how to weigh the dangers, and in choosing the least bad for the best.

A prince should also show himself a lover of excellence, giving a place to able men and honoring those who are outstanding in any art. Beyond that, he should encourage his citizens to follow their occupations in peace — in trade, in farming, in every other human pursuit — so that no one is afraid to improve his property for fear it will be taken from him, and no one afraid to open a business for fear of the taxman. Instead he should hold out rewards for whoever wants to do these things, and for anyone who thinks of any way at all of enlarging his city or his state.

A prince should also show himself a patron of ability, welcoming men of talent and honoring those who excel in any craft. He should encourage his citizens to go quietly about their callings, in trade, in farming, in every other line of work, so that no man holds back from improving his holdings for fear they will be taken from him, and no merchant from opening a trade for fear of taxes. On the contrary, the prince should hold out rewards to anyone who is willing to do these things, and to anyone who plans in any way to enrich his city or his state.

Beyond this, at the fitting seasons of the year, he should keep the people occupied with festivals and spectacles. And since every city is divided into guilds or wards, he should take account of those bodies, meet with them now and then, and show himself in his own person an example of courtesy and generosity — all the while holding the majesty of his rank firm, for that must never be allowed to slip in anything.

Beyond this, he should entertain his people with festivals and spectacles at the fitting times of year; and since every city is divided into guilds or into clans, he should take account of these bodies, meet with them from time to time, and give them an example of his own courtesy and generosity — while always, in all of this, keeping the full majesty of his rank, which must never be let slip in anything.

sections.label: Chapter XXII
sections.title: A Prince's Ministers
Concerning the Ministers of Princes

segments.text: The choice of ministers is no small matter for a prince: they are good or not according to the prince's own prudence. The first guess one makes about a ruler's brains comes from seeing the men he keeps around him. When they are capable and faithful, you can always count him wise, because he knew how to recognize their capacity and how to keep them faithful. When they are otherwise, you can always judge him badly, for the first error he made was in this choice.

The choice of his ministers is no small matter for a prince; they are good or bad according to the prince's own discernment. The first measure anyone takes of a prince and of his brains is the men he keeps around him. When they are able and loyal, he can always be reckoned wise, for he has known how to spot ability and how to hold it loyal. But when they are otherwise, no good can be thought of him, since the first blunder he makes is the choosing of them.

No one who knew Messer Antonio da Venafro as the minister of Pandolfo Petrucci, prince of Siena, could help judging Pandolfo a most able man for having Venafro as his minister. For there are three kinds of brains: one understands things on its own; the second discerns what others understand; the third understands neither on its own nor through others. The first is most excellent, the second excellent, the third useless. So it necessarily followed that if Pandolfo was not in the first rank, he was in the second: for whenever a man has the judgment to recognize the good and the bad in what another says and does, then even if he has no invention of his own, he can tell his minister's good work from his bad, praise the one and correct the other; and the minister, who cannot hope to fool him, keeps himself good.

No one who knew Messer Antonio da Venafro as the minister of Pandolfo Petrucci, Prince of Siena, could fail to judge Pandolfo a very able man for having such a minister. For there are three kinds of mind: one that understands things for itself; one that grasps what another has understood; and one that understands neither for itself nor through anyone else. The first is excellent in the highest degree, the second is good, the third is useless. So it follows of necessity that, if Pandolfo did not stand in the first rank, he stood in the second; for whenever a man has the judgment to tell good from bad in what another says and does, even if he has no invention of his own, he can still recognize the good and the bad in his minister's work, praising the one and correcting the other. Then the minister can have no hope of deceiving him, and is kept honest.

But as for how a prince may know his minister, there is a test that never fails. When you see a minister thinking more about himself than about you, and hunting his own profit inside everything he does, a man made that way will never be a good minister, and you will never be able to trust him. For the man who holds another's state in his hands must never think of himself but always of his prince, and must never put before him any business that is not the prince's own.

But there is one test that never fails by which a prince may take the measure of his minister. When you see the minister thinking more of himself than of you, and seeking his own profit in everything he handles, such a man will never be a good minister, and you will never be able to trust him. For a man who holds another's state in his hands ought never to think of himself but always of his prince, and ought never to bring to the prince's notice anything that does not concern the prince.

And on the other side, to keep the minister good, the prince should think of him in turn: honor him, enrich him, bind him with obligations, share the honors and the burdens with him — so that the minister sees he cannot stand without the prince; so that abundant honors leave him wanting no more honors, abundant riches leave him wanting no more riches, and his full load of responsibilities makes him dread any change of regime. When ministers, and princes in their dealings with ministers, are made this way, each can trust the other; and when they are otherwise, it ends badly for one or the other, every time.

On the other side, to keep his minister loyal, the prince ought to be mindful of him: to honor him, make him rich, put him in his debt, share with him both honors and burdens — so that the minister sees he cannot stand without the prince, and that the heaping of honors leaves him wanting no more honors, the heaping of riches no more riches, the weight of office no more office. When ministers, and princes toward their ministers, are so disposed, they can trust one another; and when they are otherwise, the end will always be ruinous for the one or for the other.

sections.label: Chapter XXIII
sections.title: Avoiding Flatterers
How Flatterers Should Be Avoided

segments.text: I do not want to leave out an important topic, and a mistake princes can hardly defend themselves against unless they are very shrewd, or choose their men very well. I mean the flatterers, and the courts are full of them. For men take such pleasure in their own doings, and deceive themselves about them so thoroughly, that they can barely protect themselves from this plague; and the attempt to protect yourself brings a danger of its own — the danger of becoming despised. There is no way to guard against flattery but to have men understand that telling you the truth does not offend you; yet when everyone may tell you the truth, the reverence goes.

I do not want to leave out an important branch of this subject — a danger princes are seldom saved from unless they are very prudent and choose their men well. I mean flatterers, of whom courts are full. Men take such delight in their own affairs, and deceive themselves about them so easily, that they can scarcely be guarded against this plague; and in trying to guard against it they run the risk of falling into contempt. For there is no other way to protect yourself from flatterers than to let men understand that telling you the truth does not offend you. But once everyone may speak the truth to you, your reverence dwindles.

Therefore a prudent prince takes a third way. He chooses wise men from his state, and to them alone he gives free leave to speak the truth to him — and only on the matters he asks about, nothing else. But he should ask them about everything, hear their opinions, and then decide by himself, in his own manner. With these counselors, singly and together, he should carry himself so that every one of them knows the more freely he speaks, the more welcome he will be. Outside of them he should listen to no one, go straight after the thing once decided, and be stubborn in his decisions. Whoever does otherwise is either wrecked by the flatterers, or changes course so often under the pull of contrary opinions that he comes to be despised.

A wise prince must therefore take a third course: choose the wise men of his state, and give them alone the freedom to tell him the truth — and then only on the matters he asks about, and nothing else. But he should question them on everything, hear their opinions, and afterwards decide for himself, in his own way. With these counselors, both singly and together, he should conduct himself so that each of them knows the more freely he speaks the better he will be regarded. Beyond these men he should listen to no one, hold to the course he has resolved on, and be steadfast in his decisions. Whoever does otherwise either comes to grief through flatterers or is forever shifting with the swing of conflicting advice — and from this his standing falls.

On this point I want to give a modern example. Fra Luca, servant of Maximilian, the present emperor, said of his majesty that he took counsel with no one, and yet never did anything the way he wanted. This came of his doing the opposite of what I have described. For the emperor is a secretive man: he tells no one his plans and takes no advice on them. But as the plans go into effect they begin to show and be discovered, and then the men around him begin to talk him out of them; and he, being pliable, is turned aside. So what he does one day he undoes the next; no one ever understands what he wants or intends to do; and no one can build on his decisions.

Let me bring forward a recent example. Fra Luca, the man of affairs to Maximilian, the present emperor, said of his master that he took counsel from no one, yet never carried anything through his own way. This came of his following the very opposite of the course set out above. The emperor is a secretive man: he tells his designs to no one and takes no opinions on them. But as he puts them into effect they begin to be revealed and known, and at once the men around him cross them; and being pliant, he is turned aside. So the things he does one day he undoes the next, no one ever understands what he means to do, and no one can rely on his decisions.

A prince, therefore, should always take counsel — but when he wants it, not when others want to give it. In fact he should discourage anyone from volunteering advice on anything unless he asks for it. But he himself should be a generous asker of questions, and then, about the things he asked, a patient hearer of the truth; indeed, when he learns that anyone out of some scruple is keeping the truth from him, he should let his anger show.

A prince, then, should always take counsel, but when he chooses and not when others choose; indeed he should discourage everyone from offering him advice unasked. But he should be a tireless questioner, and afterwards a patient listener on the matters he asked about; and if he learns that anyone, for whatever reason, has held the truth back from him, he should let his anger be felt.

Many people suppose that a prince who gives an impression of prudence owes it not to his own nature but to the good advisers around him. They are certainly deceived. For this is a general rule that never fails: a prince who is not wise himself cannot be advised well — unless by chance he hands himself over entirely to a single man of great prudence who governs everything for him. In that case he might indeed be well governed, but it would not last long, because that governor would in short order take the state away from him.
