Some think that a prince who gives an impression of wisdom owes it not to his own gifts but to the good counselors around him. They are plainly deceived, for here is a rule that never fails: a prince who is not wise himself can never be well advised — unless by chance he hands himself over entirely to some one man, a man of great prudence, who governs him in everything. In that case he might indeed be well governed, but not for long, because such a governor would soon strip him of his state.

But taking counsel from more than one, a prince who is not wise will never get counsels that agree, and he will not know how to reconcile them himself. Each counselor will think of his own interest; the prince will know neither how to correct them nor how to see through them. And counselors come no other way, because men will always turn out bad for you unless some necessity makes them good. So the conclusion is this: good counsel, wherever it comes from, must be born of the prince's prudence — the prince's prudence is not born of good counsel.

And if he takes counsel from more than one, a prince who is not himself wise will never get their advice to agree, nor know how to reconcile it. Each counselor will think of his own interests, and the prince will not know how to correct them or see through them. Nor could it be otherwise, for men will always turn out badly on you unless some necessity makes them good. The conclusion, then, is this: good counsel, wherever it comes from, must be born of the prince's own wisdom, and not the prince's wisdom of good counsel.

sections.label: Chapter XXIV
sections.title: Why Italy's Princes Lost Their States
Why the Princes of Italy Have Lost Their States

segments.text: The measures set out above, prudently observed, make a new prince seem an old one, and settle him faster and more firmly in his state than if he had grown old in it. For a new prince is watched far more closely in his actions than a hereditary one; and when his actions are recognized as able, they take hold of men far more, and bind them far tighter, than ancient blood does. For men are taken much more by present things than by past ones, and when they find the present good they enjoy it and look for nothing else — indeed they will mount every defense of such a prince, so long as he does not fail them in the rest. And so he will have a double glory: to have founded a new principality, and to have adorned and strengthened it with good laws, good arms, good allies, and good examples — just as the man born a prince who loses his state through lack of prudence carries a double shame.

The advice set out above, carefully followed, will make a new prince look long-established, and will fix him in his state at once more securely and more firmly than if his line had sat there for ages. For the doings of a new prince are watched far more closely than those of a hereditary one; and when they are seen to be able, they win him more men and bind them tighter than ancient blood ever could. Men are taken more by present things than by past ones, and when they find the present good they relish it and look no further; indeed they will defend such a prince to the utmost, so long as he does not fail them in the rest. So it will be a double glory for him to have founded a new principality and adorned and braced it with good laws, good arms, good allies, and a good example — just as it is a double disgrace to a man born a prince who, through want of wisdom, loses his state.

And if you consider the lords who have lost their states in Italy in our times — the King of Naples, the Duke of Milan, and the rest — you will find in them, first, one common defect in the matter of arms, for the causes discussed at length above; and then you will see that some of them either had the people for enemies, or, if they had the people friendly, did not know how to secure the great men. Without these defects, states are not lost that have sinew enough to keep an army in the field.

And if we consider those lords who in our own times have lost their states in Italy — the King of Naples, the Duke of Milan, and others — we will find in them, first, one common defect in their arms, for the reasons set out at length above; and next, we will see that one of them either had the people against him, or, if he kept the people friendly, did not know how to secure himself with the nobles. For without these defects, no state with the strength to field an army can be lost.

Philip of Macedon — not Alexander's father, but the one Titus Quintius defeated — did not have much of a state, measured against the greatness of the Romans and of the Greece that attacked him. Yet because he was a military man who knew how to hold the people and secure the great, he sustained the war against them for years; and if in the end he lost his grip on a few cities, the kingdom stayed his.

Philip of Macedon — not Alexander the Great's father, but the one beaten by Titus Quintius — had little territory beside the greatness of the Romans and of Greece who fell upon him; yet because he was a warlike man who knew how to keep the people close and secure himself with the nobles, he held out against them for many years, and though in the end he lost a few cities, he kept his kingdom all the same.

So let these princes of ours, who held their principalities for years on end and then lost them, blame not fortune but their own laziness. In quiet times they never once considered that things can change — it is the common defect of men not to reckon on the storm while the sea is calm — and when the hard times came, their thoughts ran to flight and not to defense, and they hoped the people, disgusted by the winners' insolence, would call them back. That plan, when all others are gone, is good; but it is very bad to have let the other remedies go for its sake. You should never accept a fall on the faith that someone will be there to pick you up. Either it does not happen, or, if it happens, it brings you no safety — because that kind of rescue is a coward's defense and does not depend on you. The only defenses that are good, that are certain, that are lasting, are the ones that depend on you yourself and on your own strength.

So let our princes, who have lost their states after holding them so many years, not blame fortune but their own sloth. In quiet times they never imagined a change could come — it is the common failing of men not to reckon on the storm while the weather is fair — and when hard times finally came, they thought only of fleeing, not of defending themselves, trusting that the people, sickened by the conquerors' insolence, would call them back. This course may serve when no other is left, but it is wretched to have set aside every other remedy for it; for no man should let himself fall in the belief that someone will come along to pick him up. Either no one does, or, if he does, it brings you no security, since a rescue that does not depend on yourself is no rescue at all. The only defenses that are sound, sure, and lasting are those that depend on yourself and your own prowess.

sections.label: Chapter XXV
sections.title: Fortune, and How to Resist Her
What Fortune Can Do in Human Affairs, and How to Withstand Her

segments.text: I am well aware that many men have held, and hold, the opinion that the affairs of the world are so governed by fortune and by God that human prudence cannot correct them — that there is no remedy at all; and on this account they might judge that there is no point sweating over anything, and that we should let ourselves be governed by chance. This opinion has gained more credit in our times because of the great upheavals in affairs that have been seen, and are seen every day, beyond anything anyone could have guessed. Thinking it over, I have myself leaned some way toward their opinion at times. Nevertheless — so that our free will is not extinguished — I judge it may be true that fortune is arbiter of half of our actions, but that she leaves the other half, or close to it, for us to govern.

I am well aware that many men have held, and still hold, that the affairs of the world are so governed by fortune and by God that human wisdom cannot steer them, and that there is no remedy against them at all. From this they conclude that there is no point in sweating over things; one may as well let chance rule. The opinion has gained more credit in our own day, given the great upheavals we have seen, and still see daily, beyond anything any man could have guessed. Turning it over in my mind, I am at times half inclined to share it. All the same, so as not to extinguish our free will, I judge it true that fortune is the arbiter of half our actions, but that she leaves the other half, or nearly, for us to govern.

I compare her to one of those ruinous rivers that, when they grow angry, flood the plains, tear down trees and buildings, lift the earth from this bank and lay it on that one. Everyone flees before the water; everyone gives way to its fury, powerless to stand against it anywhere. And yet, though rivers are made this way, it does not follow that men in quiet weather cannot prepare — with embankments and dikes — so that when the waters rise again they either run off down a channel, or their rush is neither so wild nor so ruinous. It is the same with fortune. She shows her power where no ordered strength stands ready to resist her, and she turns her floods where she knows no dikes and no embankments have been raised to hold her.

I compare her to one of those raging rivers that, when they flood, drown the plains, tear up trees and buildings, and strip the soil from one bank to throw it down on the other. Everything flees before it; everyone yields to its fury, powerless to hold it back. And yet, for all that, it does not follow that men cannot take precautions in calm weather, raising banks and dykes, so that when the river swells again the water runs off through a channel and its force is neither so wild nor so destructive. It is the same with fortune: she shows her power where no skill has been prepared to resist her, and turns her fury wherever she finds no banks and dykes built to hold her in.

And if you consider Italy — the seat of these upheavals, and the country that set them moving — you will see an open plain without dikes and without a single embankment. Had she been protected by proper strength, as Germany, Spain, and France are, either this flood would never have made the great changes it has made, or it would not have come at all. And let this be enough said about resisting fortune in general.

And if you look at Italy, the seat of these upheavals and the very thing that set them in motion, you will see a country with no banks and no defenses whatever. Had she been defended by proper skill, as Germany, Spain, and France are, either this flood would not have wrought the great changes it has, or it would never have come at all. So much, then, for resisting fortune in general.

But narrowing myself to particulars, I say that one sees a prince prosper today and fall tomorrow with no visible change in his nature or in any quality he has. This, I believe, comes first from the causes already discussed at length: the prince who leans entirely on fortune falls the moment she turns. I believe, further, that the man prospers who matches his way of proceeding to the quality of the times, and likewise that the man fails whose proceedings are at odds with the times. For in the things that carry men toward the end each one aims at — glory and riches — you see them proceed differently: one with caution, another with a rush; one by force, the other by craft; one by patience, the other by its opposite; and each can arrive by his own road. You also see two cautious men, one reaching his goal and the other not; and again two men prospering equally by opposite methods, one cautious, the other impetuous. All of this comes from nothing but the quality of the times, which either agrees with a man's way of proceeding or does not. From this follows what I said: that two men working differently produce the same effect, and of two working alike, one arrives and the other does not.

But coming closer to particulars, I say that a prince may be seen flourishing today and ruined tomorrow without having changed his nature or any quality in himself. This springs first, I believe, from the causes already discussed at length: the prince who leans wholly on fortune falls the moment she turns. I believe too that the man who matches his way of acting to the temper of the times will succeed, and the man whose conduct is out of step with the times will fail. For in the things men do to reach the end each has before him — glory and riches — we see them go about it differently: one with caution, another with daring; one by force, another by cunning; one by patience, another by its opposite — and each by his own method may arrive. We also see two cautious men, one of whom reaches his goal while the other fails; and two men succeed equally though one is cautious and the other headlong. All of this comes from nothing but whether or not their way of acting suits the temper of the times. Hence it follows, as I said, that two men working in opposite ways reach the same result, while two working in the same way, one arrives and the other does not.

On this also hangs the swing of prosperity. If a man governs himself with caution and patience, and times and affairs revolve in a way that makes his method the right one, he prospers; but if times and affairs change, he is ruined, because he does not change his way of proceeding. And no man is found so prudent that he knows how to fit himself to this — both because he cannot swerve from what his own nature inclines him to, and because, having always prospered by walking one road, he cannot be persuaded to leave it. So the cautious man, when the moment comes to strike out, does not know how to do it, and down he goes; whereas if he could change his nature with the times and with affairs, his fortune would not change.

Shifts of fortune turn on this as well. If a man governs himself with caution and patience, and the times and circumstances run his way, he flourishes; but if the times and circumstances change, he is ruined, because he does not change his way of proceeding with them. And there is hardly a man to be found wise enough to bend to this, partly because he cannot break from the bent his nature gives him, and partly because, having always prospered by going one way, he cannot bring himself to leave it. So the cautious man, when the moment comes to be bold, does not know how, and is ruined. Had he changed his nature with the times, his fortune would not have changed.

Pope Julius the Second proceeded impetuously in everything he did, and he found the times and circumstances so agreeable to his way of proceeding that things always came out well for him. Consider his first campaign, against Bologna, while Messer Giovanni Bentivogli still lived. The Venetians did not like it; neither did the King of Spain; with France he still had the enterprise under negotiation — and nonetheless, with his usual ferocity and drive, he led the expedition in person. The move left Spain and the Venetians standing frozen, the latter out of fear, the former out of appetite to recover the whole Kingdom of Naples; and at the same time it dragged the King of France in behind him, for the king, seeing him already in motion and wanting the Pope as a friend against the Venetians, judged he could not refuse him troops without an open insult. So with one impetuous stroke Julius accomplished what no other pontiff, with all human prudence, would ever have accomplished. Had he waited in Rome until his plans were settled and everything arranged, as any other pontiff would have done, he would never have succeeded: the King of France would have found a thousand excuses, and the others would have raised a thousand fears.

Pope Julius II went about everything with headlong force, and he found the times and circumstances so suited to that way of acting that he always came off well. Take his first campaign against Bologna, while Messer Giovanni Bentivogli was still alive. The Venetians were against it, so was the King of Spain, and he was still in talks with France about it — yet with his usual boldness and drive he set out on the expedition in person. That move left Spain and the Venetians standing still and irresolute, the latter out of fear, the former out of their hope of recovering the kingdom of Naples; and it pulled the King of France along behind him, for the king, seeing him move and wanting the Pope's friendship to bring the Venetians down, found he could not refuse him. So Julius, by his headlong action, brought off what no other pope, with all the ordinary prudence in the world, could have managed. Had he waited in Rome until everything was settled and arranged, as any other pope would have done, he would never have pulled it off — because France would have found a thousand excuses, and the others raised a thousand fears.

I will pass over his other deeds, which were all of a piece, and all of them turned out well; and the shortness of his life never let him taste the contrary. For if times had come that required him to proceed with caution, his ruin would have followed: he would never have swerved from the ways his nature inclined him to.

I will leave his other actions aside, for they were all of a piece, and all came off; the shortness of his life spared him the reverse. But had times arrived that called for caution, his ruin would have followed, for he would never have turned aside from the way his nature drove him.

I conclude, then, that since fortune changes and men stand stubborn in their ways, they prosper so long as the two run together, and fail the moment they part. For my own part I judge this: it is better to be impetuous than cautious, because fortune is a woman, and if you mean to keep her down you must beat her and shove her. And plainly she lets herself be won by such men sooner than by those who proceed coldly. And so, like a woman, she is always the friend of the young — because they are less cautious, fiercer, and command her with more audacity.

I conclude, then, that since fortune changes while men hold stubbornly to their ways, men flourish while the two are in step and fail when they fall out. For my part, I hold that it is better to be bold than cautious, because fortune is a woman, and if you mean to keep her under you must beat her and knock her about. She lets herself be mastered by such men more readily than by those who go to work coldly. And so, like a woman, she is always the friend of the young, because they are less cautious, fiercer, and command her with more audacity.

sections.label: Chapter XXVI
sections.title: Exhortation to Free Italy
An Exhortation to Liberate Italy from the Barbarians

segments.text: Having considered everything discussed above, I have been asking myself whether in Italy, right now, the times are ripe to honor a new prince — whether the material lies here that would give a prudent and able man the occasion to shape it into a form that would bring honor to him and good to the whole body of her people. And it seems to me that so many things now run together in a new prince's favor that I do not know what time was ever more fit for one.

Having weighed everything set down in the discourses above, I have asked myself whether the present moment is ripe to honor a new prince, and whether there is matter here to give a wise and capable man the opening to shape a new order that would do him honor and the people of this land good. And it seems to me that so many things now come together in favor of a new prince that I cannot think of a time more fit than this.

If, as I said, the people of Israel had to be slaves in Egypt for the power in Moses to show itself; if the Persians had to be crushed by the Medes for the greatness of Cyrus's spirit to be known, and the Athenians scattered for the excellence of Theseus to appear — then now, for the worth of one Italian spirit to be known, Italy had to be brought down to her present extremity: more enslaved than the Hebrews, more servile than the Persians, more scattered than the Athenians; without a head, without order; beaten, stripped, torn, overrun; made to endure ruin of every kind.

If, as I said, it was necessary that the people of Israel be held captive to make plain the skill of Moses; that the Persians be ground down by the Medes to bring out the greatness of Cyrus; and that the Athenians be scattered to reveal what Theseus could do — then now, to lay bare the skill of an Italian spirit, it was necessary that Italy be reduced to her present pass: more enslaved than the Hebrews, more beaten down than the Persians, more scattered than the Athenians; without a head, without order, beaten, despoiled, torn, overrun; bearing every kind of ruin.

And though before now a glimmer showed in one man, enough to let us think God had ordained him for her redemption, still we saw how afterward, at the very height of his course, fortune cast him off. So she lies there as if lifeless, waiting for whoever it may be that can heal her wounds — put an end to the sacking of Lombardy, to the extortion of the kingdom and of Tuscany — and clean out the sores that have festered now for so long. See how she prays God to send someone to redeem her from these cruelties and this barbarian insolence. See how ready she is, how willing, to march behind a flag — if only someone would raise one.

And though one man lately showed a spark that made us hope God had ordained him for our redemption, fortune cast him off at the very height of his rising. So Italy, left as if without life, waits for the one who will heal her wounds, put a stop to the ravaging of Lombardy and the bleeding and taxing of the Kingdom and of Tuscany, and cleanse the sores that have festered in her so long. You can see how she begs God to send someone to lift her out of these cruelties and barbarous outrages; you can see how ready and willing she is to follow a banner, if only someone will raise it.

Nor is there anyone now in view in whom she can place more hope than in your illustrious house, which — with its fortune and its ability, favored by God and by the Church, of which it is now the head — can make itself the leader of this redemption. That will not be very hard if you hold before your eyes the deeds and the lives of the men named above. They were rare and marvelous men; but they were men, and none of them had an opportunity as good as this one: their enterprise was not more just than this, nor easier, nor was God more a friend to them than he is to you.

And there is no house in which she can place more hope, just now, than your own illustrious house, which with its fortune and its skill, favored by God and by the Church it now heads, might lead this redemption. It will not be hard, if you keep before your eyes the deeds and the lives of the men I have named. They were rare and wonderful men, but men all the same, and not one of them had an opening better than the one before you now; their undertakings were no more just than this, nor any easier, nor was God more their friend than He is yours.

Here justice is great: for war is just for those to whom it is necessary, and arms are holy where there is no hope left except in arms. Here the willingness is very great; and where the willingness is great, the difficulty cannot be great, provided your house takes as its mark the methods of the men I have held up. Beyond this, extraordinary things without precedent have been seen here, God leading the way: the sea has opened; a cloud has shown the road; the rock has poured out water; manna has rained down. Everything has run together toward your greatness. The rest you must do yourselves. God does not want to do everything, lest he take from us our free will and the share of the glory that falls to us.

Here the cause is wholly just — for that war is just which is necessary, and arms are holy when there is no hope but in arms. Here the will is altogether ready, and where the will is great the difficulties cannot be great, so long as you follow the example of the men I have set before you. Beyond that, here are extraordinary signs, beyond all precedent, worked by the hand of God: the sea has parted, a cloud has shown the way, water has poured from the rock, manna has rained down. Everything has come together for your greatness. The rest you must do yourselves. God will not do everything, for He will not take from us our free will and the share of the glory that is ours.

And it is no wonder if none of the Italians named before could do what we may hope from your illustrious house, or if in so many revolutions and so many campaigns of war in Italy it always looks as if military virtue were spent. The truth is that her old institutions were bad, and no one has appeared who knew how to find new ones. Nothing brings a newly risen man so much honor as the new laws and new institutions he devises: when they are well founded and have greatness in them, they make him revered and admired. And in Italy the material is not lacking — it will take any form you can give it.

And it is no wonder if none of the Italians named before now have managed to do what we may hope for from your illustrious house; nor that in so many upheavals in Italy, and so much waging of war, it has always seemed as if her warlike skill were spent. The reason is that her old order was bad, and no one has known how to find a new one. Nothing brings a man more honor than to lay down new laws and new institutions when he himself is newly risen; and such things, when they are well founded and have greatness in them, make him revered and admired. In Italy there is no shortage of material to take shape under any form you please.

Here there is great strength in the limbs, if only it were not missing in the heads. Look at the duels and the small combats: how superior the Italians are in strength, in dexterity, in quickness of wit. But when it comes to armies they make no showing. And all of it traces back to the weakness of the heads: the men who know are not obeyed, every man thinks he knows, and no one until now has known how to lift himself, by ability or by fortune, so far above the rest that the others would yield to him. That is why, over so long a time, through so many wars in the past twenty years, whenever an army has been all Italian it has always failed the test. The first witness is Il Taro; then Allesandria, Capua, Genoa, Vaila, Bologna, Mestri.

Here there is great prowess in the limbs, if only it were not wanting in the head. Look at the duels and the fights of a few against a few, and see how far the Italians surpass others in strength, in skill of hand, in resourcefulness. But come to armies, and they make no showing at all. The whole fault lies in the weakness of the leaders. The men who know their business are not obeyed, and every man thinks he knows it himself, since to this day no one has risen so far above the rest, by skill or by fortune, that the others would yield to him. This is why, through all the long stretch of these past twenty years, every army wholly Italian has always given a poor account of itself. The Taro is the first witness, and after it Alessandria, Capua, Genoa, Vailà, Bologna, Mestri.

If your illustrious house, then, means to follow those excellent men who redeemed their countries, one thing is necessary before all others, the true foundation of every such enterprise: to arm yourself with your own troops, for there can be no more faithful, truer, or better soldiers. And good as each man of them is singly, together they will be better still when they see themselves commanded by their own prince, honored by him, and kept at his charge. These arms must be prepared, so that with Italian strength we can defend ourselves against the foreigner.

If, then, your illustrious house means to follow those rare men who delivered their own lands, it must before all else, as the true foundation of every undertaking, provide itself with arms of its own; for there can be no soldiers more faithful, truer, or better. And good as each of these men is by himself, all together they will be better still once they find themselves commanded by their own prince, honored by him, and kept at his charge. It is necessary, then, to be furnished with such arms, so that Italian prowess can defend Italy against the foreigner.

The Swiss and the Spanish infantry are counted terrifying, it is true; yet each has a defect, so that a third order of troops could not only stand against them but be confident of beating them. For the Spaniards cannot withstand cavalry, and the Swiss have reason to fear infantry that meets them in close combat as stubbornly as they fight. So we have seen, and will see again by experience, that the Spaniards cannot hold against French cavalry, and the Swiss are broken by Spanish infantry. Of this last there is no complete proof yet, but a taste of it was given at the battle of Ravenna, when the Spanish infantry met the German battalions, which keep the same order as the Swiss: the Spaniards, with the agility of their bodies and the help of their bucklers, got in under the Germans' pikes and stood there safe, cutting at them while the Germans had no remedy; and had the cavalry not charged them, the Spaniards would have finished them all. Knowing the defect of both these infantries, then, one can order a new kind, able to stand against horse and unafraid of foot — and this will be done by the kind of arms chosen and a change of formations. These are among the things which, ordered fresh, give reputation and greatness to a new prince.

And though the Swiss and the Spanish infantry are reckoned terrible, each has a flaw, so that a third order could not only stand against them but be counted on to beat them. For the Spaniards cannot hold against cavalry, and the Swiss have reason to fear infantry whenever they meet men in the field as stubborn as themselves. We have seen it, and will see it again: the Spaniards cannot hold against French cavalry, and the Swiss are broken by Spanish infantry. The last we have not yet seen proven to the full, but there was a taste of it at the battle of Ravenna, when the Spanish foot came up against the German battalions, who keep the same order as the Swiss. The Spaniards, quick of body and shielded by their bucklers, slipped in under the German pikes and struck them safely from below, while the Germans had no defense; and had the cavalry not charged them, the Spaniards would have cut them down to the last man. Once you know the defect of both these kinds of foot, then, you can raise a new one that will stand against cavalry and not fear infantry. This calls for no new weapons, only a change in the order of them. And it is reforms of just this kind that win a new prince repute and greatness.

This opportunity, then, must not be let slip, so that Italy, after so long, may at last see her redeemer. I cannot express with what love he would be received in all the provinces that have suffered these foreign floods; with what thirst for vengeance, what stubborn faith, what devotion, what tears. What doors would be shut against him? What people would refuse him obedience? What envy would set itself against him? What Italian would withhold his homage? To every one of us this barbarian rule stinks. Let your illustrious house take up this cause, then, with the spirit and the hope in which just enterprises are taken up; so that under its banner this country may be made noble again, and under its auspices Petrarch's words may come true:

This chance, then, must not be let slip, so that after so long Italy may see her deliverer at last. I cannot say with what love he would be received in all those provinces that have suffered under these foreign floods; with what thirst for revenge, with what unshakable faith, with what devotion, with what tears. What gate would be shut against him? What people would deny him obedience? What envy would stand in his way? What Italian would refuse him homage? This barbarian rule stinks in the nostrils of every one of us. Let your illustrious house, then, take up this charge with the spirit and the hope in which just undertakings are taken up, so that under its standard this country of ours may be made noble again, and under its leading the words of Petrarch may come true:
Virtù contro al Furore prenderà l'arme, e fia il combatter corto: ché l'antico valore negli italici cuor non è ancor morto.
Virtue against fury will take up arms; and the fight will be short: for the ancient valor in Italian hearts is not yet dead.
Valor against fury / shall take up arms; and the fight shall be short; / for the ancient courage / in Italian hearts is not yet dead.
